en: The "Chronological Compilation of the Orthodox Lineage of the Śākya School" is an ancient precedent established by former sages. When a king possesses virtue and officials maintain their integrity, they can cause all the states to comply with and practice these principles.
Upon the issuance of proclamations and edicts, the world was as one family and the Middle Kingdom as one person, and the ancient statutes were fully implemented.

Subsequently, when the vapors of the Three Luminaries and Five Peaks diverged and the royal ordinances were established, the system of allied states persisted: annual missions and occasional audiences, followed by biennial audiences and formal assemblies.
They met again and formed an alliance. Those who administered the government were more rigorous than in the affairs of the feudal lords.

They selected those capable of understanding the actions of the four states, distinguishing the clans and lineages of the great officers, their ranks and positions, and their nobility, meanness, competence, and incompetence. They employed those skilled in diplomatic speech;

thus, although the laws were not explicitly proclaimed, the administration of affairs could be verified. The sage’s pen condensed them for completeness, making the subtle manifest and recording the hidden.

The essence of punishing evil and encouraging good remains intact. Descending from this point, Sima Junshi (Sima Guang) held the talents of his era in his grasp, yet he carried his own limitations with him;

though he spent half a lifetime on it, he produced but a single work. How could Ban Gu or Fan Ye have hoped to reach such heights? Among the followers of Śākyamuni, those who dwell in crags and caves and humble themselves find their fame to be all the higher;
those whose positions are low find their Way to be all the more solemn. Across the four seas and ten thousand *li*, they stand alone...

The *Yunshen te* (Cloud-Body Treatise) refers to what is called "chronological compilation" (*biannian*) in the *Wulun*. If the gates and portals crumble and collapse, and the barbarians come to insult us—when they arrive in such numbers, who is there that is not like them?
Who else but sin could cause this? When employing the methods of Sima Qian and Ban Gu, there were indeed circumstances beyond one's control.

Although the style follows Qian and Gu, in making the subtle manifest and the hidden intentions clear, and in punishing evil while encouraging good, I have never ceased to draw upon their principles in secret.

The Old Chapters. This is the work of the orthodox tradition. The Basic Annals (*benji*) strictly establish the founding ordinances; the Hereditary Houses (*shijia*) manifest the preservation of those ordinances.

The Monographs (*zhi*) detail the laws enacted, thereby honoring those capable of implementing them. The various Biographies (*zhuan*) branch out like flowing rivers, while the Records (*jì*) stand firm like towering mountains.
Whether in agriculture or warfare, who was host and who was guest? Thus, the essential tasks are complete. This is the lineage of the school.
My learning is shallow and my insight dark; my perspective is as narrow as that of a tube. I am well aware that my words are as wild and frivolous as they are.

Yet, since the Way is weighty while my person is insignificant, what need have I to concern myself with profit or harm? Written on the tenth day of the third month in the first year of the Jiāxī era of the Huángsòng dynasty, by the śramaṇa Zōngjiàn.

Like a profound and still dharma, his spirit was long radiant; amidst the contemplation of the *Brahma* [heaven], there was a brilliant clarity that could be observed.
Zhao Shuo zhi and Chen Guan passed this down through five generations and five transmissions.

*Shimen Zhengtong*, Volume One (The original text consisted of three volumes; as it has now been made into eight volumes, this title is placed here).
The Life of the World-Honored One Śākyamuni, the Teacher of the Sahā World, and the Accounts of All Buddhas Appearing in the World:
All possess both essence and function, as well as the three bodies (*trikāya*). The first is called the Pure Dharma Body (*dharmakāya*), which is the essence.
In Sanskrit it is *Vairocana*, which here means "pervading all places. The second is called the Perfect Dharma Body, also known as...

The *vijeṣin* (Victorious Response), also called *mahāpuruṣa-lakṣaṇa* (Exalted Unique Features), is in Sanskrit *Vairocana*, which here means "Pure Fulfillment" (the retribution of self) or "Universal Radiance" (the retribution of others).

Third is the *koṭīśata-sahasra-nirmāṇakāya* (Transformation Body of a Hundred Thousand Myriads), also called the *hīna-vijeṣin* (Inferior Response)—referred to as the transformation body for those of great capacity, while for those of small capacity it becomes the inferior response.
In Sanskrit this is *Śākyamuni*, which here means "Able Benevolent One" and "Silent Sage"; these all refer to the functional aspect (*upayoga*). Furthermore, this...
The Sahā world undergoes formation, abiding, destruction, and emptiness, each lasting twenty intermediate kalpas of increase and decrease; this is called one great kalpa.

The current kalpa of abiding is named the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa), during which one thousand Buddhas appear in the world. During the first eight kalpas, time passed empty with no Buddhas appearing.
Then, during the ninth kalpa of decrease, from the time when the human lifespan in Jambudvīpa was eighty-four thousand years, every hundred years...
The lifespan decreases by one year [at a time]. When it has decreased to sixty thousand years, Krakucchanda Buddha appears;
when it is forty thousand years, Kanakamuni Buddha appears; when it is twenty thousand years, Kāśyapa Buddha appears;

and when it is one hundred years, Śākyamuni Buddha appears. Thus it continues decreasing until it reaches ten years. Then, the sons' lifespans double those of their fathers, increasing again until it reaches eighty-four thousand years.
When the human lifespan reaches eighty thousand years during the tenth *kalpa* of decrease, Maitreya Buddha appears.
In this manner, through the fifteenth *kalpa* of decrease, nine hundred and ninety-four Buddhas appear in succession. This continues until the twentieth *kalpa* of increase, when Ruci Buddha arises.
Once the *kalpa* of decrease has concluded, it then enters the *kalpa* of destruction. Furthermore, regarding this Bhadrakalpa...

The kalpa that has passed is named the Adorned Kalpa (*Vibhūṣaṇakalpa*); the future one is named the Constellation Kalpa (*Tārakakalpa*). In both, one thousand Buddhas appear in the world, as detailed in the *Sūtra of the Names of Three Thousand Buddhas*.

Now, following the World-Honored One’s manifestation of the two types of response—the superior and the inferior—he bestowed the two teachings of the gradual and the sudden, each displaying the eight phases of enlightenment.
Thus, I have compiled this Record of the World-Honored One’s Life.
Śākyamuni Buddha is the "inferior response-body" (hīna-nirmāṇakāya). This inferior response-body manifests through the eight phases of manifestation for the sake of śrāvakas:
namely, descending from Tuṣita, entering the womb, birth, renouncing the world, subduing Māra, attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and entering parinirvāṇa.

While those of the Tripitaka and Shared Vehicles (the three vehicles) as well as ordinary worldlings at the stage of the "vast ground" all perceive this body, the text here specifically mentions "śrāvakas" because they are those who directly receive and follow the Buddha's teachings.
Speaking from the perspective of those whose faculties and nature are particularly dull: if one refers to the Supreme Response Body (vairocanābhisambodhi), it is said to be Vairocana Buddha.

The eight manifestations of this Supreme Response Body correspond to the Bodhisattva, namely: descending to be born, entering the womb, dwelling in the womb, initial birth, renouncing the household life, attaining enlightenment, and preaching the Dharma.
[The Buddha] entered parinirvāṇa. As for the Bodhisattva, he is one of the distinct and perfect [teachings]. Regarding his descent:

on the level of the Small [Vehicle], as the *Puyao jing* (Sutra of the Manifestation of Light) states, the Bodhisattva dwells in the Tuṣita Heaven as the teacher of the devas; having perfected his merit and resolve, when the time arrives, he descends to become a Buddha, taking birth in the kingdom of Kapilavastu in India.
On the level of the Great [Vehicle], as the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states, the Bodhisattva [descends] from Tuṣita...

When the celestial being was about to descend with his spirit, there were bodhisattvas as numerous as the atoms in ten buddha-fields, all of whom shared the same vows and practices as this bodhisattva, even to the point that their universal conduct and vows of Samantabhadra were entirely equal to his.

Furthermore, by means of their supernatural powers, they universally manifested themselves in all Tuṣita palaces; within each palace, they appeared throughout the Jambudvīpa of all worlds in the ten directions.
Regarding the image of taking birth within the womb: the one who was briefly conceived in the womb was King Śuddhodana of Central India, of the Gautama clan.
His queen, Māyā, dreamed of a person riding a white elephant, piercing the essence of the sun, entering her right flank from the Tuṣita Heaven palace.
Consequently, she carried the child for ten months. As stated in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Vairocana..."
The Bodhisattva has already passed away from here and been born into the human world in the household of King Śuddhodana. He ascends a sandalwood pavilion and dwells within the womb of Queen Māyā.
Furthermore, the Queen says: "O noble son, as is the case with the World-Honored One today, I am his mother."
All the immeasurable Buddhas of the past likewise served her as their mother.
Furthermore, the Great Sūtra states that when the Bodhisattva descended from Tuṣita Heaven, the devas of the desire and form realms all came to attend upon him. Thus, the *Fahua jujì* says:

"Regarding the two modes of manifestation, the sūtra texts each contain accounts of birth and dharma; one should know that the characteristics of birth for the two bodies are present in both locations."
One cannot take the sandalwood pavilion as being equivalent to the solar essence that pierces the heavens;

nor can the perfection and clarity of the *sarvajñajñāna* (all-encompassing wisdom) be equated with the simultaneous exhaustion of both innate and acquired habits (*vāsanā*). Furthermore, the seven steps taken in the ten directions are used to manifest the distinction between superiority and inferiority.

Thus, we know that in both cases there is no "long-term accomplishment. Moreover, the Mahayana teaching regarding dwelling in the womb symbolizes permanence, constancy, and immutability; therefore, we know [that this is the definitive meaning].
The *Avataṃsaka* states: "Within the mother’s womb, the Bodhisattva manifests a great palace, adorned with all manner of exquisite ornaments, all of which are wondrous and beautiful;
yet he causes the mother’s body to remain stable and free from ailment. It further says: "Having dwelt in the mother’s womb, his mind is always in right mindfulness, and he is never confused.
Moreover, the *Lalitavistara* states: "Those Bodhisattvas move about freely within my belly," or...
He takes a single stride across a trichiliocosm; or he takes a single stride across worlds as numerous as the atoms in unspeakably unspeakable numbers of Buddha-fields.
Furthermore, the Sūtra says: While dwelling in the mother’s womb, he manifests residing in Tuṣita Heaven;
his birth as a youth; his life in the royal palace; his renunciation; his ascetic practices; his attainment of the Way; and his turning of the wheel of Dharma.
[They] enter parinirvāṇa. Furthermore, it is said: some see the Buddha preaching various teachings; some see him in Tuṣita Heaven;
some see him descending to dwell in his mother’s womb; some see his birth; some see his renunciation;
some see his attainment of the Way; some see him turning the wheel of Dharma; and some see him entering nirvāṇa. Jingxi says: the word "some" (或) is used in each instance.
Within these [twelve] stages, there are eight phases. Therefore, in the Hīnayāna, impermanence is defined as arising and ceasing; the stage of dwelling in the womb is not established.
As for the fact that various sūtras occasionally mention dwelling in the womb, it is counted among those stages that are not part of the eight phases. Regarding his initial birth:

in the twenty-sixth year of King Zhou Zhao, the Jia-yin year, on the eighth day of the fourth month, the Queen informed the King that she was traveling to the Lumbinī Garden and had arrived beneath the Aśoka tree.
Raising his right hand as if to pluck a flowering branch, Prince Siddhārtha then descended from his mother’s side and was born.
Immediately, nine dragons were moved to send down rain to bathe his body. He then took seven steps by himself and, raising his right hand, spoke these words:
"In the heavens above and on earth below, I alone am supreme. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "Having finished speaking, he became silent like an infant; he neither moved nor spoke.
For three years he was nursed at the breast as his mothers raised him, and he gradually grew up. Yet, the Buddha’s body is infinite."

He transcends all worlds, yet for the sake of sentient beings, he manifests as an ordinary person. Furthermore, a great sutra states that seven days after the Prince was born, his mother’s life ended and she was reborn in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
If one refers to the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, it says that the Queen grasped a branch of a golden garden tree and gave birth to the Bodhisattva;
the hosts of heavenly kings each held fragrant water and together bathed him. Moreover, a great sutra states:

When the Bodhisattva was first born, he walked seven steps in each of the ten directions. Furthermore, it is said that the Nanda Dragon King and others bathed the Bodhisattva’s body through their supernatural powers;

this is the manifestation of birth according to the Mahāyāna. Regarding the date of this birth, it is determined based on the *Zhou shu yiji* (Miraculous Records of the Book of Zhou), the *Chuanjiao fawang benji* (Chronicle of the Dharma-King Who Transmitted the Teaching), the *Han faben neizhuan* (Inner Biography of the Original Record of the Dharma in Han), and the *Bianzheng lun* (Treatise on Discerning the Correct).
The *Zhengji* (Correct Record) considers this to be the year Wuzi of King Ping of Zhou; others say it was the reigns of Kings Huan, Hui, or Ding.
The Tiantai Master Zhiyi correctly takes the period of the two Zhuangs—that is, King Zhuang of Zhou and Duke Zhuang of Lu.
Because their insights and perspectives differ, there are many such theories. At three years of age, King Śuddhodana took the Prince to visit the temple of a deity. The deity...
The elephant paid its respects. The King was startled and said, "My son is even more venerable among the heavenly deities.
Consequently, he was titled "God among Gods" (Devātideva). He then went to see the ascetic Ārāḍa to divine his fortune.

Upon seeing the Prince’s thirty-two marks, his four limbs of golden hue, and the fleshly protuberance upon his crown, the ascetic declared, "If he remains in the kingdom, he shall become a Wheel-Turning King (Cakravartin Rāja); if he departs..."
He thought to himself, "If I had studied the Way at home, I would have attained Buddhahood. It is my regret that I am now old and do not see the appearance of a Buddha.

Five years later, the King provided him with vehicles drawn by elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep; indeed, there was no toy or object of pleasure for a child that he was not given. At the age of seven...
The King established an academy and had the Prince ride in a goat-drawn carriage to the teacher’s gate. He summoned the Brahmin Bhadrayāṇī to instruct the Prince.
The texts the Prince studied were the Vedas, the five sciences, astronomy, geography, archery, charioteering, writing, mathematics, and the study of diagrams and prophecies.
At ten years of age, he remained constantly within the palace and never went outside. At last—

He competed in martial arts with his two younger brothers, Devadatta and Nanda, piercing seven iron drums, throwing elephants, contending in feats of strength, and engaging in wrestling and other games.
At the age of eleven, while playing archery in the *Gonaghu* garden, he vied with Devadatta for a wild goose.

At fourteen, having requested permission from his father the King to tour the four city gates, he encountered an old man, a sick man, and a dead man; he immediately turned his chariot back to the palace and was struck with deep sorrow.
There are three afflictions from which there is no way to escape. Grieved, he could not eat. Finally, he again traveled through the northern gate and encountered a śramaṇa;

he contemplated leaving the household life. At fifteen years of age, on the eighth day of the second month, the great ministers assembled and performed the consecration upon the Prince’s head with the waters of the four great oceans, bestowing upon him the precious seal and establishing him as the heir to the kingdom. At sixteen years of age, he went out to tour the royal fields to observe them.
While the farmers were working, the Śuddhāvāsa devas manifested as earthworms and birds that came to peck at them.
The Prince said, "Sentient beings, through the conditions of dependent origination, devour one another. He then reflected further, contemplating liberation from birth and death.

When the King heard these words, fearing his son would renounce the world, he wished to arrange a marriage immediately to please him. At the age of seventeen, he took Mahānāma, a Brahmin, [as his bride].
He took the maiden Yaśodharā as his consort, along with Gopī and Mṛgajā, making three queens.

Although they shared his daily life—whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining—morning and evening alike, there was no marital intimacy between them. Instead, he spent much of his time during the quiet nights practicing meditative contemplation.
At the age of nineteen, on the fifteenth night of the second month, he mounted his celestial horse and left the city to become a renunciant. After traveling twelve *yojanas*, he arrived at...
In the forest of asceticism where the Ṛṣi Bhadra dwelt on the Snowy Mountains, he immediately used a sharp sword to shave off his own beard and hair.
He thought of obtaining the *kāṣāya* robes; at that time, a deva from the Śuddhāvāsa heaven manifested as a hunter, wearing *kāṣāya* robes.
Since the lions of the Western Regions do not harm those who wear *kāṣāya*, the hunter had stolen these robes to enter the mountain villages. The Prince saw him.
The Prince asked, "For what purpose do you wear this? He replied, "I wear it to lure the deer.
The Prince said, "If that is the case, then clothing the body in dharma-robes serves only as an aid for killing and stealing; it is not for the sake of liberation.
May I trade with you my kāśika robe made of the seven precious gems? The hunter took it off and departed. [Then] Kauṇḍinya and the other four...
Attended by his human followers, he first practiced the concentration of the sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana-samādhi*) for twenty years.
At twenty-two, he went to the hermitage of the seer Ārāḍa Kālāma and practiced the concentration of the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana-samādhi*).
At twenty-five, he went to the banks of the Nairañjanā River and practiced various austerities.
As he practiced his conduct, the devas offered him hemp seeds and rice. The Prince consumed one hemp seed and one grain of rice daily, or ate once every seven days.
Furthermore, his father the King ordered five hundred chariots laden with provisions to go and present them to the Prince, but the Prince accepted none of them.
As the Sūtra says: "The Devaputra Manojña saw grass sprouting from the ground and piercing the flesh of the Bodhisattva as it grew upward."
It reached his elbows. Some say his calves pierced through his knees and spiderwebs hung from his brows, though the source for this has not been seen.

As for the crane’s nest upon his head and the venomous snakes entwined around his body, these were events from the time the World-Honored One was practicing the causal stages; they were not his ascetic practices of today.
Subsequently, when the six years were completed and his physical form and spirit were withered and emaciated, he went to the river to bathe. Having emerged, Nanda and Nandabalā...
The two daughters of the Brahmin offered milk-rice. At that time, Śakra Devānām Indra, named Śrī, held pure grass and presented it to the Prince, who spread it as a seat of grass.
At thirty-one years of age, during the seventh night of the second month in the fifth year of King Mu’s reign (the Jia-shen year), he subdued a demonic army of thirty-six billion.
However, among the minor [biographies], those that list his subduing of Māra refer to the Tripiṭaka Bodhisattva.
Once Śākyamuni had emerged from his dwelling and was about to attain enlightenment, he was disturbed by the celestial Māra of the desire realm; therefore, it was necessary to subdue him.
If a Bodhisattva abiding on the stages has already analyzed and destroyed ignorance, then all their bodies and lands must pertain to beyond the realms.

How could there be a celestial Māra attached to the five desires to be subdued? For this reason, these characteristics do not appear among the [first] eight stages. This is the Bodhisattva’s subduing of Māra.
Having done so, he emitted a great radiance and immediately entered meditative absorption.

On the eighth day, as the morning star appeared, he attained sudden and great enlightenment, achieving Perfect Awakening and being titled the World-Honored One (*Bhagavān*). On that same day, his younger cousin Ānanda was born (some say on the tenth day).
Previously, the World-Honored One had pointed at Yaśodharā and said, "Six years hence, you shall give birth to a son. When this time arrived, a son was born, named Rāhula.
O Hula, two sages passed away seven days before the site of enlightenment. The World-Honored One lamented that they did not witness the turning of the Wheel of Dharma.
After another seven days, he conferred the five precepts upon Yaśodharā’s father. On the forty-ninth day, he accepted the parched grain and honey from the elder Trapusa;
he conferred upon him the Three Refuges and the five precepts, naming him Trapusa. According to the *Trapusa Sūtra*, he received [the protection of] the Four Heavenly Kings.
Each was given a stone alms bowl. Brahmā King erected a hall of the seven treasures, and Śakra Devendra established a throne of the seven treasures, entreating him to preach the Dharma.

According to the Mahāyāna, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "Furthermore, one sees him leave home and proceed to the site of enlightenment, where he attains equal and perfect awakening and sits upon the lion throne;
one also sees the Tathāgata, when he formerly practiced the bodhisattva path, showing reverence before all Buddhas."

Reverently making offerings. The Brahmajāla Sūtra states that one may leave the household life at seven years of age. The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra records Śāriputra asking the Most Victorious One (the Buddha):
"For what reason did the Bodhisattva first manifest six years of ascetic practice to subdue the heavenly Māras, and only afterwards attain perfect enlightenment? He replied:

When a bodhisattva practices the *prajñāpāramitā* with skillful means (*upāyakauśalya*), they penetrate the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) and realize that there is, in reality, no asceticism (*duṣkaracaryā*).

Nevertheless, in order to subdue the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they manifest such practices. Furthermore, although the Lord of the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātupati*), the celestial Māra, is by nature disciplined and gentle and thus truly should not be destroyed, he manifests his subjugation for the sake of transforming sentient beings. This is because those non-Buddhists claim for themselves: [text continues]
He was foremost among those capable of practicing asceticism. He even witnessed the Bodhisattva lying upon thorns, or lying upon cow dung, or wearing tree bark, or again being naked;

or eating roots of grass, or eating leaves of trees, or eating once every six days, or passing his days drinking only water, or consuming nothing at all. Through such various forms of ascetic practice, he passed six years.

There is no deficiency whatsoever. However, in reality, Bodhisattvas do not engage in such ascetic practices; rather, they perceive themselves as having them while actually being in the process of delivering sentient beings.
Based on these passages, it appears to be a form of Mahāyāna asceticism. Nevertheless, it is ultimately a Mahāyāna that has been extracted from within the gradual [vehicle].
This is not the Mahāyāna of sudden instruction through transformation. The same applies to the subduing of Māra. If the Great Sūtra says:
"Having been born in Jambudvīpa for seven days, he further manifested the shaving of his hair. It also says:

"Furthermore, it was seen that when the Tathāgata was practicing the bodhisattva path in the past, he reverently made offerings at the abodes of various Buddhas. It also says: "The Bodhisattva should [practice] through asceticism..."
He tested his own mind by eating one sesame seed per day for seven days; he did the same with non-glutinous rice, mung beans, and so forth, each for seven days.
To his great disappointment, there was no benefit whatsoever. He thought to himself, "How does this differ from the ascetic practices of the Hīnayāna?

It is simply a matter of discernment. Drawing from the current to seek the source, and following the fragrance to investigate the root, I have compiled the "Genealogy of the Southern Peak (Nanyue) of the Northern Qi.

Regarding all phenomena, the mind is free from discrimination. When wisdom (*prajñā*) is predominant, it follows from clarity; when clarity is predominant, it follows from accumulation; when accumulation is predominant, it follows from loftiness.
Sōngduo followed Shenzui; Shenzui followed Mingzui. From Mingzui to the Master, there were seven generations in total. They had cultivated only the seven stages of expedient means of the Hīnayāna.

Prajñāpāramitā. Śāriputra, a bodhisattva mahāsattva should train in the prajñāpāramitā in this manner.

The treatise asks: "If one attains all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*) and the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), and cuts off all afflictions along with their habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) within a single moment of mind, why is it now said that one 'fulfills all-knowledge' and 'attains the knowledge of all aspects'? Therefore, it is said thus. Furthermore, although [these] are attained within a single moment of mind, there is still a sequence of beginning, middle, and end, just as a single moment of mind possesses the three characteristics: arising conditioned by abiding, and abiding conditioned by cessation.
Likewise, this applies to the mind, mental factors, dissociated formations, as well as bodily and vocal actions. Through the knowledge of the Path, one fulfills all-knowledge; through all-...

What was previously described as the knowledge of all modes is itself omniscience (*sarvajñatā*). The knowledge of the path (*mārgajñatā*) is named the Vajra Samādhi.

When the Buddha first generates the mind of enlightenment, it is already both omniscience and the knowledge of all modes; at that time, the habitual tendencies of the afflictions are severed. Omniscience—[one]...

He observed that the three types of knowledge (*trijñāna*) described in the treatises are actually attained within a single moment of mind. Furthermore, since the fruit is attained within a single moment of mind, the cause must likewise be so.
How could one attain [the fruit] through preceding and succeeding stages? Therefore, when this contemplation is perfected, one realizes at that moment the three wisdoms within the One Mind;

with the simultaneous negation and simultaneous illumination, one enters the stage of the First Abode (Prathamābhūmi), the rank of the Non-arising Patience (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). This is why [Zhiyi] points distantly to Nāgārjuna as his teacher;
although he did not behold Nāgārjuna’s face, he had already beheld Nāgārjuna’s mind. For this reason, our school takes the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* as its foundational authority.

Chapter Seventeen: The Fourteen Truths, Verse 17. "Of those dharmas produced by causes and conditions, I say they are empty;

they are also called provisional designations, and they are also called the meaning of the Middle Way. Suddenly awakening alone, he realized at once that all teachings are nothing other than dharmas produced by causes and conditions.
Yet these causes and conditions are not fixed as existing, and emptiness is not fixed as empty. Emptiness and existence are non-dual; thus, names are established.

All these refer to the Middle Way. The Master walked alone along the Yellow and Huai Rivers; at that time, none could rival his transformative influence. He gathered several hundred disciples, held in high esteem by both the monastic and the laity.

He transmitted the oral instructions of mental contemplation to Huisi. Huisi attained the purification of the six sense faculties, which corresponds to the ten stages of faith (*śraddhā*) of the Perfect Teaching, the thirty minds of the Distinct Teaching, and the ten Brahma-conducts of the *Avataṃsaka*, as well as the Iron Wheel stage of the *Ratnakūṭa-vaipulya-sūtra*. It is like discerning the kind of wood by its smoke, or seeing [the essence] through its manifestation.
The crane knows the pond. Such is the realization of his disciples; the relative heights of the Master’s stations can be known even without being spoken.

An ancient sighed, saying: "Those who wear the sky do not know its height; those who tread upon the earth do not know its thickness. As the history of the monks has been lost to transmission, it cannot be recorded in full—how regrettable!

This is merely a colloquial expression. Nanyue Huisi was surnamed Li and was a native of Wujin (in Chenzhou).
From his youth, he was characterized by broad-mindedness and compassion, earning the respect and submission of his village neighbors.

He once dreamed of a foreign monk who exhorted him to leave the household life; struck with awe and awakened by this auspicious omen, he took leave of his kin to enter the Way. Upon receiving full ordination, he withdrew from worldly society.

His devotion to the Way grew ever more profound. For ten years he constantly recited the *Lotus Sūtra*, and for seven years he specialized in the practice of the Vaipulya repentance rites and the *dharmasamādhi* of constant sitting.
He took only one meal per day and did not accept separate invitations. When he was staying in a thatched hut, a rustic man set it on fire.
He was immediately stricken with a severe illness and subsequently sought to repent for his transgressions; his ailment was then healed. He rebuilt his thatched hut and recited the sutras as before.
Furthermore, he dreamed that you [the deity] told him, "Previously, you received the ritual of the precepts, yet it was not supreme. How could it have opened the way to the Right Path?

Thereupon, he obtained the forty-two-fold *saṃghāvaśeṣa* *karmavācanā* for the perfection of the full precepts. Upon waking, he redoubled his efforts, never abandoning his constant practice from dusk until dawn.
Through these ascetic practices, he eventually beheld the traces of his conduct throughout three lifetimes. Furthermore, he dreamed that Maitreya and Amitābha preached the Dharma to him.
He also followed Maitreya and various eminent companions to the assembly at the Dragon Flower (Nāgapuṣpa) tree. Overcome with emotion, he wept bitterly; this led him to redouble his diligence.

Consequently, upon reading the *Sūtra on the Sublime Samādhi*, he marveled at the merits of meditative concentration (dhyāna). Thereupon, he traveled north to the Qi dynasty to seek out and receive instruction from those who held the correct [teachings].

He received [the instructions]. Day and night he applied his mind; after the first three weeks, he gave rise to a slight degree of calm observation (*śamatha-vipaśyanā*) and beheld the signs of the wholesome and unwholesome karma of his entire life.

His vigor increased manifold, and he subsequently experienced the eight tactile sensations (heavy, light, cold, hot, rough, smooth, soft, and coarse), which gave rise to the fundamental first dhyāna. Suddenly, obstacles to dhyāna arose:
the four limbs became limp and weak, he could not bear the weight of walking, and his body no longer followed his mind. He then observed to himself, "I am now ill."
All these arise from karma. Karma originates from the mind; fundamentally, there are no external objects. By turning back to perceive the source of the mind, karma cannot be apprehended.

The body is like a cloud or a shadow; its appearances exist, yet its substance is empty. Having contemplated in this way, inverted perceptions are extinguished, the nature of the mind becomes pure, and all suffering is eliminated.

Furthermore, one gives rise to the concentration of emptiness (*śūnyatā-samādhi*), and the mind and its objects suddenly open up in clarity. As the year of the Dharma draws to a close, I lament that there is nothing [to be grasped].
He realized that he had been deluded by dullness and that his life had passed in vain; deeply filled with shame and remorse, he leaned his body against a wall.

Before his back even touched it, he suddenly attained awakening to the Lotus Samādhi and all the various Dharma gates. Later, when he went to report his realization to masters such as Jiao and Zui, they both granted him their approval.
As he refined his practice over a long period, his previous insights grew ever more profound, and he became renowned throughout the Shōyō region.
His reputation spread far and wide, and his disciples increased daily. He then expounded and illustrated the teachings of samādhi and prajñā to guide both himself and others.

Among the diverse assembly, both refined and coarse, disputes arose; yet he was not harmed by their resentment or malice, which were like the most virulent poisons. When followers of heterodox paths devised schemes against him, those plots failed to cause him harm.
He then looked upon his followers and said: "Even when the Great Sage was in the world, he could not avoid slander; how much more so for me?"
"Without virtue, how could I escape this retribution? This retribution is the result of past deeds; when the time comes, it must be endured. This is a private matter.
However, as the mandate of the Qi dynasty is about to collapse and the Buddha-dharma should perish, to which direction should I go to avoid this calamity?

Suddenly, he heard a voice from the sky saying, "If you wish to cultivate meditative concentration, you may go to Wudang. Nanyue is a mountain for entering the Way. At the beginning of the Wuping era, he led his disciples southward.

He stayed at Dàsū Mountain in Gāozhōu for several years, and his followers gathered there like a marketplace. As the region lay on the border between the Chen and Qi dynasties, beacon fires frequently flared up, leaving the assembly no peace of mind.
In the second year of the Guāngdà era of the Chen dynasty, he finally departed for Nányuè Mountain, whereupon he addressed the assembly:

After a long time, he ascended Mount Chidi (Red Emperor Peak). There he encountered the Spirit of the Mountain, who said to the Master, "Disciple, may you yield your dwelling to me?

Upon encountering level ground, he stopped and established a shrine for the deity. He had the image of the Mountain God (Yueshen) carved, which still sits upon a stone drum today at Shangfeng Temple.

He went further to a dense thicket and said, "This was an ancient temple where I entrusted my third life.

He pointed out the spot for someone to dig, and indeed they found monastic utensils as well as the foundations of a hall made of layered bricks. He immediately constructed a platform there and preached the *Prajñāpāramitā* to the assembly.

At that time, there was an immortal from the Nine Immortals Observatory named Daoist Ou-yang Cheng, who perceived that the mountain possessed an auspicious aura.

[The remains were] concealed. His spirit-bones were returned to their origin. It was because the Master had once said: "These Daoists have no cause to harm me;
yet one day they will surely don my *kāṣāya*, enter my monastery, and destroy my physical remains. He further informed the God of Mount Tai, saying: "I am in peril."
"The disciples shall likewise encounter difficulties; now, seven hundred years have passed, and indeed this prophecy has been fulfilled. Alas!
Were it not for those with the six sense-faculties purified and endowed with great supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), how could one penetrate the past and future so thoroughly?

As the Master was about to pass away, he preached the Dharma at the Great Assembly Gate for several days, reprimanding them with bitter urgency until those who heard him were chilled with fear. He then said: "If there are ten people..."

"Those who do not begrudge their own bodies or lives, who constantly practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, the *Pratyutpanna*, and the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, and who perform the Vaipulya repentances and the asceticism of constant sitting—for such as these, I shall personally provide whatever they require and will surely benefit them.

If there is no such person, I shall depart far away. Yet, no one answered. He then dismissed the assembly, collected his thoughts, sat cross-legged, and with palms joined, invoked the Buddha to come and welcome him.
He passed away on the twenty-second day of the sixth month in the ninth year of the Dajian era.
His age was sixty-four. He entrusted the Dharma to his chief disciple, Zhiyi. Regarding the master’s writings, he dictated them orally;
his disciples composed the sentences and phrases, with little need for revision or alteration. He produced two fascicles of the *Forty-two Letter Gate* and the *Practice of Non-contention*.

He produced one fascicle each of the *Men* (The Gates), the *Shilun xuansui ziyi anlexing cidi chanyao* (The Essential Methods of Meditation on the Sequential Stages of the Peaceful Practices According to One’s Own Intent as Explained in the Commentary), and the *Sanzhiguanmen* (The Gate of Contemplation of the Three Knowledges).

Furthermore, he used gold donated by a lay devotee to transcribe twenty-seven fascicles of the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* and one complete set of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, which were stored in a precious lapis lazuli casket.
Their adornment was so magnificent and dazzling that it opened the minds of the multitude; he then requested that they be preached.
He expounded upon the two sutras according to the text, and there was nothing in his profound exegesis that was not illuminating. Later, he requested Zhiyi to lecture on them in his stead.

When they reached the section on "one mind encompassing all practices," Zhiyi harbored a doubt. The Master said, "What you have doubted is merely the sequential meaning of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*."

"This is not yet the perfect and sudden (yuantun) purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*. Zhiyi further inquired about the stage of realization attained by his teacher. [The teacher replied: 'It is the tenth bhūmi. The teacher said: 'No.
My lifelong hope was to enter the stage of the Bronze Wheel-turning King (*tāmracakra*). I regret that I led disciples too early; thus I benefited others at the expense of myself.'"
He merely possessed the iron wheel [of sovereignty]. He once composed a text of vows to entrust to his disciples, which stated in brief:

"All those among the clergy and laity of this world who earnestly request offerings are all dispatched by evil Māras; they are not true spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). At first, they feign earnestness."
They appear to have good intentions, but subsequently they plot [against us]. Both the wrathful and the virtuous Māras are not to be trusted.
From this day forward, you should not believe them. All scholars should likewise be regarded as untrustworthy, like enemies feigning friendship.
Alas, alas! This is inconceivable. It is the same in every realm of all kings; choose with care, choose with care.
Zhezhe. The Master’s physical appearance was exceptionally prominent; his ears were adorned with the *bhadra-kuṇḍala* (ear-rings), and his crown was marked by a *uṣṇīṣa* (fleshly protuberance).
His gait was like that of an ox or an elephant—neither leaning nor slanting, but perfectly upright. In former times, he used only a single hempen robe to ward off the cold;

regarding items made of silk or cotton, he would not accept anything that involved the destruction of living beings. Auspicious omens occurred in succession: the water in his flask was always full, and his offerings were strictly prepared, as if attended by celestial youths.

As for the Protector (Weizhe): he sometimes manifested forms large or small, and sometimes remained in silent concealment of his body; his extraordinary fragrances and marvelous colors were beyond counting. The *Chuan deng lu* states:
Master Zhi sent someone to say to Sida, "Why do you not go down the mountain to transform sentient beings?
Why do you gaze at the clouds and stars? Sida replied, "The Buddhas of the three periods have been swallowed by me in a single mouth; what more is there?"
It is said that the sentient beings were highly capable of being transformed. According to the Master’s old inscription, he was born in the thirteenth year of the Tianjian era of the Liang dynasty;
since this was the time when Daoyi entered nirvana, those words cannot be relied upon as authoritative.
Attached is the "Dharma-gate of the Lotus Sūtra Meditation" composed by the Great Master Dàshàn of Wǔrén. He attained the Samādhi of Compassion.

Zhèng Sēngguǒ, the Interior Historian of Héngyáng, was frequently praised for the Master’s virtue by the County Magistrate Chén Zhèngyè, yet he showed no sign of faith or inclination. One day, they went hunting together.
A herd of deer surrounded him. He said to Chen, "You once praised the Great Goodness Chan Master for possessing the power of the Samādhi of Compassion.
Today, what will he do with these deer? Chen led his attendants and together they chanted, "Namo Great Goodness Chan Master!
Instantly, the herd of deer flew out into the air. The Grand Secretary bowed in shame and submission. This was similar to the case of Ge Fan, who invoked Guanyin.
Regarding the name "Sound" (Śabda): when the flock of geese he raised took flight, people saw a mass of snow crossing the sky amidst the clouds;
how is this any different [from Avalokiteśvara]? (*Guanyin Ganying Ji*). The Minister Wu Mingche once inquired, saying: "How great is the true virtue of the Dharma Flower Chan Gate at Mount Nanyue?
He replied: "In terms of faith and reverence, there are three thousand; in terms of karmic excellence, four hundred. Sengzhao has attained the deepest meditative concentration. Zhiyi...
He was unimpeded in preaching the Dharma; it would have been most excellent had he possessed both [wisdom and skillful means] together.

For the Master was renowned as being equal in fame to Zhiyi. Zhiyi’s Way was like the raising of the sun and moon, its radiance illuminating all under heaven; surely he must have possessed both concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) in their entirety.

Yet, Nanyue alone designated the Master by that specific title. When the Master passed into *parinirvāṇa*, extraordinary flowers rained from the heavens for seven days. The stage of realization he entered was exceedingly profound.

This may be known. Dharma Master Xuanguang was a native of Silla. From his youth, he possessed brilliant insight and felt weary of worldly existence; he sought a teacher to cultivate the pure conduct (*brahmacarya*) with single-minded devotion.

Upon reaching adulthood, he crossed the vast ocean to seek the Dharma in the Central Kingdom. Arriving at Mount Heng, he met the Great Master [Huisi]. The Master examined the origins of his disposition and bestowed [the teachings] upon him.

He received and practiced the *Anrakugyō* (Peaceful Practices) chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, applying himself with diligence and without error. Before long, he realized the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*.
Zhiyi said to him, "What you have realized is true and not false. Guard it with wholesome mindfulness and advance toward Bodhi.
Return to your native land and employ skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), so that all who are like caterpillars may become wasps. The Master then returned south to Jiangnan.
While he was about to board a sea-going vessel, before he had even reached the harbor, he suddenly beheld multicolored clouds bewildering his eyes and elegant music filling the air.
Scarlet staffs and rainbow banners arrived with the sound of proclamations. A voice from the sky said, "The Heavenly Emperor summons the Chan Master Xuanguang of海东 (Haidong).
The Master folded his hands and declined, yet he saw only green-clad attendants leading him forward. After a short while, they entered a palace that was by no means like a human dwelling.
At the palace, as the imperial guards were arrayed in formation, there appeared a multitude of fish and shellfish emerging from their burrows, interspersed with spirits and deities.
They all said, "The Celestial Emperor has descended to our Dragon Palace to invite the Master to expound the Dharma-gates already realized; we have received profound benefit.

Having ascended the jeweled hall and further climbed the lofty pavilion, he conversed as if in response to questions for seven days until the conclusion. The Emperor personally saw him off, [turning toward] where his boat had previously been moored.

The boat drifted out onto the ocean and would not advance. The Master boarded it once more; the crew said it had been only half a day. The Master returned to Mount Wŏngsan in Ungju, where he took up residence in a thatched hut.
It subsequently became a great monastery (*bopang*). He preached the Dharma to guide and transform others, bringing enlightenment to a vast multitude.

One person ascended the hall to receive the prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*), and one person entered the fire-light samādhi (*tejodhātu-samādhi*). [One person] entered the water-light samādhi...
There were two [who remained]. His various disciples were like birds perched upon Mount Sumeru; they were all of one color.
Afterward, they fled and dispersed, with no one knowing where they had gone. Among the twenty-eight figures depicted in the Shadow Hall of Mount Nanyue, the Master occupies one of them.

Dharma Master Huicheng’s surname was Duan; he was a native of Liyang. He left the secular life at Shizhu Temple and recited more than twenty fascicles of Mahāyāna sūtras, including the *Lotus Sūtra*, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*, and the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*.
Having received full ordination, he traveled to Jianye, where he happened upon the Great Master Chengshi lecturing.
Students were packed shoulder to shoulder, and he listened for ten years until the principles and phrasing were almost entirely mastered. He was then about to return home.
From his native district, he traveled to Mount Kuang and heard that Dashi (Sengzhi) was spreading the teachings on Mount Nanyue. He went there to rely upon him.
Dashi said, "The scholarship you have pursued in your life would not even produce smoke when held against my hand; it has been a waste of effort—what a pity!

Having previously relied on commentaries and sub-commentaries to derive understanding from others, the Master, once he had received this instruction, resolved to burn them all in indignation. At that time, there were several dozen practitioners of Chan.

The people there were all men of established reputation. Fearing that he might not be able to keep pace with them because he had arrived late, the Master continued from night until day, sitting in meditation with eyes open for fifteen years.
He further entered the practice halls of the Vaipulya, Avalokiteśvara, Lotus, and Prajñāpāramitā sūtras, undergoing trials to eliminate his karmic obstructions.

After practicing this for three years, demons and ghosts were entirely eradicated, and he subsequently attained the *Sattvabhāṣā-vyākaraṇa-samādhi* (the Samādhi of Understanding the Languages of Sentient Beings). He...

As for the "one who closes his eyes": though his realization of the Way may be clear when his eyes are shut, he loses it upon opening them. Compared to the Master [Huisi], there is a vast difference between them, as distinct as heaven and earth.
Sida said: "Zhiyi first attained samādhi and subsequently realized dhāraṇī; Huicheng and [Hui]ji—these two disciples were equal in both practice and understanding.

When the Master reached Zhijiang, he founded Chanhui Temple; all the labor involved in its construction, including the timber and masonry, was provided by laypeople. His virtue and conduct were exemplary.
What was summoned soon came to pass. While the construction of the hall was lacking a central beam, suddenly in the sixth month the river rose in flood.

He dreamed that there was a wooden beam in the middle of the current; he went to fetch it, and upon inspection, it was indeed so. The lay devotee Dianhong became the master of the vihāra, but he suddenly passed away.
The Master was summoned to his residence, whereupon Dianhong revived and said: "At first, I was seized and brought before the King. There I saw the Master ascending the hall and saying: 'I and..."
"This man has not yet finished establishing his meritorious works together with me; I pray you will pardon him. The King rose and prostrated at his feet, ultimately complying with his request.

When the Ruler of Chen heard of this, he summoned him, but the Master resolutely refused to go. The King then sent Jiang Zong and others to welcome him, saying, "If the Master does not consent, there is no need for you to trouble yourself to return.
The royal messengers wept profusely as they forcibly led him onto the boat; the Master then threw himself into the water and stood upright.
At the side of the pond, he again entreated him, saying, "If I do not receive [the precepts] from you, there will be no place for me to even scatter my body in dust.
Following this, he went to the imperial palace, where he was specially granted the Imperial Precepts (Dìjièfǎ) before returning. Thereupon, the temple was bestowed the name Chanhui Temple.

Once, while the Vinaya Master Chang was sleeping with the Master, he felt for lice on the ground in the darkness of night. The Master immediately knew of it. When they parted at dawn, the Master said: "Yesterday..."
One night, a lay donor suffered from the cold and was in great distress; [Huisi] felt constant shame for this and took it as a perpetual warning.

One day, he told his disciples, "Quickly lay the foundation for the main hall; I shall lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. Shortly thereafter, Zhiyi arrived from Yùquán, and they discussed profound principles together.
After a long while, Huisi passed away at the age of seventy-three. Prince Xiāngdōng erected a stele within his palace.
Dharma Master Huichao’s surname was Shen, and he was a native of Danyang. By nature, he was gentle and magnanimous. In his youth, he followed the monastic life and recited the *Lotus Sūtra*.

Having heard that Sengzhi of Guangzhou was preeminent in both samādhi and prajñā, and equally skilled in the Vinaya, and that he shared a bond of mutual respect with Zhiyi, Huichao respectfully approached him to request instruction.
Sengzhi remarked, "The inner treasury of Huichao’s spirit is such that he is one who has attained the stage of patience (*kṣānti*). Later, when Huichao traveled to Mount Heng, he again...
The Wise One recited the sutras along with his companions for years. Later, he withdrew to Zhongnan Mountain, where for eight years he attained the Way and greatly enhanced his three types of wisdom.
When the Daye era began and fortune rose, an imperial decree invited him into the inner palace. At the dawn of the Great Tang, his honor was esteemed throughout the capital.
The Master recited the sutras for over fifty years, totaling more than ten thousand fascicles. When he was bedridden with illness, he addressed the assembly, saying:

"Coming and going is my constant way; I do not rejoice in long life, nor do I grieve at death at nightfall. The emptiness of the primary truth and the contemplation of pure wisdom are my staff. Having spoken thus, he passed away facing west.
His final instruction was that his body be left exposed among the pines and rocks as an offering to birds and beasts. His disciples...
In accordance with the instructions, he remained there for over a month; his complexion remained as if he were alive. He returned and used the remains to build a stupa within a cave.

Dharma Master Huimin was a native of Hedong. At the age of nine, he left the secular world and devoted himself to pure conduct. It took him only one month to master the recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
When fifteen years had passed, he requested the Dharma from Gwangyeong of Silla; his brilliance was so outstanding that scholars praised him.

Another fifteen years later, he returned to Sigwangheung Temple in Haeyang to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. A wondrous fragrance wafted through the air, and snapping fingers repeatedly resonated in mid-space.

The assembly gathered like clouds, all declaring it an auspicious omen. Later, he moved to Tongxuan Temple, where for seventeen years he cultivated the Way with his disciples, never crossing the threshold of his room.

At the end of the Sui dynasty, when the realm fell into chaos and famine struck the region of Wu, the fourfold assembly fled in search of safety; yet Bao-min alone remained to face death, devoted to meditation and recitation.
During the flourishing of the Great Tang, he resided at Nanjian Temple, where two rabbits and a tiger lived together in harmony. One day—
A rare fragrance filled the room. The assembly questioned the Master about it, and he said, "I shall depart on a later day.

Birth and death are the constant nature of humanity. Life is like drifting clouds; each of you should contemplate impermanence and strive early to attain liberation. As scheduled, he passed away peacefully.
The lineage of the Great Master Zhizhe, the Founder of the Tiantai School and Master of Spiritual Wisdom, is truly noble.
Alas! For descendants to discourse upon the virtues of their ancestors is a difficult task indeed. Even Zaiwo, Zigong, and Youbo possessed a profound knowledge of Confucius;
yet Mencius said: "Their wisdom was sufficient to know the Sage, yet they did not stoop to flatter him."

What they hold dear—how could this not be because virtue has its heights and its depths? That which is lofty is beyond the reach of titles and appellations; what can be titled and named is but a mere trace.
If some were to record it with a private mind, how could they escape the reproach of "favoring what one is personally fond of"?

Is this not indeed difficult? Nevertheless, as for great virtue, magnificent achievements, noble discourse, and sublime intentions—how could these be known by a neighbor? It is not for you... [to judge].
Who, then, shall record his legacy? For this reason, I have gathered various texts to compose this "Genealogy of the Patriarchal Teacher.

Zhiyi, courtesy name De’an, was surnamed Chen. He was a native of Huāróng County in Jīngzhōu (present-day Jīngmén Commandery). His father, Qǐzǔ, was a *sànqí* (attendant-at-large) under the Liáng dynasty and a Marquis of Kāiyáng County.
His mother was Xu. She conceived after dreaming that she had swallowed a white rat; on the night of the full term of her pregnancy, in her chamber...

The inner chambers were brightly illuminated. He intended to set out the sacrificial vessels and offerings as a celebration, but before the mats were spread, the fire was extinguished and the broth grew cold;
thus, the rites could not be completed. His eyes shone with double pupils, and his eyebrows were parted into eight colors—these are the auspicious marks of an emperor or king.

Although his parents concealed them, people already knew of them. Furthermore, he would naturally fold his hands in prayer when lying down and always face west when sitting. At the age of seven, he delighted in visiting monasteries. Under the protection of...
A monk orally transmitted the "Universal Gate" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* to him, and he mastered it after reciting it once.

On the fifteenth day, before a Buddhist image in Changsha Commandery, he vowed to become a śramaṇa to uphold the True Dharma. That night, he dreamed of an auspicious elephant entering through the window with its trunk and stroking his head three times.
Consequently, he grew deeply weary of the prison of domestic life and went to Faguoyuan Monastery in Xiangzhou to have his hair shaved under the monk Faxu. Soon thereafter...
He went to see Vinaya Master Huikuang, who was thoroughly proficient in the Vinaya-piṭaka. Continuing his journey, he visited Dashi at Mount Dasu in Guangzhou.
Upon seeing him, Dashì marveled, saying, "In the past, we heard the Lotus Sūtra together at Vulture Peak. Pursued by our karmic affinity from former lives, you have come here once more.

He then conferred upon him the Pu-xian (Samantabhadra) ritual arena and expounded for him the Four Practices of Peaceful Bliss (*catur-āśvāsa-caryā*). After seven days had passed, he recited the sūtra...

When the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* reached the "Past Deeds of Bhaiṣajyarāja" chapter, he attained a sudden and great awakening through the passage: "This is true diligence; this is called the true Dharma-offering to the Tathāgata.

He clearly illuminated the *Lotus Sūtra*, like the light of the sun reaching all myriad forms, and he thoroughly penetrated the characteristics of all dharmas, like a pure breeze wandering through the vast void.
He was about to certify his realization to his teacher when the teacher said: "It is not you who do not realize it; it is not I [who do not certify it]."

[The Master] did not recognize it. The samādhi he had entered was the preliminary skillful means (*pūrvayoga*) of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. The dhāraṇī he had manifested and maintained was the "Dhāraṇī of the Initial Turning.
From this day forward, even if there were thousands or tens of thousands of Dharma-preachers with texts, they could never exhaust your eloquence by searching for it;
you shall be the foremost among all who preach the Dharma. He once commanded [the Master] to lecture on his behalf, using his own hand...
Holding the wish-fulfilling gem, he sighed upon taking his seat, saying: "It may be said that the Dharma has been entrusted to a Dharma-minister; the Dharma-King has nothing more to do.
Thus, the path between teacher and disciple flourished, and their fame spread far and wide. Regarding the *Pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*, it is the turning from the provisional into emptiness.
Regarding the *Koṭīśata-sahasra-pratyāhāra-dhāraṇī*, it is the turning from emptiness out into the provisional. Regarding the *Dharma-nirghoṣa-upāya-dhāraṇī*, these two serve as...
Through these skillful means (*upāya*), one attains entry into the Middle Way, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

What is here called "the beginning" refers to the five stages (*pañca-varga*) and the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), which serve as the preliminary preparation (*pūrvopāya*) for ascending to the stages of abiding (*vihāra*), where true cultivation begins. Thus, the ten levels of faith constitute the preparatory stage.
When [Zhizhe] informed Master Si Da that he was about to depart, Si Da said: "You have a karmic affinity with the state of Chen; if you go, you will surely bring benefit."

His fame shone brightly. When he first entered the capital, he was invited by Shen Junli to reside at Waguan Temple (the temple’s name was Shengyuan; it was located west of the city, with its front overlooking the river and its rear perched upon lofty peaks.

It was an ancient site from the Liang dynasty, standing two thousand fifty feet high—the very place where, as Li Bai said, "the sun and moon hide behind its eaves and beams. It still existed during the time of the Prince of Li [Yang Guo]).

There, he first lectured on the wondrous meaning of the *Lotus Sūtra*, explaining the various sūtras of a lifetime according to the Five Periods and Eight Teachings. By imperial decree, the high officials were to suspend their court duties for one day to listen to the Dharma.

Thereafter, he lectured on the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* for the benefit of all students who came to him, and expounded the *Cidi Chanmen* (The Gate of Gradual Meditation) as an essential means for purifying the mind.
At times, he established a community of meditation practitioners at Lingyao Monastery; at times, he disseminated the teachings of *śamatha-vipaśyanā* on Mount Yuquan;

and at times, he lectured on the *Benevolent Kings Prajñā-pāramitā Sūtra* for the Emperor of the Chen dynasty, to whom the Emperor performed the ritual of three prostrations. Furthermore, he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon the Sovereign of the Sui dynasty, who...

He was bestowed with the title of "Wise One" (Zhìzhě). For over sixty years, he transformed and guided the seven assemblies across more than sixty prefectures; the benefits conferred were immeasurable.

However, as his followers became numerous while those who attained awakening remained few, he feared that this might instead hinder his own practice. In the ninth month of the seventh year of the Daye era, he ceased all worldly ties and sat in meditative retreat at Mount Tiantai to fulfill his long-held vows.
At times, upon Mount Huading, he subdued both the fierce and the mild demons, causing malevolent spirits to flee in disarray. Or...

He established a *fangsheng chi* (refuge for released creatures) at the bend of the sea, extending for three hundred *li*. At times, while he preached the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, the mountain valleys turned the color of lapis lazuli;
at other times, he heard a divine being announce that the temple was completed and designated it with the name Guoqing. These are but the broad outlines;
the details are preserved in separate biographies. One night, as he sat alone preaching the Dharma until dawn, Zhixi addressed him, saying, "I do not know what you saw last night."
For what reason? He replied: "A monk from India came and said to me: 'The karmic conditions are like firewood; the illuminating function is like fire; the auxiliary support is like wind.
When these three are complete, the path of transformation can finally proceed. At night on Mount Huading, he granted that we might influence one another."
Now my capacity for activity is nearly exhausted, and my auxiliary support has also ceased; therefore, I have come to inform you.

Furthermore, the Great Zen Master Si of Mount Nanyue and Zen Master Xi have instructed me to preach the Dharma, and they have also spoken on my behalf, saying that it has been a long time since we have looked toward one another across the Flower-Adorned World (Saha).
"When my time has come to an end, you should go; we shall see you off. I bowed twice and assented.

This was the manifestation of the signs of death. In the tenth month of that year, Emperor Yang sent an envoy to welcome him. Consequently, he followed the envoy to the Great Buddha statue at Shicheng.

There, manifesting illness, he said, "Shicheng is the western gate of Tiantai; this great Buddha is a sacred image destined to appear here. Since it is so auspicious, one should apply one's mind with utmost diligence for the last time. He then addressed Zhiyue, saying, "My life will end here."

Do not advance further. Take fragrant water to rinse your mouth and recite: the Ten Suchnesses, the Ten Realms, the Three Contemplations, the Fourfold Accommodation, the Four Noble Truths, the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination, and the Six Pāramitās. Each of these dharma-gates encompasses all dharmas;
they are all capable of penetrating the mind and reaching the Pool of Coolness. If one can, within the context of illness, master these various dharma-gates, this is the twenty-fifth [gate].

"A person may be entrusted with a hundred pieces of gold. To one who wished to offer him medicine, he replied: 'Can this medicine dispel illness and prolong life? Illness does not unite with the body;

what, then, would the medicine dispel? Life does not unite with the mind; what, then, would the medicine preserve? He then ordered [the man] to chant the title of the *Lotus Sūtra*, and then offered this praise:
'The Dharma-gate is the father and mother; wisdom and understanding arise from it. Its fundamental and manifest traces are vast and great, subtle and..."
How wondrous and unfathomable! Today, the chisel is laid aside and the strings are severed. After a short while, he was again ordered to chant the title of the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*.
He praised it, saying: "The forty-eight vows adorn the Pure Land; though the lotus ponds and jeweled trees are easy to reach, no one goes there.

Even when the signs of the fiery chariot appear, if one repents for a single thought, one may still attain rebirth—how much more so for those who cultivate the holy practices through the熏習 (*vāsanā*) of precepts and meditative concentration!"

"The power of the Way is truly not in vain. He further said, "A merchant entrusts gold to another; a physician departs leaving behind medicine. Although I am not quick-witted, this madman is pitiable.
He then orally transmitted the *Guanxin lun* (Treatise on Contemplating the Mind) and commanded Zhiyue to prepare a bed, facing east with his back toward the wall and facing west.
Zhi Lang asked, "I do not know at what stage he passed away, nor where he has gone. After we, his disciples, what lineage shall we look up to for veneration?"

He replied, "I do not lead a multitude; I have merely purified my six sense-faculties and sacrificed myself for others to the extent of the five stages of faith. He was asked, "From where were you born?

He said, "All my teachers and friends have come from the presence of Avalokiteśvara to welcome me. He was asked, "Who is it that one may take as a model and revere? He replied, "It is Avalokiteśvara."
The four *prātimokṣa* and three *samādhis* were present therein. Having finished speaking, he chanted the names of the Buddhas of the Western Quarter as if entering meditative concentration.
This was on the twenty-fourth day of the eleventh month in the seventeenth year of the Kaihuang era, the year of Ding-si.
His worldly age was sixty, and his monastic seniority (śrāmaṇeraka) was forty. The assembly welcomed his entire remains and buried them in the southwest corner of Fulong.
Emperor Wen dispatched an envoy with an imperial decree to enshrine his stupa; every year, an envoy was sent to open the stupa for offerings.
When Lu Zhengli arrived as the envoy, the entire body was no longer to be seen. Later, the King of Wuyue, Qian Zhongyi, posthumously conferred upon him the title Fakong.

Venerable Baojue was posthumously conferred the title of Great Master Linghui in the fifth month of the third year of the Qingyuan era (1197), at the request of the local governor of Jingmen Commandery (as recorded in the *Xingshuai zhi*). Regarding the teachings expounded by the Master, he did not rely on written texts or phrases;
