At seven years of age, he entered Cesheng Temple to become a disciple of Master Huizheng. He could memorize ten thousand words a day. II.
He received the ten precepts and attended upon the Venerable Zhiyi at Guangzhai Temple, where he deeply investigated the *guanmen* (contemplation gates) and repeatedly received his seal of approval.
Among his fellow disciples, he was foremost in wisdom and understanding; thus, he was able to compile the Master’s subtle words for circulation in later generations.

Indeed, the Venerable Zhiyi’s preaching was like clouds and rain, yet it was the Master alone who was able to fully comprehend and uphold it. He personally recorded the origins of these events, saying: "Fortunately..."

Ah, this consecration! Formerly, at Jianye, I first heard the scriptural text; subsequently, at Jiangling, I reverently received the Profound Meaning (*xuanyi*). Later, returning to Mount Tai, I encountered the Crane Forest (*helin*).

Traveling back and forth between Jingzhou and Yangzhou, the journey spanned nearly ten thousand *li*. Through piecing together what I had heard before and after, I have only just managed to hear it once.

Not only have I heard what I had not heard before, but even those who have heard it have not yet understood its unfolding and its contraction; my drilling and admiring [of these teachings] grow ever more profound.

Jue Jiangao deeply regretted that his karmic conditions were insufficient for a second or third encounter, leaving him with no ground upon which to seek further instruction—like a calf longing for its mother’s milk.

He repeatedly contemplated these words, fearing that if he were to fall away in the future, it would be a tragedy for his attainment of Nirvana. He clarified the text as if carving it into wood or stone;

whereas the current edition refers to "fields" or "villages," he followed the sacred scriptures to record and transmit them. Furthermore, he composed the *Profound Meaning of the Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*. From [this point]...

Preface: In the tenth month of the tenth year of the Daye era, I took up residence south of Mount Tiantai. Peering through the tube of a narrow view, I have ventured to provide an explanation of the meanings of the Great Master Zhiyi’s teachings.
Having encountered the end of the Sui dynasty, bandits and rebels roamed at will; the seas were turbulent and the mountains were desolate, leaving me without paper or brush anywhere.
He concealed his traces at Wozhou; beneath the shaded groves, he sat upon arrows. He scrutinized the sacred texts until his robes were worn out and his provisions exhausted;

he continued to plant millet and gather firewood, laboring with diligence both day and night for five years in total. On what day did he not face the threat of war and fire? Sustaining himself on vegetable food and water, with ice for a bed and clouds for a covering, he dwelt alone and solitary.
In his dreams, he drew forth his thoughts to unroll and unfold the scroll of the eternally abiding Dharma, thereby offering his repayment [to the Buddhas].
With his body and hands, he praised the Dharma of liberation, offering heartfelt gratitude from both mind and speech. In the second year of the Renshou era, he entered the capital by imperial decree;

throughout the nine months of summer, he propagated the teachings, and the ladies of the six palaces looked up to him with reverence. The Emperor dispatched an envoy to escort him back, bestowing upon him most generous gifts.
On the seventh day of the eighth month in the sixth year of the Zhenguan era, he passed away at Guoqing Temple at the age of seventy-two and with fifty-two years of ordination. At first...
He manifested illness, and a rare fragrance filled his chamber. As he approached the end of his life, he instructed his disciples, saying:

"The *Maitreya Sūtra* states that on the day the World-Honored One entered parinirvāṇa, various famous incenses were burned, and the smoke rose like clouds. You should burn much incense; I am about to depart.

He then set forth his final exhortations, the words and principles of which were so poignant and profound that all the disciples were moved to realization, none of whom failed to shed tears. Suddenly, he rose and joined his palms, as if [he were seeing something].

He was deeply revered. As he was about to pass away, he recited the names of the Four Holy Ones of the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) ten times each with his own mouth, and then suddenly departed this life.
Previously, in the first year of the Zhenguan era, his fellow student Zhi-xi had passed away and said at the moment of death: "I have been born in Tuṣita Heaven.
I see the rows of precious thrones of my former teacher [Zhiyi] all occupied by people; there is only one throne that is empty. A celestial being there said: "After a period of time..."
Six years later, the Dharma Master Youding came to ascend this seat. Calculating the years and deliberating on the period, he examined the records and found them to be unerring.

The *Fuxing* (Commentary on the Practice) states: "While the Great Master was alive, he constantly aspired to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven; yet at the time of his death, he said that Avalokiteśvara had come to welcome him.

One should know that in guiding beings, he adapted to their capacities and established his teachings in accordance with conditions; thus, one cannot apply a single standard. On the ninth day of this month, he was interred in the temple."

At Nanshan, in the past, when the Dharma Master Zhi was in the Chen dynasty, he wished to establish Guoqing Temple. He had already marked out the foundation and felled timber, yet his aspirations were not yet fulfilled.
He entrusted the Master with the task of construction, requesting that it be carried out according to the original design. At the beginning of the Daye era, Emperor Yang went on a southern tour.

Because the Buddhist temple had newly been completed, the Master went out of the mountains to welcome him. The Emperor granted him an audience and offered words of comfort; the Master’s responses were as swift as echoes, and the Emperor’s favor toward him grew even more profound. He then dispatched—
Zhang Qianwei, an Attendant Censor Extraordinary, escorted him back. The Emperor bestowed upon him three thousand rolls of silk and three hundred pieces of felt to provide a meal for the monks.

Upon the completion of the temple, he further embellished the buildings, creating a magnificent sight throughout the region west of the sea. The Master’s spiritual power was boundless; both the hidden and the manifest were transformed by his influence.
There was an elderly man who fell ill, and though treated with a hundred medicines, he could not be cured. His son prayed for salvation, and the Master burned incense and recited the Lotus Sūtra.
The patient was cured when the fragrance entered their nostrils. Le Anlingnan said, "Anzhou Creek is deep and the trees are dense;
the paths are impassable. The Master lingered there, cherishing its beauty, and looking back at it, he vowed, "If this place becomes level and open, I shall come here to preach the sutras.
Less than ten days had passed when white sand surged forth everywhere, as smooth as a jade mirror. He then preached the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra*.

He fulfilled his vow. One day, as he struck the bell to lecture on the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, pirates suddenly arrived. The monastics and laypeople were terrified and scattered, but the Master remained composed and unperturbed.
The ringleader, upon reaching the gate, instead beheld military banners gleaming in the sun; those bearing weapons stood over ten feet tall, fierce and spirited. The bandits fled in total disorder.
During his leisure from lecturing at Fulong, the Master gathered his disciples to pile stones and build a stupa, intending it as a memorial.
Two pieces were obtained to serve as the gate for the stupa. One named Guangying had previously transported a stone, which everyone suspected was too thick and large;

they were just about to seek another when the Master raised his staff and struck it, causing it to split instantly into two parts of equal thickness, which were used to fill the stupa’s doorway like a pair of matching seals.
Among the works authored by the Master were the *Nirvāṇa Xuán* in two fascicles and commentaries (*shū*) in ten fascicles. In the *Xuánwèn*, it says: "Since ancient times..."

Regarding the transmission and translation [of the scriptures]: among those who, like Master Kumārajīva, were destined for the world and attained the inner sanctum of his teaching, there was only Sengzhao.

When Sengzhao composed the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*, people of the world took such delight in its flavor that they could not put the volume down from their hands. How is this so? I answer: The eminent monks possessed such magnificent virtue that the sun and moon were held within their hearts.

Since I did not personally receive instruction from them, their gateway is difficult to perceive. However, when one composes a treatise, the discourse should be grand and not trivial; it is not merely a matter of three... [text fragment].

It is a treasury. Its discourse does not extend beyond the boundaries [of the provisional teachings]; it is neither the Separate nor the Perfect [teachings]. To return to the source and point toward the ultimate, one sees only the meaning of the Shared Teaching (Tongjiao).
Master Shi’s two-fascicle *Commentary on the Treatise on Contemplating the Mind* (*Guanshin lun shu*) was included by him in the *Suihan lu* (Catalogue Arranged by Case).

He further remarked that by examining its expositions, one knows it belongs to the stage of "Entering the Ranks" (*ru pinwei*). However, renowned scholars of Jiangzhe have occasionally doubted its authenticity. *The General Meaning of the Eight Teachings*, Part One.
*Fajie cuan* (Collection of the Dharma Realm), five volumes; *Guoqing bailu* (The Hundred Records of Guoqing), five volumes; *Zhizhe biezhuan* (A Separate Biography of Zhizhe), one volume.

Other works for which the original manuscripts were missing cannot be recorded in full here. The Dharma was entrusted to Zhiwei. The King of Wuyue posthumously conferred upon him the title "Venerable Total-Mastery" (*Zongchi*).

The eulogy by Gushan states: "He could speak at three months of age; he left home at an early age. With his staff he struck and split stone; his words caused white sand to gush forth. Incense flowed to heal the sick; the bell was struck..."
He crushed heterodoxy. What Zhixi observed was verified without error. Chunzhi praised him, saying: "In the Buddha’s world, Ānanda was the most learned and honored;
in the Tiantai school, Zhanran possessed a prodigious memory, while Zhizhe was as eloquent as a surging river. His Dharma-son [Zhixu] held all teachings like the ocean receives its tributaries.

He maintained a vegetarian diet and water-abstinence while compiling the Great Teachings; he used an ice-sled and snow-blanket to expound the Heroic Sūtras during times of turmoil. Thus, amidst chaos, he convened the council.
It was through the most arduous toil that this was achieved; how could it be easy for later generations to receive its bounty?
Attached [is the record of] my younger brother, Dharma Master Puming, surnamed Zhu. A native of Kuaiji, from his youth he set his resolve apart from ordinary children. He gathered sand...

To perform meritorious deeds, he cut *haomao* grass to construct a temple and stupa. A monk who was begging for alms happened to say, "Since you already possess a virtuous nature, you should go to Mount Tiantai to leave the household life;
there, the Primordial Relying Bodhisattva manifests his body to preach the Dharma.

Consequently, in the fourteenth year of the Dajian era, he crossed mountains and overcame ridges to arrive at Mount Tiantai, arriving just as the Master of Wisdom (Zhiyi) was in the midst of a lecture before a seated assembly.
Once the assembly had dispersed, he prostrated at his feet and took refuge, vowing to remain as the master’s disciple for the remainder of this life.

The Wise One smiled and said, "Drawn by the牵引 (karmic attraction) of past conditions, we have now met. Thereupon, he served him with diligence, never flagging from morning until night, devoting himself exclusively to seeking the methods of dhyāna.

He practiced the Fangdeng Banzhou Guanyin Chanmo (the Vaipulya Pratyutpanna Samādhi and Avalokiteśvara Repentance) and recited one volume of the Lotus Sūtra. Although it was the midst of deep winter, he did not wear any cotton or flossed-down clothing;
he maintained rigorous discipline while practicing the Way. Seeing him, Master Sengyun said, "Your name is Fajing; it is not a particularly auspicious title. You should change it to Puming.

This name signifies 'Universal Radiance,' which illuminates and comprehends the three periods of time. When the repentance was completed, he informed Zhiyi of this. Zhiyi said, "Since you have attained clarity through the darkness..."
As indicated therein, it is appropriate to abandon the old and follow the new. The Wise One (Huiyuan) went to Yuquan and ordered the casting of a great bell for use at Fulong.
The monastics and laypeople of Jiangling vied with one another to manage the project. As the casting was about to begin, a blind man came to observe;

sensing that the omens were inauspicious, he felt the mold and found it cracked and broken. Consequently, they doubled the amount of earth and recast it, stipulating that those with incomplete limbs must not come. Thus, the bell was successfully produced with a resonant *keng*.
Xuan’s reputation resounded for seven thousand *li*. When he arrived at Guoqing Temple, obtaining water was quite difficult as the ground was full of gravel and stones.
He thought to himself, "If these stones could produce water, would that not be wonderful? As soon as he finished speaking, a spring gushed forth, providing for everyone near and far.
He once cast a sixteen-foot statue of Vairocana; moved by this, a mysterious person offered him gold. However, the lecture hall at Guoqing was narrow and small, and the Master wished—

He expanded upon this matter and discussed it with Zhang’an. Zhang’an advised him not to make the changes. Shortly thereafter, Zhou Xiaojie, the Prefectural Governor of Kuozhou, offered a cypress pillar and arrived by sea.
As Zhang’an was heading toward Chicheng, he saw the Master standing over ten *zhang* tall, towering above the treetops, accompanied by dozens of attendants.
The Master spoke to Zhang’an, saying, "Do not press your remonstrances; what he desires shall surely be accomplished. Thus spoke Zhang’an.
Moved by its spiritual wonders, he joined his palms toward the grove and said, "I dare not further remonstrate; I shall follow entirely according to your virtuous will.
On the day the hall was first constructed, it moved the Mountain King (Shanwang). At dawn, a profound resonance arose, appearing like the roll of thunder;

trees were uprooted and branches toppled over a distance of about one pace, extending from the foot of Fulong Hill all the way to the temple. By sunset, it returned to its original position with a loud clattering sound.
He struck [the meditation seat] with such force as if he had just arrived. The attendant of his room constantly heard him speaking, yet when he went secretly to observe, he saw no distinct form.
Listening to his words, they were solely exhortations to cultivate goodness. When his time was up, he manifested his passing; he changed his robes and entered nirvana. Two nights and one day passed.

He bent his left third finger. The Master did not keep private wealth; whatever offerings he received, he gave away immediately. He commissioned ten statues made of gold and copper and read the Tripitaka twice.
He performed acts of benefit with single-minded devotion, and gold and silk were spontaneously sent to him to provide for his livelihood.
Zhiyue was surnamed Zheng and was a native of Nanyang. While his father sought a marriage alliance for him, he vowed to renounce the world. His father complied with his wish.

Having shaved his hair, he traveled to various regions and encountered Zhiyi at Jinling, where he requested instruction from the Master as his teacher. Zhiyi transmitted the methods of Chan to him, and he attained a profound understanding of the Five Gates and Six Wondrous Principles.
He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* ten thousand times and became the foremost among the disciples. When Zhiyi withdrew to conceal his traces on Mount Tiantai, the fourfold assembly [followed him].

He was entrusted with this responsibility. For twenty years, he guided others with steady and skillful instruction, never failing the weighty trust placed in him; thus, he became the refuge for the two assemblies and the ancestral home to which the four divisions of the sangha returned.

On the anniversary of the death of the Venerable Zhiyi, the Emperor of Sui issued an edict to provide offerings for a thousand monks, and the Master further supplemented this with his own surplus funds.

When Empress Wenhuang passed away, a vegetarian feast was established, and his prayers were always efficacious. Yet, despite these honors, he never sought to remain permanently at the Imperial Palace.
On the twenty-third day of the eleventh month in the twelfth year of the Daye era, he manifested illness and passed away lying on his right side.
Mountains collapsed and the earth shook, as witnessed and heard by all. He was seventy-four years of age.
In the sixteenth year of the Kaihuang era, the Koryo monk Prajñā sought the methods of Chan at Fulong. Before long, he attained realization.
The Master of Wisdom (Zhiyi) said to him, "You have a karmic affinity with this place; you must dwell in a secluded and quiet location to accomplish sublime practice.
Six or seven *li* from here is the peak of Huading, which was the site of my former head-dhūta practices. Go there to study the Way and advance in your cultivation."
There will surely be profound benefit; do not worry about food or clothing. Since I received the instructions of the Way, my shadow has not left the mountains for sixteen years.
In the second month of the ninth year of the Daye era, I suddenly arrived at Guoqing on Fulong Mountain and secretly informed my virtuous friends that my life span was nearing its end.
He came to bid farewell to the assembly. After several days, he passed away without illness. When his coffin was carried out through the temple gate, it turned in a circle as a gesture of parting;
at that moment, his eyes opened, but they closed again upon reaching the mountain. All who witnessed this were moved to give rise to the aspiration for the Way.

In the seventh year of the Dajian era, Fahuan of Qinghe attended upon Zhiyi at Tiantai. Having received the transmission of *dhyāna*, he sat in silent meditation amidst the forest, never dwelling in a room.
He would sometimes emerge from meditative absorption only after seven days, reporting his realization to the Master.

The Master said, "This is the second stage of the *vipaśyanā* (contemplation) within the *pratisarga* (liberation). Mountain deities frequently harass and test you, yet you remain serene and unmoved. Great!
On the thirtieth day of the second month in the seventh year of the Jiande era, he passed away at Guoqing Temple at the age of sixty.

His secular surname was Gu, and his religious name was Dazhi; he was from Kuaiji. Having entered the monastic order, he served Zhizhe, who, upon seeing him, remarked that his physical form and spirit were refined and liberated.
He lived in high places above the world to establish his present name. He recited the *Sūtra of the Wondrous Dharma* with such profound stillness that his voice was clear and resonant;

those who listened forgot their fatigue. Furthermore, on Mount Lu, he practiced the "Ambrosia" (*amṛta*) and "Dhūta" (ascetic) disciplines. At times he threw himself before ferocious beasts, yet they would always avoid him.
When his store of grain was exhausted, he sustained his life solely on cakes and fruits. Thus for seven years, he never ceased his meditation and recitation.

During the Daye era, when Buddhism was suppressed, he lamented that the Great Dharma was declining. He subsequently donned mourning clothes and wept bitterly before the Buddha for three days, vowing to sacrifice his physical form to clarify and propagate the orthodox teaching.
He traveled to the Eastern Capital and submitted a memorial, saying: "I pray that Your Majesty will cause the Three Jewels to flourish.
This humble monk shall burn one of my arms at Mount Song to repay the grace of the state. The Emperor granted his request.

He then assembled the seven assemblies of the Sangha and prepared a great vegetarian feast. For three days he abstained from food; he then ascended a large wooden scaffold, wrapped his arms in cloth, and doused them with wax.

He set them ablaze like torches, and the light pierced through the crags and grottoes. Those who saw him were struck with grief that entered to the very marrow of their bones, yet his countenance remained unchanged.
Sometimes he recited the scriptures, sometimes he praised the virtues of the Buddha, and he preached the Dharma for the multitude with a voice that never ceased until the fire was extinguished.
He descended from the platform, sat in the full lotus posture, and entered meditative absorption. Seven days later, he passed away, leaving behind more than seventy sheets of his "Vow Text.
His intention was to serve as a spiritual friend to all sentient beings; those who read it were so moved that none failed to shed tears.

Zhi Zao of Linhai, surnamed Zhang, was seventeen years old when both his parents passed away. After he had completed the period of mourning, he contracted an illness that resisted medical treatment for a long time.
Thereupon, during a quiet night, he exerted himself despite his ailment to step out into the courtyard and lay down facing the moon, single-mindedly recollecting the Bodhisattva Candraprabha.
I only pray that Your Great Compassion may rescue me from this deep-seated illness. For ten days, I focused my mindfulness;
then, one night, I dreamed of a person whose form and color were extraordinary, coming from the east and saying to me, "I have come specifically to treat your illness.

He immediately brought his mouth to my body, sucking and rinsing it in succession for three nights. Because of this, I gradually recovered. I clearly realized that the Triple Gem is my refuge, and I took full reliance upon them.
At Anjing Temple, Li Huipei took [Huisi] as his teacher. Having heard that Zhiyi was a virtuous guide for the world, he submitted himself to him and requested instruction.

He was then sent to perform the *Lotus Sūtra* repentance ritual for two seven-day periods. On the first night, having completed the repentance, as he was about to sit upon his bed, he saw a nine-headed dragon emerge from the earth and ascend into the void.
The following morning, he reported this to Zhiyi, who said, "This signifies the Nine..."
He said, "When sentient beings hear the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, they will shatter the ground of ignorance and enter the emptiness of the Dharma-nature.
Furthermore, while he was practicing at Baolin Monastery, during his initial night of repentance, someone came and shook the door panels. Huizao asked, "Who is there?"

He replied immediately, "I am merely looking at the lamp. This was repeated several times. A virtuous monk named Hui Cheng, who resided in the monastery, heard this and said, "That hall has long been haunted by an evil spirit.
Now that it hears this sound, the ghost will seize a person. At dawn, Hui Cheng knocked on the door and called out, but there was no response.
He walked around the hall and lamented, "Alas, alas! That man is lost! Then Dao opened the door. Hui Cheng—
He said, "Are you still alive? I thought that last night my son had already killed you; that is why I lamented.

Cheng consulted with Prince Yongyang, who dispatched several dozen men armed with weapons to guard him. Baoyao said, "Life is determined by karma; how could protection possibly exert any influence over it?
I pray that you gentlemen will lead your troops back to the city. He then informed the Prince, and after the guards departed...
At night, ghosts entered the hall, pounding the walls and striking the pillars, roaming throughout the east and west.

Although there were six lamps within the hall, five were immediately extinguished, leaving only one for the practitioner to sit in meditation and recite the sutras; yet he remained calm and fearless. This continued in this manner until the twenty-first day.
When the ritual was about to conclude, he saw a youth in blue robes who praised him, saying, "Excellent! Having spoken, he vanished. He once went to attend a gathering.
I prostrate. On his route through Shanxi at Li Xing Village, he begged for food. The host inadvertently served him poisonous mushrooms; having finished eating, he continued on his way.
When the host ate the remainder, they all vomited and suffered diarrhea, nearly dying. A neighbor brought medicine to pursue the Master, reaching him only after ten *li*.
The Master hurried to him and found he was unharmed. He asked, "For what reason have you come to seek me? [The monk] related the preceding events in detail.

The Master smiled and said, "I have no other ailment. You may discard your medicine and return; for the power of the Way has permeated me, and the poison could not harm me. This was in the first year of the Daye era.
When the Emperor traveled to Jiangdu, [Zhizhe] was sent by the command of the presiding monk to attend an audience in the inner palace.
Upon seeing him from afar, the Emperor rose from his seat to bid him sit. He then dispatched the Palace Attendant Lu Zhengfang to escort him back.

For the sake of Zhizhe, he hosted a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks, ordained forty-nine men into the monastic order, and bestowed upon the temple two thousand bolts of silk, three thousand bushels of rice, along with incense, clarified butter, and other offerings.

Furthermore, he constructed earthen walls on four sides for a period of six years. He traveled to Yangzhou to pay his respects [to Zhiyi], who dispatched Xu Gongyuan, a Palace Attendant and Vice Minister, to escort him back.

For the sake of Zhizhe, he hosted a vegetarian feast for a thousand monks, ordained one hundred people into the monastic order, and bestowed one thousand bolts of temple property, along with one bolt of silk as a donation for each monk.
He visited him nine times in total. He passed away in the twelfth year of the Zhenguan era.
Zhi Xi of Yingchuan was surnamed Chen. His ancestors had resided in Min and Yue due to official postings. From childhood, he harbored a desire for renunciation from worldly life.
At the age of twenty, he joined Zhi Zhe to leave the household life and receive full ordination. He applied himself to the practice of *dhyāna* with the urgency of one whose hair is on fire.

Residing at Fulong, he constructed a majestic and orderly complex; however, only the Sūtra Terrace remained unfinished. On Mount Xianglu, there were many *cinnamomum* and cypress trees, which were occupied by a deity whom no one dared to approach.

He looked askance at them. They all requested that the Master cut them down. The Master said, "I fear the mountain deities protect and cherish them; we must not act rashly. Later, he dreamed that wood from Xianglu Peak was being delivered to him.
Once he had finished using it for his construction projects, he then took [the remaining trees] and used them; their dimensions were perfectly suited for his needs, with nothing lacking.

Previously, Zhiyi had made an agreement with the residents along the river to donate the area for the release of living beings and to forever cease all hunting and fishing. This remained so for many years.
As they drifted further away, they again established the altar on the bank and paid homage to the stupa of Zhiyi (Zhìzhě) with Master Li. They burned incense and offered prayers.
Shortly thereafter, a fisherman saw them standing upon the bank; thinking they were drifting with the current, he called for a boat to go and rescue them, but by then they had already vanished.

As this news was passed from one person to another, people reformed their evil ways and followed the good, ceasing their fishing and hunting. The monk Fayun (Fǎyún) then intended to travel to Xianglufeng (Incense Burner Peak) to practice meditation.
As he sat, the Master admonished him, saying, "That mountain deity is fierce and violent, while your power of the Way is weak. Be careful not to go.

Yun did not follow this advice, and after traveling for one night, the deity immediately manifested his form and drove Yun back. After Yun had explained his intentions, the deity conceived a deep sense of reverence and admiration.
Suddenly, the bronze bell of Dongshan resounded, shaking the mountains and valleys. The Master said, "This is calling for me. Prepare a bath of fragrant water for me."
On the seventeenth night of the twelfth month, he sat in the lotus posture and preached the Dharma while holding his *cintāmaṇi*.

He then immediately became silent. The assembly wept incessantly. He opened his eyes again and admonished them, saying: "All that is born must perish; such is the nature of worldly phenomena. Is this truly cause for sorrow? Now I depart from you;
do not disturb my mind. He further said: "I have practiced meditation for nearly fifty years; I have not betrayed the trust [of the Sangha]."

Practice giving! You should exert yourself and do not let your time pass in vain. When asked about his place of rebirth, he replied: "According to my dream, my report is that I shall be reborn in Tuṣita.
The palace is blue in color and is located to the northwest of the heavens. I saw my former teacher there;
all those attending him were seated upon jeweled thrones, with only one throne empty. When I inquired why this was so, he replied: 'Six years hence, you shall receive the empowerment (abhiṣeka).'"
When he was about to ascend [to his deathbed] to preach the Dharma, on the morning of the eighteenth day, he said to his disciples: "Prepare yourselves for the early meal; my life will not last long.

A layperson climbed the mountain to inquire after his illness; when the meal was finished, the man took his leave to return. The Master, mindful that he had come from afar, tried to detain him earnestly, but could not keep him.

He said, "Since you will not stay long, you must depart quickly; it will surely rain. At that time, the bright sun was shining in the sky, entirely free from clouds. Yet, shortly thereafter, a torrential rain poured down.
When the sun reached its zenith at midday, he passed away while sitting in the lotus posture. Everyone heard the sound of stringed instruments and pipes in the air.
His remains were enshrined in a stūpa two hundred paces in front of the stūpa of Zhizhe. He was seventy-two years of age. Initially, the Master paid his respects...
He prostrated eighty-four thousand times before the Jewel Stūpa of King Aśoka and circumambulated it several thousand times. He was moved by a purple-textured mark appearing on his right arm;
it was square, bright, and remained visible for the rest of his life. As he approached his death, he told his disciples: "The various sages have sealed me—how could this be in vain?
It is certain that I shall be reborn in the Inner Court."

Fuyang et al., disciples of the Sūn clan who relied upon the Great Master (Zhizhe), requested that he expound the Mahāyāna teachings at Fayin Temple in Yuhang during the twelfth month of the ninth year of the Zhenguan era.
On the first day of the new year in the tenth year, the deity of Gaoting Temple requested to receive the Bodhisattva Precepts, stating:
"When the Meditation Master passed through the temple grounds, your disciple was away on a journey; for this reason, we now [make this request]."

A person came from afar seeking a master to bestow the precepts upon him. The master immediately prepared an incense burner and lit the incense, saying, "I shall receive the Bodhisattva precepts for you, my patron.
Once the deity had received the precepts, he took his leave. At midnight the following day, [the patron] burned incense, shaved his head, bathed, and put on new, clean robes.
Facing west, he sat in the lotus posture and recited the names of Amitābha, Avalokiteśvara, Mahāsthāmaprāpta, and Zhiyi (the Wise One) for the sake of Huifa.
The Master explained the meaning of the Three Contemplations (*sanguan*), saying: "This was received directly from the Great Master’s own lips. Having finished speaking, he passed away.

Thousands of miles away, my heart feels a vast distance from the Way. From this point on, we have become newly parted; it seems as though we are separated by the vicissitudes of life.

Having attained the essential meaning and explored profound stillness, I have no mind to compete for profit or fame. As the autumn night deepens within my thatched cottage, who will accompany me in the sound of reciting the sutras? (A further eulogy follows.)
He was not born apart from the three realms. Our Great Master possessed the extraordinary mark of the white tuft between his brows and the wondrous appearance of a full moon.

His pearl of precepts shone everywhere; his ocean of wisdom was boundless. He was a mass of merit for humans and devas; all gazed upon him with reverence. Thereupon, both monastics and laypeople were drawn to him in devotion and requested that he remain as their refuge.
The Master said, "This was not my original intention. The multitude replied, "Whether by restraining him as a nun or by compelling him to stay, it shall not be against our will, O Disciple."
[The Emperor] said, "Why must it be Koryo to benefit living beings? The Master replied, "The conditions have already matured; you should go yourself.
Though [the Emperor] declined, he could not refuse him, and so the Master stayed. The Transport Commissioner Gu Chenghui donated his residence to establish the Chuanjiao Monastery.
During the Taiping Xingguo era, it was renamed Baoyun to manifest its auspiciousness. Since the Master’s arrival, two cycles of twelve years had passed; Zhi Li and Zun Shi were [his disciples].
He was the foremost among the disciples. Those who ascended to the hall or reached the gate [of his teachings] were beyond counting. His writings were numerous;

however, only the titles of the *Sūtra on Contemplation* Commentary (*Guan jing shu ji*) and the *Wondrous Praise of the Light* (*Guangming xuanzan shi*) remain. He lived to the age of sixty-two during the first year of the Duan-gong era.
On the eighteenth day of the tenth month, he manifested illness. Three days later, he passed away reclining on his right side.
After his cremation, his disciples collected the remains and enshrined them in the northwest corner of the monastery at Mount Yuyang.

Seventy-seven years later, the Master Zongzheng, the Dharma Master Wenhui of Yanqing, seeing that the brick enclosure was about to fall into ruin, piled up stones to construct a square mound for it and erected a stele.
As for the matter: before long, the monastery’s entrance was altered, and the stupa was likewise destroyed.

In the seventh month of the Dingwei year of the Xuanhua era, Dongzhi from Chang requested that the monk Ruowen of Mount Wushan provide a record of the relocation of the remains for the sake of future generations.
The inscription briefly states: "Within the sunlight, his bones appeared sometimes blue, sometimes yellow, sometimes red, or white. They grew...
It grew upon the bones. All who saw it were filled with joy, prostrated themselves, and marveled at such an unprecedented occurrence.
In the *gengchen* year of the Xiangshu era, the abbot of the monastery, the monk Zhiquan, once again carved the inscription for the stupa and the poems and eulogies of the King of Wuyue.

He commissioned artisans to fashion a seated statue and renovated the bone stupa. During the Chunxi era, the presiding monk Zongying further established the Zhenzu Hall (Hall of the Patriarchs) along the eastern corridor.

He painted portraits of the four patriarchs (the Wise One [Zhiyi], Tianming, India, and Zhili). Both Weihe and Wang Shihao praised them with verses. The Master’s eulogy runs briefly as follows: "The lineage descended from Mount Tai;
the succession was maintained through times of rise and fall. There were two possessing divine feet—true sons of the Lion King. Ciyun and Fazhi harmonized like the *xuan* and *chi* flutes.
All men say that the Master harbored brilliance and nurtured excellence; his roots were firmly planted, standing alone as a single trunk."
*Shuangzhi*. According to the *Caʼan Jiaoyuan Yishi* (Remnants of the Teaching Garden at Caʼan): "At that time, as the Tiantai Way had become attenuated, it relied upon the Master to sustain it.

He transmitted the Dharma to Fazhi and Ciyun, thereby establishing the school once again. This is what is called the life-vein of the Tiantai sect. The Master preferred to address people by their place of origin;
thus, those of the Shanjia school today are all referred to as "Tongxiangren" (People of Tongxiang). — *Guanzhuan'an* (Observations from Zhuan’an).
The Eulogy says: To call all people "countrymen" is like cold clouds clearing away lightning or withered wood sprouting spring.
It is through the power of his resolute vow that he has returned; I take refuge in him, the reincarnation of Tiantai. Zongyuan’s Record states: "I have previously investigated his life and deeds."
There was no one at all who could distinguish between its large and small features. By the time it reached Baoyun Monastery, there remained only a single portrait hall;

it was merely handed down by tradition that between his two eyebrows, the white tuft of hair (ūrṇā-kośa) would extend to a length of five or six feet when unfurled, and be retracted within them when rolled up.
He was truly a great being among the Sangha. Later, the monk Zongxiao of Yinqu compiled the Master’s life and deeds and inscribed them upon a stele.
I have further compiled these into a separate collection titled *Baoyun Zhenzu* (The Resounding Ancestors of Baoyun), which follows the *Jiaoxing Lu* (Records of Teaching and Practice) of Siming.
Thus, the words and deeds of Master Tong may be examined in detail.
Regarding the ancestral lineage of the Great Master Fazhi, the Restorer of the Teaching and Contemplation:
originally, the two disciples who emerged from Baoyun were roughly equal in their understanding and practice;

yet, it was only Siming who earned the title of "Restorer of the Patriarchal School" because his merit in propagating and protecting the Dharma was profound. Had he not been so exceptional, the humble lanes would have remained but a mere record.
He was attached to his friends; yet, out of reverence for Zhanran alone, he carried rice on his back. He held the authority to ward off insults;
for when one person is respectfully served, ten million people will all be respectfully served. "There is no second moon in heaven; in the human world there is but one monk"—whose verse is this?
Once Zhāng'ān had passed away, Jīngxī followed in his footsteps. When Zhāng'ān was gone, Jīngxī died next; this man succeeded to the former's teachings and emulated the latter's legacy.

The light of the Great Teaching of one family has reached its zenith through these three virtuous men; whose words are these? [This concludes] the second record, the Genealogy of the Dharma-Wisdom (Dharmajñāna) Family of the Patriarch.
Zhili, courtesy name Yuoyan, surnamed Jin, was a native of Siming. Initially, his father Jing’s lineage had no heir, and his sincere resolve...
He was deeply devoted [to the Dharma] and prayed to the Buddha with his wife, Li. One night, he happened to dream that a Brahman monk gave him a son, saying, "This is Rāhula.
When the Master was born in the year of Jiǎng-gēngshēn, they named him Rāhula, the Son of the Buddha. His spirit was pure and his countenance bright; his physical bearing was extraordinary.
Even while still a young child, he did not conform to the ways of the common crowd. At the age of seven, he encountered the death of his mother and wailed in mourning.

He did not cease his efforts, for he felt that the toil of filial duty was difficult to repay; thus, he became urgent in seeking ordination. His father patted him in approval and marveled at him, and did not thwart his resolve.
He first served Master Hongxuan of Taiping Xingguo Temple as his preceptor. At fifteen, he received full ordination and immediately began to investigate the Vinaya section.
At twenty, he studied the Tiantai teachings under Master Zibao Yun, becoming a member of the assembly. Only three days had passed when the First Seat said to him:

Regarding the *Dharmadhātu-krama* (The Sequence of the Dharma Realm), when he was about to uphold it (*Dharmadhātu-krama*, Volume Three, for the instruction of beginners), his teacher asked, "What is meant by the 'Dharma Realm'?
Zuo replied, "It is that which is the perfect fusion and non-obstruction of the great universal characteristics of the Dharma-gate.

The teacher said, "Since it is perfectly fused and unobstructed, how can there be a sequence? Zuo remained silent. After nearly a month, he began to lecture on the *Heart Sūtra* himself; everyone [was amazed].

Upon hearing this, he was struck with awe and spread the news far and wide, saying that the Dharma teachings were now truly dependent upon him. After two years had passed, his father dreamed that Zhizheng was kneeling before Zhizhong;
Zhizhong held a water jar and poured its contents into the Master’s mouth. The flow was like a spring, and the receiving was like a valley.

From that time on, he attained a transcendent realization of the Perfect and Sudden teachings and contemplations (*yuan-dun jiao-guan*). He immediately took over from Zhizhong to lecture and teach. This continued for several years until he encountered Zhizhong [who passed away].
He returned to stillness. Furthermore, he dreamed that his own head was pierced through and fastened upon his left arm as he walked. Ciyun explained this, saying:
"Does this not signify, at the beginning, the reception of training—just as Ānanda poured water from one vessel into another without distinction?

And at the end, it signifies the transmission and upholding of the Master’s *jñāna* (primordial wisdom), walking for the sake of transformation with his head as the foremost. From this, he gave rise to great diligence and became endowed with great wisdom.
He remained at ease in the open air, his brilliance illuminating the heavens. Whenever he engaged with a single disciple, they would surely say he had "ascended the dragon";
whenever he resolved a point of doctrine, the assembly would surely say he had "subdued the deer. Thus, though he did not seek to propagate the Way, it was heard throughout the four quarters;

though the multitude did not wait for an invitation, they came from a thousand *li* away of their own accord. During the Chunhua era, he accepted an invitation to Chengtian Monastery in his native commandery, where he stayed for four years before being transferred.

At Yanqing Monastery, he devoted himself exclusively to lecturing and repentance rituals. For over forty years, he never for a single moment departed from the offerings of incense and lamps, nor did he ever for a single night cling to the warmth of his bedding.

He even offered the front and rear courtyards of this monastery—where the abbots had resided—to the Master, so that it might forever serve as a residence for the ten directions and become a center for the transmission and propagation of the Tiantai teachings.

The Dharma is for the purpose of settling the community and cultivating the Way. Because the master’s dwelling was dilapidated and ruined, he commissioned the Tiantai monk Jueyuan to solicit donations for its reconstruction.
Once all matters were fully prepared, the master grew deeply apprehensive that his life would not last long and that the project might otherwise fall into disarray;

thus, he entrusted it to future worthies, stipulating that only those who excel in succession should reside there, rather than confining it to his own descendants. He subsequently composed a covenant of precepts to ensure this.
In response, he instructed his disciples, including Li Cheng and others, composing two chapters: "The Precepts" and "The Vow. The precept text states in brief:

"Moreover, regarding the regulations established by our Great Master Śākyamuni, as you have heard: there is the three-month summer retreat (*varṣā*), the eight impurities, and the prohibition against maintaining children or grandchildren.

One’s vocation is not that of a layperson. How, then, should one understand to whom the four requisites were originally intended to be given? If one clearly understands this, one does not violate the scriptures."

If one violates the precepts, one will incur evil retribution in the present and be consumed by fire in the future. How much more so for me, who initially received this dwelling with a mind directed toward the ten directions;
yet, upon its renovation, I have established these buildings specifically for the purpose of gathering students—how could I dare to treat them as my own private property? Furthermore, it is said:

"However, in our school, there are those who possess five virtues; regardless of whether they are near or far, I shall appoint them to reside here. Subsequently, all the deliberations were in agreement. The first was:

to have studied the Tiantai teachings from the outset and not to engage in concurrent lecturing on other subjects. The second was: to investigate with refined precision and profound reflection, remaining distant from superficiality and falsehood.

The third was: to have a reputation for the virtue of the precepts, rectifying oneself while dealing with others. The fourth was: to be able to distance oneself from honor and fame, never bowing down to them.

My Way has five aspects: first, the excellence of both rhetoric and discernment; second, being quick in encouraging and guiding others. Why is this? If one merely lectures on everything, they will stray from what I have illuminated;
if one is frivolous and hypocritical, they will mislead those who follow their teachings. If one maintains the virtue of the precepts, they will bring glory to their transformative guidance;

if one enjoys a wide reputation, they will consolidate their supreme achievement. Only then can one use discernment to clarify the meaning and use guidance to win over people. Furthermore, it is said: "If you still do not fear my words..."

"I have made a vow. The divine spirits shall witness it; may calamities and blessings not be granted in error. You must be cautious! The brief words of the oath state: 'I humbly consider that since the Tathāgata manifested his signs, he has long resided upon Vulture Peak;
since Sudatta turned his heart toward the Dharma, the site was first established at Jeta’s Grove. When the Brahma King offered his palace, he invited [the Buddha] to preach the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa*;
when the chamber for the sick was established, profound discourse arose. As for the maintenance and upholding of the True Dharma, all these matters depend [upon us].'"
Regarding the stupas and temples, the succession of the Four Reliances has continued their legacy, all clearly manifesting where they dwell.

Since the Dharma texts are proclaimed by people, people must necessarily rely upon a place. Although this site is situated within a village, it is much like a mountain forest; to the west it reflects the light of the lake, and to the east it connects with the colors of the wilds.

The buildings extend far and wide, providing a sufficient refuge for habitation. After [the Master’s] passing, a hall was constructed here to propagate the Dharma in this degenerate age; thus, the *Sūryagarbha-sūtra* describes it as a place where the Tathāgata wanders.
Cease. The *Lotus Sūtra* states that this is the Buddha’s enjoyment realm. Now, in this humble chamber, I shall forever contemplate the penetration of the scriptures.

Looking up to all Buddhas, may they look upon me with compassion and the Four Reliances; may they take pity and accept me, so that this vulgar and lowly person may naturally become adorned, eternally dwelling in the perpetual radiance, and find peace in the future.
May the Way flourish within the inner court, and transformation spread throughout the City of Fragrance. May I always encounter good teachers and gather wise students from afar, spreading like stars.
The Dharma-torch shines universally throughout the ten directions; the transmission of the fundamental vehicle spreads continuously across the three periods of time.

May the Emperor’s longevity be uninterrupted and his wondrous lineage flourish ever more. Should there arise in the future wicked factions or malevolent hordes who, by seizing special privileges and forming cliques, commit acts of arbitrary extortion and plunder, abolish the propagation of Prajñā, or obstruct the practice of the Way—I have already offered this place to the Triple Gem, looking up to them in reverence.

[He] transmits [this teaching]. Such a person thereby uses divination to usurp the place where the Buddha’s enjoyments are received; it is also the destruction of the place where the Wheel of Dharma is turned;

it is also the sowing of discord within the harmonious community of trainees. This person shall bring about the extinction of the Triple Gem and commit the most grievous sin of severing the study of Prajñā.
One should wish: "If my followers or even others should intend to seize and occupy my [place]..."
Regarding those who transmit the Dharma: if they move their minds, they shall immediately fall into madness and delusion; if they move their mouths, they shall lose their voices and remain mute;
if they move their hands or bodies, they shall be seized by wind-disorders, or suffer from burns and gangrene, or be harmed by venomous snakes, vipers, scorpions, and all such creatures.
They shall endure every affliction, including malignant sores and pus, blindness, deafness, muteness, and the loss or mutilation of limbs—every manner of calamity—until their very lives end.

In the end, one shall fall into the Avīci Hell; as the world undergoes formation and destruction, one shall be reborn there again and again, with no time of escape. The remaining retribution in the future shall be twice that of the preceding kalpas.
It would be better to let my life be ruined, it would be better to have my life cut short, it would be better to have my eyes destroyed, than to have my physical form and life destroyed.
I shall never cast a spell to cause this person to encounter such sufferings.

To destroy my abode would be to sever the roots of merit and the lineage of *prajñā*—the bodhi of myself and all sentient beings—and it would likewise sever the wise ones' teaching on the contemplation of the life-span.

Furthermore, they extinguish the power of the Tathāgata’s remaining transformation. To state it briefly, they destroy the life-span of the Triple Gem throughout the ten directions and the three periods of time, and they destroy the eye of the True Dharma.
They open the gates to the three evil realms for all sentient beings and close the path to nirvāṇa for all humans and devas.
The retribution for this person’s sins is inconceivable. We look up with aspiration to all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
The devas, nāgas, and spirits shall protect this person, preventing them from giving rise to such an evil thought for even a single moment, let alone allowing it to reach the point of destruction.
During the early Jingde era, there were two versions of the *Guangming xuanyi*—an extensive and an abbreviated one—circulating in the world.

At that time, Master Ciguang En composed the *Fahui ji* (Record of Elucidation) to explain the abbreviated version, stating therein that the extensive version contained ten sections on the contemplation of the mind (*guanxin*) and so forth.
[This] preface was likely added by later generations, who then proceeded to critique [the text] based on four alleged errors.
Furthermore, its two disciples, Masters Qing and Min, jointly composed difficult arguments to support their position, desiring to abolish the "Extended Version" (Guǎngběn).

When Bǎoshān Xìn sent a letter requesting the Master to adjudicate the matter, the Master said: "To judge what is right and wrong approaches the nature of contentious debate; this is not my intention. Moreover, these two gentlemen are..."
"Our school has had predecessors in this; you should not reject it so hastily. Xinxing made a sincere and repeated request, saying, "The Dharma-drums are sounding in competition;
which shall take precedence and which shall follow? The Master yielded out of deference but could not decline, and thus composed the *Fuzong shinan* (Rescuing the School and Dispelling Difficulties).

In it, he strove to rescue the texts of the *Shifa guanxin* (Contemplating the Mind through the Ten Dharmas) in its expanded version and others, while refuting the errors of those who fail to understand the "setting forth the movement" (*fayun*) and the "discrimination of objects" (*jianjing*), as well as the "contemplation that traverses the dharmas" (*guancheng lili fa*).

The Qing disciple Fǎtiān Zhāo and Gūshān Yuán further composed the *Biàn'ébó* (Discriminating Errors) and the *Bōshì nán* (Refuting and Resolving Difficulties). These were not merely attempts at rescue or exaltation;
rather, the two schools engaged in a series of exchanges, formulating arguments and posing challenges back and forth for five [periods] over the course of seven years.
Yet [the debate] was not yet concluded. The Master dispatched his disciple Benru to engage him in discussion; in the end, Benru’s arguments were able to prevail.
Subsequently, the Master’s dharma-grandson Jizhong compiled the preceding and following ten rounds of discourse and titled them the *Ten Treatises on the Meanings* (*Shiyi shu*).

Furthermore, such works as the *Sānqiānjùzào dìngjìng liǎofǎ yòngguān* (The Contemplation of the Realization of Dharma-Function through the Three Thousandfold World) serve as true guides for later students.

Indeed, the Way of the Tiantai and Huayan schools was on the verge of becoming extinguished like cold ashes; that it was revived by this Master is nothing short of a feat of turning back heaven itself.
While he was at Yanqing Temple, he practiced the Samādhi of Constant Practice within the Qixin Hall for a period of ninety days.
The area where he had circumambulated became marked by the tracks of a chariot wheel. During the military fires of the Jianyan era, these traces were obliterated;
those who hear the words of the elder monks can do nothing but increase their sense of poignant regret. In the third year of the Xianping era, there was a great drought.

The Master, together with the two masters Wen-shi and [the other], jointly performed the *Guangming* Repentance to pray for rain. When after three days there was still no response, they then removed [the altar].
They prostrated themselves on the ground and made a vow before the Supreme Deity, saying:

"If the Buddhist rites are about to be completed and we do not receive a descent of sweet rain, each of us shall burn off one hand as an offering to the Buddha. Before their repentance was finished, a heavy rain had already drenched the earth.

During the Tian-sheng era, when Duke Zeng Ru (Gongliang), the Xuanjing Gong, was attending upon the Duke of Chu, he was appointed to govern Siming. One day, while visiting Yanqing Temple, the Master...
Previously, a monastery deity had appeared in a dream and told him, "Tomorrow the Senior Official will arrive; you should prepare the rites to welcome him.
When the official arrived, the Master informed him of the dream, saying, "How could such a thing be? You should simply keep it in mind within your heart.

It was only upon his great prostrations that the official realized the Master’s dream was indeed true. Thereupon, he petitioned the court to grant land and construct a residence, whereupon the Dharma seat was grandly inaugurated.

Consequently, Yanqing became a monastery of great renown, and the temple also depicted his image and enshrined it there. At the beginning of the Tianxi era, when the Master was nearly [seventy] years old, he said to his disciples:
"To forget one's body for half a verse and to throw oneself into fire for a single phrase—such was the mind of the Sage for the sake of the Dharma.
How much more so now that the time since the Buddha has grown long and those who treat the Way with contempt are numerous; I cannot simply cast away my life."

If one allows indolence to arise through alarm, then the wind of courageous diligence will be lost. Thereupon, he restricted the number of monks to ten who entered into the practice of repentance, vowing to complete it in three years and then collectively cremate their own bodies.
He further declared: "I vow to offer this as a true Dharma-offering, while keeping the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) in my heart.

At that time, Yang Yi, a Hanlin Academician, admired the Master’s spiritual conduct and held him in high esteem upon hearing of his reputation; he devoted himself with great diligence to dispatching messengers on the postal relay system.
He earnestly entreated him to remain in the world and further raised objections based on the sentiments of joy and revulsion. The Master replied:
"Throughout the day one may shatter all forms, yet all dharmas are thereby established; throughout the day one may establish all dharmas, yet the dust of afflictions is thereby completely exhausted.
Realizing that he could neither be constrained by reason nor retained through words, Lord Yang wrote a letter to Ciyun of India, requesting him to travel from Hangzhou to [the capital].

Ming refuted his arguments. Furthermore, he sent a letter to Li Yigeng, the Prefectural Governor and Director of the History Bureau, secretly instructing the neighboring communities to provide universal protection so that [the pagoda] would not be permitted to be burned.

In the year of the Emperor Zhenzong’s birthday, Master Yang visited Chancellor Kou Qun and recommended [himself], whereupon the Master was honored with purple robes for his virtue. Subsequently, the Director of the Secretariat, Ma Zhijie, requested Yang—

Yang Gong composed a stele inscription for his late father’s spirit way (shendao). When offered a reward for his calligraphy (runbi), Yang Gong accepted none of it; he requested only that the Master be granted a posthumous title.

Consequently, Ma submitted a memorial to request an imperial decree to accept the reward. The Emperor immediately summoned Yang Gong to question him. Yang Gong then reported on the Master’s practice of casting off the body (yishen).
The Emperor deeply praised and sighed in admiration, and addressed Yang Gong with great earnestness, saying: "Simply convey my intention; I request you to retain [the reward]."
"If you remain in this world, I shall grant you a title as Master. You should not decline such an honor for the sake of refining my writing.
Thereupon, he specially conferred upon the Master the title of *Dharmajñāna* (Fazhi Dashi). Thus, the Master’s original vow was finally fulfilled.

The Emperor subsequently dispatched the eunuch Yu Yuanqing to travel far to the Master’s quarters, ordering him to perform repentance rites (*sānti*) and bestowing generous gifts. Yu wished to understand the essential meaning of these repentance rites.

He then composed the *Essential Principles of Repentance*, which is now widely circulated in the world. The *Record of Remnants from the Garden of Teaching* states: "The Inner Secretary, Master Yang, was asked:
'To what kind of person does the Pure Land belong as its realm? and 'Are both the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* the teachings of Māra?
These were questions posed by using principle (*li*) to subvert phenomena (*shi*). The Master then [responded] with phenomena that are identical to principle."
He replied to him, saying: "There is no further principle beyond this very seeing and hearing. [The other] asked: "How far apart are Buddha and Māra?
Later, in his letter of thanks, the Master said: "Only the patriarchal style of Shaoshi is fundamentally the smiling gaze of Vulture Peak;
it extends to Huangbo’s severe blows upon Linji and Chuanzhi’s wielding of the oar before Jiashan. This was how the Master used Chan to resolve the matter.

[This was] the teaching. The Master [Zhaoqing] replied again, yet [the Japanese monk] did not at all grasp its meaning. Indeed, in the past, Chan and the Teachings (Dharma) consulted one another; however, this was not the case here.
Thus we know that the Great Master’s skillful means must possess its own inherent substance.
The Japanese National Teacher Enchin once dispatched his disciples Jikishō and others to carry twenty-seven questions to inquire about the essentials of the Dharma. The Master answered them.

All attained its wondrous essence. Later, Guǎngzhì succeeded him on the seat [of the Dharma]. He again dispatched two of his disciples, Shàoliáng and others, carrying a *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* written in golden characters as a formal gift of audience.
They wept with grief and paid their respects, requesting to study under his guidance for three years. Their realization of the Way was fully perfected.
Upon returning to their country, they widely propagated the Tiantai teachings. Duke Cèng erected a stele at his pagoda, which records these events in detail.
According to the *Jiaoxing lu*, there is further recorded a text titled "Answers to the Ten Questions from Japan. However, it is not known who the master of that country was.

When the Master was about to pass away, he again gathered ten monks to perform the Great Compassion Repentance for three years and the Guangming Repentance for seven days to mark the occasion of his peaceful extinction.
On the fifth day, he sat upright in the full lotus position and gave instructions to his disciples.
He said, "Birth must inevitably be followed by death; this is simply the constant law of nature. You all should diligently cultivate the Way without allowing for any interruption.
Following my instructions is equivalent to having me still alive. Having finished speaking, he suddenly recited the name of Amitābha Buddha several hundred times and passed away in an instant.
This was on the fifth day of the first month in the sixth year of the Tiānshèng era, at the hour of Wù (7–9 p.m.). He was sixty-nine years old, with fifty years of ordination seniority.
4. After being left in an open niche for fourteen days, his fingernails and hair had grown long, and his countenance appeared as if he were alive.
On the twenty-fourth day of that month, he was cremated outside the southern gate of the commandery. Prior to this, a rare and fragrant incense-like aroma had been perceived.

When the fire was extinguished, his tongue remained intact, and five-colored śarīras were found in numbers beyond counting. (Recorded on the twenty-ninth day of the seventh month in the second year of the Mingdao era.)

The sacred remains were enshrined in a stupa to the left of Chonghwamun Hermitage. To this day, there are still śarīra relics preserved within a lapis lazuli bottle, which are reverently installed atop the Daebigak Hall.
Among his disciples who ascended the hall, there were over a thousand; they penetrated the profound depths of his teachings and led their followers with great vigor.
These included Jeok-jeon, Gak-chong, Bon-nyo, Chong-gu, In-gak, Hye-tae, Bom-jin, and Sang-hyeon.
He had twenty such [senior] disciples, four hundred and seventy-eight disciples who received the Dharma from him, and seventy disciples whom he ordained with his own hands.
Zhao Qingxian (Yuan) composed a stele for his conduct, which is complete; the *Sanxue Lu* records his achievements in detail. The epitaph for his stupa by Secretary Hu (Fang) states briefly: "Alas!
When the Great Master appeared in this world, was it not for a purpose? Could it have been anything other than for the sake of Jetavana?"
The Dharma belongs to an age of decadence; did you, Master, establish and support it? When the teachings of Tiantai were being disseminated, did you, Master, cause them to flourish and shine?
There are carriages outside the gate, yet the sons of the house no longer mount them; did you, Master, cause them to mount them?
There is a pearl within one's garment, yet the intoxicated person does not realize it. Do you, O Master, cause them to awaken to it? Do you manifest a "city of transformation" on the perilous path?
Do you provide a "floating bag" upon the great ocean? Is this to repay the kindness of the Buddhas, or to act as an envoy of the Tathāgata?
This is not so. How could he have cultivated his mind toward the Way with such devotion and sacrificed himself for the sake of the assembly to such an extent?

However, the accounts currently presented regarding the eight kingdoms, Aśoka, and other matters are merely traces of the Tathāgata’s transformative manifestations. If these are to be judged according to the principles of the Tiantai teachings:

Thus, there are instances where the four teachings mutually possess or lack certain elements; where the *pariccheda-bhava* (segmented existence) and *parināma-vaśitā-bhava* (transformative existence) differ in their presence or absence;

and where the *janma-kāya* (birth-body) and *dharma-kāya* (truth-body) differ in their integrity or fragmentation. Students should further investigate these matters deeply: namely, that all four teachings may simultaneously exist, or that all four teachings may simultaneously be absent;

that the *zang* (Tripitaka) and *tong* (Shared) teachings may exist while the *bie* (Distinct) and *yuan* (Perfect) teachings are absent; that the *bie* and *yuan* teachings may exist while the *zang* and *tong* teachings are absent; and that while the *dharmatā* (nature of reality) is absent, the *pariccheda-bhava* exists.
There is also the case where [the relics] are entirely pulverized, and both [types] exist together. Regarding the existence of both in the four teachings, the *Miaoxuan* states:
"Entering parinirvāṇa beneath the twin trees, when the fuel is exhausted and the fire is extinguished, he leaves behind śarīra as a field of merit for all humans and devas.

This refers to the śarīra of the Universal Buddha (*sāmānya-buddha*). The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The Tathāgata accepted the offering of eight *hu* and four *dou* from the elder; having entered extinction, he left behind..."
The eight *hu* and four *dou* of śarīra refer to what is taught in the Tripitaka (Zang) school. If they exist in the Separate (Bie) and Perfect (Yuan) schools, this symbolizes permanence:

although the body has entered extinction, these śarīra are left behind to signify that it is not extinguished. As for their absence in all four teachings: [this refers to the case where none are present].

When the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings speak of "non-existence," this expresses the meaning that in these two teachings, [phenomena] are extinguished like ashes and do not arise again.

When the *Bie* (Distinct) and *Yuan* (Perfect) teachings speak of "non-existence," this expresses the meaning that in these two teachings, [the nature of reality] is eternally abiding and does not perish. Regarding the case where the *Zang* and *Tong* have "existence" while the *Bie* and *Yuan* have "non-existence": it is because the *Zang* and *Tong* truly possess arising and ceasing, they are said to have "existence.

It is because the *Bie* and *Yuan* do not discuss arising and ceasing, they are said to have "non-existence. Regarding the case where the *Bie* and *Yuan* have "existence" while the *Zang* and *Tong* have "non-existence": this refers to those of sharp faculties.
When Bodhisattvas receive the distinct or perfect [teachings] and perceive the existence of śarīra, they should instruct those Bodhisattvas of dull faculties who dwell in emptiness.

When they perceive no śarīra—since the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is non-existent, yet there is existence within the realm of segmented birth (*paricchinna-jāti*)—the capacity for response ceases and the manifestation should turn toward cessation.

Thus, one knows that the Dharmatā-kāya Buddha outside the realms does not exist; whereas as for those within the realms, since they possess bodies born of segmented birth and are subject to arising and ceasing, they do exist.
Regarding those that are entirely fragmented yet complete: these are like the whole-body *śarīra* of Prabhūtaratna and the fragmented-body *śarīra* of Śākyamuni.

Demolish monasteries and nunneries; dismiss monks and nuns to become commoners. Entrust bronze statues and the like to the Salt and Iron Commissioner to be melted down for coinage;
cast iron statues and the like into agricultural implements. Melt down gold and silver statues and deliver them to the Ministry of Revenue (Du-zhi) for distribution to the nobility and commoners.

All existing gold and silver statues must be surrendered to the authorities within one month; those who fail to comply shall be punished according to the law. This applies to both the two capitals and all [other regions].
Each prefecture along the roads maintained one temple. In the third month of the sixth year, the Emperor consumed gold elixir;
he suffered from feverish agitation and madness, unable to speak for ten days before his death. The high ministers welcomed the Imperial Uncle, King Gwang, and installed him on the throne;

he was Emperor Xuanzong. He changed the era name to Dazhong. In the fifth month, by imperial decree, eight additional Buddhist temples were established in each of the Left and Right Monastic Districts. Thus...
He executed twelve individuals, including the Daoist Liu Xuanjing, and arrested twenty-four others, including Zhao Guizhen and Deng Yuanqi, all of whom were charged with deluding the late Emperor.

Having long practiced this Way, our reforms have been excessive and the state of affairs has not yet flourished. if there are veteran and renowned monks capable of restoring and rebuilding them, [they shall be permitted to do so].
He was permitted to reside there as abbot, and no one was allowed to prohibit him. At that time, Shi [Dao]yi criticized him, saying:

In the third year of Taiping Xingguo of the Great Song Taizong Emperor, the King of Wuyue, Qian Zhongyi,
surrendered his territory and recommended the monastic leader Zan Ning, ordering him to escort the precious stupa containing the true-body relics to the imperial court.

Six years later, an imperial edict ordered Ning to compile the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song*. After some time, he was again appointed by edict as a compiler at the Historiographic Institute (*Shiguan*).
In the fourth year, the Tripiṭaka Master Tian Xizai translated the *Ratnarāja-sūtra* and other scriptures. In the eighth year, an edict was issued to ordain novice monks throughout the empire.

The origins of this lineage have already been made manifest through its accumulation; now, as the regions are extended and the teachings established, they serve to express our reverence and veneration.

It is decreed that all prefectures, provinces, armies, and surveillance stations throughout the empire shall establish halls for the Holy Ancestor (Shengzu) within the Tianqing Observatories, enshrining sacred images along with their attendants, and shall receive the ritual vessels and insignia from the Yuqing Zhaoying Palace.

Although the Imperial Court bestowed the title "Xianlie" (Manifest Valor) upon it, the Great Master Zhizhe alone had not yet received an honorary posthumous title. It has been observed that Zhizhe...
At the Daochang Temple, the temples of Lord Guan and his sons, as well as those of the Dragon King, have long been sites for prayers;
