I have observed that during last winter’s drought, General Gao Ziyong personally offered prayers at the temple, whereupon the auspicious omen of the "three whites" appeared.
Throughout the spring rains, the moisture was granted without fail, resulting in a bountiful harvest of silkworms and wheat. In the sixth month, however, a sudden and intense heat set in;

for several months there had been no rain, and the parched crops were on the verge of withering. The people were filled with anxiety. When our army again offered supplications as before, sweet rain descended immediately. Several...
The sun did not cease its course. My original army had selected the twelfth day of the ninth month for a grand review of over one thousand righteous volunteers and militia.
However, it coincided with days of continuous wind and rain, which hindered the training exercises. Furthermore, the late rice was still in the fields and had not yet been harvested;
there was fear that it might sprout anew. Upon learning this, High Ziyong, the Military Governor, personally visited the shrine, whereupon the skies immediately cleared.

The hearts of the people were greatly gladdened. It is known that this year the five grains have been harvested in double measure across all districts; this is truly due to manifest merit, the benefits of which reach the common people.

We request that the local authorities seek out and issue official notifications in accordance with the established regulations. Furthermore, the Qiang tribes of Fu Prefecture are to be entrusted to Jingling County.

The Secretary-General Jia’uo personally investigated the matter and learned that at the end of the fourth month in the third year of the Shaohui era, when the weather was dry and no rain had fallen, the commoners of Dangyang County, including Du Xing and others, came before the deity at Yuquan Temple to pray.
On the fifth day of the fifth month, heavy rain fell continuously, resulting in a bountiful harvest. This was commissioned by the Pacification Commandery of this circuit.
On the fifteenth day of the fifth month, Deng Jian, who was managing public affairs, personally visited the shrine to offer prayers.
As soon as he arrived and offered incense and the prayer text, a heavy rain fell immediately. On the following day, he again requested sacred water to take back for further supplication;

before they had even reached the borders of the prefecture, torrential rain poured down, ceasing only after three days. Furthermore, on the eighth day of the seventh month in the fifth year of the Shaohui era...

Knowing that during the summer months in Jingmen Commandery, Gao Ziyong observed a severe lack of rain, causing the fields to crack like tortoise shells, he commissioned Dong Junming, the Magistrate of Dangyang, to personally visit the spirit temple to offer prayers; immediately, the rains fell.
Throughout the four quarters, he obtained responsive manifestations; thus, the administration of his deeds was extended.

Consequently, a second memorial was submitted to Li Bisheng, the District Magistrate of Yidu County in Xiazhou, requesting that he personally go forth to verify the facts and confirm the existence of the aforementioned miraculous responses from the recent past.
It is hoped that Your Majesty will graciously bestow an imperial edict granting the title of Great Master Zhizhe to him. We humbly await the imperial decree. Hereafter—

The memorial was forwarded to the Ministry for investigation and reporting. The Shangshu Sheng (Ministry of State Affairs) subsequently issued a directive to the Taichang Si (Court of Imperial Sacrifices) to conduct an inquiry.

Upon receiving the report, [the Ministry] noted that according to the petition submitted by the military unit, they had prayed for snow during last winter’s drought; they prayed for rain during the parching heat of the sixth month;

they encountered wind and rain during the autumn maneuvers in the ninth month; and they prayed for clear weather before the late-ripening grain could be harvested. As for the officials tasked with this investigation:

Upon further investigation into the matter, none of the aforementioned items were found. However, it was reported that between the fourth month of the third year of the Shaoxi era and the seventh month of the fifth year of the Shaoxi era, there were responses to prayers for rain, all of which were consistent with previous records.

As these matters have not yet been adjudicated according to the provisions of the relevant statutes, we request that the local Circuit Transportation Commission be notified to report this to the Ministry. This Ministry has already... [omitted].
Aside from the previous submission to the Hubei Circuit Transport Commission, we have now received a report from Jingmen Commandery.
It has been recently verified that the title of "Great Master Lingji of Dahong Mountain in Suizhou, Jingxi Circuit" has already been upgraded to the eight-character posthumous title:
"Great Master Yuantong Yinggan Ciren Lingji. Our commandery was just about to submit a request to apply the same title to Great Master Zhizhe. Please grant this accordingly.
Regarding the posthumous titles conferred upon the Great Master Ji, this is a special case of imperial grace.

While the draft for the conferment was prepared, on the tenth day of the sixth month in the second year of the Qingyuan era, an imperial decree was issued to investigate the spirit shrines reported as having miraculous efficacy by various prefectures and counties across the circuits.

The relevant authorities, however, were constrained by minor formalities and had not yet fully completed the process of submitting the required reports. This delay over many months has resulted in a failure to fulfill the intent of bestowing honor and veneration. (5)

On the ninth day of the month, the Three Ministries jointly received a sacred edict ordering the Ministry of Rites and the Court of Imperial Sacrifices to immediately examine the relevant regulations and submit a proposal for swift implementation regarding those who have been recommended as having manifested spiritual efficacy within the Daoist and Buddhist traditions. Upon examination, it was found that the articles of the code indeed provide for such matters.
Regarding those marked with the plus sign (合), all shall be titled "Great Master" (大師). For each of the preceding two characters, add two more.
We hereby request that you examine our previous petition and graciously grant the posthumous title of "Great Master Zhizhe of Yuquan" in its entirety for implementation by this ministry.
This shall be further transmitted to Taitsi Temple to verify according to the regulations. Now, based on the report from Taichang Temple, which has been verified by the Hubei Transport Commission:
A memorial was submitted to the Great Master Zhizhe, requesting that his native temple be granted an official title.
At that time, it was observed that although the status of the Great Master Zhizhe was well-known through various scriptures, the specific posthumous title to be conferred was not recorded therein.

Now, based on the report submitted by Jingmen Commandery stating that the Great Master Zhizhe has never previously been granted a title for his native temple, the local Circuit Transportation Commission has conducted an investigation into the original documents.
The memorial for protection has already been submitted. According to the statutes of the preceding period, the official decree should propose the conferment of a two-character title.

We request that the Ministry [of Rites] prepare the formal application, and that the Imperial Court issue an edict for the Department to confer the title. Based on the report from the Court of Imperial Sacrifices (Taichang Si) regarding the existing status, we await further instructions.
[The Emperor’s] Decree: It is hereby commanded that the title "Great Master Linghui" (Linghui Dashi) be conferred.

He maintained that only the laws and edicts of the imperial ancestors were authoritative; as for those works based on the scriptures of the two schools or those not contained within the canon, they lacked a foundation in the authentic scriptural texts.

upon death, they are buried naked. These are not recorded in the *Zangjing* (Canon) and lack a basis in the scriptural texts.

They falsely claim that the Buddha rejected affection for his teacher, whereas the Buddha spoke with tears falling. They speak of the appearance of the Great and Small Ming Kings, citing the *Kaiyuan Jing*, the *Guodi Bianwen*, and the *Qi* [dynasty records].
Regarding the discourse on the heavens and the various sects such as the Wulai-zi (Five-Coming Sons), their origins may be traced to a single source.

The Great Qin, also known as Persia. In the twentieth year of the Kaiyuan era, an imperial edict declared: "Mani is originally of heterodox views, yet falsely claims to be Buddhism, deceiving and deluding the common people.

While traveling through the Central Kingdom, [the Emperor] first established a temple there; thus it was named accordingly. When intending to instruct people, one must surely follow the original source.

Therefore, the Boshisimiao (Persian Temple) in the two capitals should be renamed Daqin (Great Qin). All such temples existing in the prefectures and commanderies throughout the empire shall follow this precedent.

In the third year of the Dali era, an imperial edict was issued for the establishment of a temple by the Uyghurs, which was granted the name Dayun Guangming (Great Cloud Radiance). In the sixth year, an edict was issued for Jing, Yue, Hong, and other [regions].
In each prefecture, one Dayun Guangming Temple was established. In the third year of the Huichang era, an imperial edict ordered that all Mani temples throughout the empire be abolished.
Seventy-two female Manis in the capital died; as for the various Manis of the Huïgür in this country and elsewhere, they were exiled to various circuits, and more than half of them perished.
In the fifth year, an edict was issued concerning the Daqin Mu-hu and the Huo-xian.
More than two thousand people were all compelled to return to secular life; however, the root had not yet been eradicated, and at times the branches continued to spread.
In the sixth year of the Zhenming era of the Liang dynasty, the Manichaeans of Chenzhou enthroned Mu Yi as their Emperor.

An army was dispatched to suppress them, capturing Mu Yi and his remaining followers, who were then shackled and sent to the imperial capital to be executed in the marketplace. Initially, the local customs of Chenzhou had favored the practice of heterodox paths. Relying on...
The Buddhist teachings established a school of their own, known as the "Highest Vehicle" (Shangshang Chéng). They abstained from eating pungent vegetables or meat.

Yet, in their efforts to convert the common people, they mixed their practices with lewdness and impurity; they gathered at night and dispersed by day. The Regional Inspector, Prince Huì Wáng Yǒunéng, committed many illegal acts, which led to the rallying of these demonic rebels.

Though they were repeatedly suppressed, they were not fully pacified. It was only during the Zhēnmíng era that they were completely eradicated through execution. During the Later Táng and Shí Jìn periods, they rose up again in secret.
They appoint one person as their leader, and all matters are submitted to his authority. Sometimes they depict a demon king seated upon a throne, with the Buddha washing his feet for him.
They claim that while the Buddha teaches the Mahāyāna, this [practice] is the "Supreme Vehicle" (Anuttarayāna). This is merely a shadowy imitation of Buddhism, what is known as a "semblance path.
There are bhikṣus who, driven by hunger and cold, often follow them in pursuit of profit. Those with discernment should keep far away from such people.

This teaching seduces people until they fall into hell. Beware! As for the present followers of Māra, because they survived the period of banishment during the Huichang era, they are no longer called *Huixian* (Fire-worshippers);
and because they survived the executions during the Zhenming era, they are not termed *Mani*. Their teachings remain as they were.
Therefore, the laws prohibit them. As for those known as the "White Lotus," in the early years of the Shaoxing era, there was one in Wujun...
The śramaṇa Maoyiuan of Yanxiang Monastery once studied under the Dharma Master Fan of Beichan.

Following the Tiantai tradition, he produced the "Diagram of the Four Perfectly Interpenetrating Lands," the "Text and Verses for Morning Liturgy and Repentance," and the "Four-Phrase Buddha Recitation in Five Tones.
He exhorted men and women alike to jointly cultivate pure karma and was titled the "Master of the White Lotus. His followers were known as the "White Lotus Vegetarians" (Bailiancai).
People also call them the "Mao-shami Vegetarian" sect. There were those who brought this matter to the authorities, who further charged them with the crime of serving demons;
consequently, they were exiled to Jiangzhou. Later, there was the Xiao Mao-shami, who again gathered the remaining followers; however, his understanding did not equal that of Ziyuan.
Furthermore, as the lay practitioners (baiyi) transmitted the teachings from one to another, there were inevitably errors, with the sole exception of the precept on "carefully protecting life."
Regarding the so-called Baiyun (White Cloud): during the Daguang era, a monk named Kong Qingjue from Baoying Temple in the Western Capital claimed descent from the lineage of Confucius.

He came to reside at the Baiyun Hermitage in Hangzhou, where he perused the Buddhist scriptures and established a system of four fruits and ten stages to distinguish between the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna vehicles.
He composed several treatises that circulated among the common people; his followers honored him as "Master Baiyun."

Furthermore, he named his followers the "White Cloud Vegetarians" (Báiyún cài) and also the "Ten Grounds Vegetarians" (Shìdì cài). Yet, when discussing the four fruits of arhatship, he was ignorant of the opening of provisional means to reveal the ultimate reality;

when discussing the ten grounds, he did not understand the distinctions between the Shared, Distinct, and Perfect vehicles. Thus, though he wished to challenge the Chan school, he failed to do so effectively.

The teachings and contemplations of Nai lacked a point of return and instead became demonic doctrines. By the power of his own delusion within the ocean of awakening, he presented these fallacies to the authorities and was sentenced to exile in Enzhou.

He taught for twenty-five years, with a constant attendance of over a thousand people, and many attained the Dharma. His deportment was upright and serene.
He did not keep any superfluous possessions. When a thief entered his room at night, he stripped off his clothes and gave them to him, guiding him along a side path so that he might escape.
Not long after, weary of social engagements, he returned to live in seclusion at a thatched hall, keeping only six items with him.

On the morning of the seventeenth day of the seventh month in the sixth year of the Xining era, he rose and washed himself, took leave of the assembly, and passed away while sitting in the full lotus posture.
He was sixty years of age and forty-one years since his ordination (*varṣa*). Initially, his teacher had left a final instruction that the coffin must not be closed until Su Dongpo arrived.
Four days later, Dongpo entered the mountains; he saw the master seated in the lotus position as if alive, and the crown of his head was still warm.
Twenty-one years after the master’s passing, while Dongpo was in exile at Huizhou, the disciple Master Huijing of Siyi entrusted this account to Chanlinzi Dao.

He secretly sought out the eulogy written by Su Shi. Furthermore, he said: "While I was in Hangzhou, I dreamed that I reached the West Lake where there was a great hall with a plaque inscribed 'The Descent of Maitreya.

Figures such as my old friend Haiyue Biancai were all practicing the Way within it. He then composed three quatrains in rhymed prose to mourn him, saying: "I wish to seek his traces, yet I am forced to dampen my robes;

In truth, he was originally unborn and cannot be said to have perished. Though the world speaks of his passing, his spirit remains unspent; How could the moonlight of his wisdom ever be extinguished? His fame has spread throughout the eight directions, Yet he alone has returned to the source of the Dharma. I offer this verse to console his soul; May he rest in peace within the realm of Nirvana."
Tonight, the moon over Master Sheng’s lecture hall shines; the entire courtyard remains as cold as frost.

Birth and death are like the bending and stretching of an arm, yet our attachment to this world brings us such bitter sorrow. You, Lètiān, are no guest of Penglai; rely instead upon the Western Paradise as your host.
You wish to inquire into the causes of drifting clouds arising and ceasing, yet finding no opportunity, you see only your own body in a dream. Rest your mind and dwell well.

Wang Wendu: "Why must this principle be further questioned of others? Later, Cānliáo went to Ying River to visit Zīyóu, saying, "Since Biàn-cái was able to obtain an inscription from you because of Zīzhān, would it not be fitting for Hǎiyuè alone to have one as well?
Zīyóu also composed an inscription for him. When the Master came to Tiānzhú, he first arrived at Héjiàn, where an old man wearing a cap and sash crossed a bridge toward him.
Bowing low, he welcomed [the guest] as they entered the gate, but he lost his place while lecturing. At that time, he dreamed that Zhang’an struck his mouth with a golden probe, saying:
"Since you are diligent in instructing others, you shall attain eloquence and wisdom. He once suffered from a chronic spleen ailment that did not subside;

he dreamed that a celestial deity took a golden basin filled with water and told him to close his eyes. The deity washed his intestines, and once the washing was complete, restored them. Upon waking, the pain ceased. (Recorded in the *Wuyue*)
There was a great drought. Prayers were offered to the Avalokiteśvara image from India, but no response was received. At that time, the Master was ill and sleeping during the day.
He dreamed of an old man in white robes and a black cap who told him, "At noon tomorrow, it will surely rain. When asked who the man was, he replied, "He is a mountain deity.
Rain fell exactly as predicted. Yang Wuweiz composed a eulogy for this, saying: "Upon the sea there is a bright moon; its single orb is forever pure and clear. The wind rolls [the clouds away]..."
Floating clouds part across ten thousand miles; a cold light shines upon the snow atop Feilai Peak.
Yuanjing’s courtesy name was Wuxiang; his surname was Xu, and he was a native of Yuqian. His family had long delighted in performing acts of goodness.
A traveler who passed by his residence pointed it out to others, saying: "There is an auspicious aura here, rising up in dense columns. A remarkable man shall be born from this."
When he was born, a lump of flesh arose on his left shoulder like a stalk of *kāśa* grass; it disappeared after eighty-one days.
His paternal great-uncle sighed and said, "This child is a śramaṇa from a previous life. Be careful not to thwart his vow; let him serve the Buddha for his entire life.
'Eighty-one' is likely his destined lifespan. When the Master reached his end, it indeed accorded with that number. At the age of ten, he followed the monks of his district.

Fayu entered the monastic order; by nature, he did not consume pungent roots or meat. Whenever he saw a lecture seat, he would invariably say, "I wish to ascend this and preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings.
At the age of sixteen, he shaved his head and received full ordination. At eighteen, he went to study under Ciyun at Tianzhu.
At that time, the master’s disciples were already numerous, and the assembly wished to turn him away. Ciyun said, "In the past, I had a most extraordinary dream; this youth is surely..."
He was a vessel for the Dharma; do not refuse him. Day and night, apply yourself with diligence to study and practice, and within a few years you will rank among his senior disciples.

After Ciyun passed away, he served Mingzhi Shao. Once, while Shao was lecturing on the *Mohe Zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) at the section on the five conditions for expedient means, he said:
Vimalakīrti said: "One should give a single meal to all beings, making offerings to all Buddhas and worthy sages before consuming it oneself.

This is one skillful means. Upon hearing this, Master [Wuzhuo] attained enlightenment and said, "Now I know that form, sound, fragrance, and taste are fundamentally endowed with the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Tears fell from him like rain. From this point on, whenever he encountered objects, he realized they were all the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). He subsequently lectured on the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* ten times.
After five years, Lü Zhen, the Governor of Hangzhou, requested that he reside at Beibao Ge. [Zhiyuan] strictly established the precepts;

those who committed even the slightest transgression were expelled, and his disciples revered him for it. After ten years had passed, Shen Gou, the Governor of Hangzhou, remarked, "Tianzhu is originally the site of the Great Being Avalokiteśvara’s practice hall;
its Buddhist rites consist of repentance through sound and voice, not a dwelling for Chan meditation. He then requested the Master [to leave].

He replaced meditation with teaching. When the Master arrived in Wu and Yue, people vied with one another to quarry the mountains and expand the monastic quarters until they reached nearly ten thousand foundations.

His multi-storied pavilions and magnificent halls stood preeminent throughout western Zhejiang. His disciples increased several-fold. Furthermore, those who offered prayers to the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) rarely failed to receive an answer.
Thus, he named his monastery "Inspired Response Avalokiteśvara" (Linggan Guanyin). At the beginning of the Xining era, Zu Wozhe was governing Hangzhou, and a critic remarked:

Displeased with his administration, [the authorities] hastily established a judicial prison at Xiali. Because of the circumstances surrounding the casting of the bell, Zhiyi was required to undergo interrogation;

fortunately, he did not fall victim to it. His residence was not a true *aranyaka* (monastic hermitage), yet he remained composed as he composed the *Jingangpi* (The Diamond Scalpel) and the *Yuan Shili Shuo* (Treatise on the Perfect Nature of Phenomena and Principle).
After seventeen years had passed, a monk named Wenjian, coveting his wealth, relied upon powerful and noble figures to—
The Commissioner of Transport (Dongzhuan Yunshi) seized [the monastery] for himself and relocated the Master to Lower Zhu. The Master did not resent this;
yet the Governor Jian was still not satisfied and sent messengers to relocate the Master to Qian. Over a year later, Jian was defeated.

Upon hearing that the Court had restored Upper Zhu to the Master, the people of Wu detested Jian during his time; consequently, donors did not arrive, and the rocks, valleys, grasses, and trees were affected by it.
It was desolate. When the Master returned, men and women gathered without being exhorted, and all things within the mountains seemed to bear expressions of joy.
Zhao Qingxian, who had been a transcendent friend of the Master, witnessed this personally and praised him, saying: "The Master has returned from India."
The mountains were empty and ghosts wailed as the Indian master returned home. The light of the *dōjō* shone brightly; he remained for another two years before finally intending to depart.
Addressing his disciples, he said, "Even our ancestral sage, though urgent in converting others, realized that it harmed his own practice.

His rank was originally that of an Iron-Wheel King, yet his realization stopped at the fifth stage. How much more so for me, a mere ordinary man? Thereupon, he took his leave and spent his final years on Nanshan.

Above Longjing, he covered the site himself with thatch and bamboo. When the rulers of Wu and Yue heard of this, they vied with one another to build him dwellings, complete with sacred images and golden-glazed tiles;
it was finished in the blink of an eye. After three years, at the request of the Prefectural Governor Deng Bowen, he moved to reside at Nanping.
A year later, when Deng departed, he returned to Longjing to spend the remainder of his life there. The Master’s lectures were held regardless of day or night. He once said: "The ghosts..."

The divine majesty and virtue were not fully manifest; many people feared him and would not listen when he preached during the day. Only when the night fell and all was quiet did they hope to hear him.
He burned his fingers as an offering to the Buddha—three on the left and two on the right—merely to maintain control over his disciples. Those who wished to emulate him [were few].
The Master said, "If it is as I say, then it shall be so. Throughout his life, he had cultivated the pure practices of the Western Paradise without ceasing for even a moment;
his power was fully realized, and there were many instances where he manifested supernatural abilities beyond the ordinary. Dongpo’s son Dai had been unable to walk since birth at the age of four.
He requested the Master to shave his head, upon which the Master rubbed the boy's crown and offered prayers for him. Within a few days, he was able to walk like any other child.

"Master, there is a man named Li, dressed in plain clothes, who practices dhyāna and contemplation with great discernment yet lacks virtuous conduct. He wishes to follow you and leave the household life.

Dongpo takes pity on him and has requested this of you on his behalf; he did not mention the man's name. It seems as though you already knew what kind of person he was. The Master refused and would not grant permission.
The madman of Xiuzhou turned toward heterodox paths to drum up followers among both the clergy and the laity, proclaiming that he would build a *stūpa* as a field of merit for the people of Wu.
Offerings poured in like clouds. However, they feared entering Hangzhou because they knew the Master could not be deceived. Having no other choice, he came;
first, he sent one hundred thousand coins to the Upper Zhi (Shangzhushan) to provide a meal for the monks, and dispatched a messenger with a message, saying: "Now..."

"Having set aside such-and-such funds for construction, I wish to provide for one hall of the Sangha. The Master replied, "That you have come from afar to spread the Dharma wind has increased the splendor of these mountains and rivers.
Your kind message arrived first, bringing me immeasurable joy and consolation. You have established this pure offering for the purpose of feeding the monks;

however, I have heard that the teachings contain explicit texts prohibiting the interchanging of funds. Since you, O Holy One, have already acted contrary to these clear instructions, I do not know how you will explain this to the Buddha."
"With what words shall I respond? I await your reply; I am currently composing this commentary. The madman was greatly startled and ashamed.

Upon seeing his disciples, even though they were his own followers, he urged them, saying, "We should merely pay him homage to transform the common people. The Master spoke with stern words: "One who has left the household life must possess the eye of wisdom before it is permissible.
He is truly a holy one, so how would I dare not show him respect? If he were merely boastful and delusory, I would know it and treat him accordingly."
This was a loss of right mindfulness. I have heard that the Sage possesses the supernormal power of knowing the minds of others; today we shall earnestly entreat him.

Tomorrow, we shall come to this mountain to observe the fast together with the Buddhas of the ten directions. Thereupon, they prepared everything according to the Dharma with solemn reverence, knelt to recite the ritual text, and burned it.
On the following day, they led the assembly out to welcome him, yet the madman did not arrive at all. All the students...

Fu. Furthermore, Tao Tan, the Magistrate of Jiaxing, had a son who suffered from possession by a malevolent spirit (*mèi*). Neither shamans nor physicians could cure him, but the Master blessed him with incantations, and he was healed.
A daughter of the Chen family in Zhuji, Yue Province, suffered from a mental illness and remained unconscious for long periods.

Her parents brought her to see the Master; he awakened her with subtle words, and she suddenly regained consciousness. He once met the monk Xizhong while eating; as they were dining, [the Master] saw a mark between Xizhong’s eyebrows.
The light was like that of fireflies. Upon grasping it, he obtained śarīra. Thereafter, these were frequently found at the places where he slept and arose.

When he was about to pass away, he entered his room (which was named Fangyuan-an; recorded by Qin Guan and calligraphed by Mi Fu). He sat in meditation to decline visitors, ceased all speech, and while eating, summoned Cānliáo and Dàoqián, saying:
"My pure practice is accomplished. If no demonic interference occurs for seven days, I shall pass away lying on my right side. This was his vow.

This was sufficient. On the fifth day, he recited a verse to inform the assembly; on the seventh day, he passed away peacefully. This was the final day of the ninth month in the year of Xinyou of the Yuanyou era.
When his stupa was completed, his disciple Huai Chu traveled to Ruyin and requested Sūn Dōngpō to compose a record for it. Dōngpō commanded me to provide the inscription.

From the Vinaya-master Jingtuzhū of Qiantang, he received the three contemplations of the Sea-Moon and Tiantai schools. He then said: "What is the use of pursuing empty fame? It is far better to cultivate actual practice.
To have pure words but turbid conduct is what the sages and saints condemn. He entered the Tianwang Monastery on Mount Nan, where he specialized in recitation and study.

He read through the five treasuries of the *Lotus Sūtra*, the four treasuries of the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā*, and the ten treasuries of the *Amitābha Sūtra*. He performed circumambulations before the True Body Stūpa ten times.

He performed three hundred thousand prostrations to Śākyamuni and one million prostrations to Amitābha. He recited the Buddha’s name five million times, performing three prostrations for each syllable.
He paid homage to the *Lotus Sūtra* three times. Yang Wuweish presented him with thirty chapters of a hymn on the Land of Peace and Bliss that he had composed.

The Master, desiring to widely transform others, subsequently depicted the three grades and nine ranks in a tableau and had it inscribed upon stone with a eulogy. He lived his life in pure abiding, never sitting with his back turned to the west.
Without illness, he passed away while in the full-lotus posture; extraordinary fragrances filled the chamber, and celestial music resounded through the sky.
If Yu was styled Zifa and posthumously titled Fajian, he was of the Ma clan of Haiyan. At the age of twenty-four, he gained renown in the local schools.
He traveled to the Juehai Hermitage on Lake Dongting, where his former residence had been torn down; there he relied upon the monk Yongming to receive ordination.

He studied under Biancai, and his reputation for the Way grew daily more eminent. When the prefecture invited him to reside at Nanping, he declined with vigor and did not go, instead remaining in service to Biancai.
Carrying his staff and sandals, he retired to Longjing for six years. There, he shared a spiritual friendship with Canliao;

while Canliao excelled at poetry and sought fame, the Master concealed his brilliance and polished away his luster, seeking no recognition from others. Upon seeing the dilapidated dwelling of the old monk Du Juehai, he provided him with inexhaustible offerings.

He constructed a pavilion to enshrine the Western Sage (Amitābha), which was preeminent in the region of the southeast. He established a Pure Society (*śuklavarṇasaṃgha*) to exhort both monastics and laypeople;
every assembly invariably gathered several hundred people. For thirty years he applied himself with diligence and advanced in practice, whereby many received the Buddha’s reception.

Zhang Cibu (Jingbei) left behind an inscription containing lines that stir boundless aspirations for rebirth in the Pure Land. On the day he first took leave of his parents, he dreamed of a person in white robes who bestowed upon him seventy...

Regarding the second strategy: when his life-span reached its end in the ninth month of the Bingwu year of the Jingkang era, he said to his disciples, "In a dream, a divine being told me that my fellow student, the monk Ze Zhang, has attained the samādhi of the practice of Samantabhadra’s contemplation and has already been born in the Pure Land.

He has long been waiting for you; how can you linger here? He then commanded the assembly to chant the *Amitāyurdhyāna Sūtra*. As soon as it was finished, he said, "The sacred image has appeared before me. My...
He departed. A verse says: "A lattice of a thousand flowers in the void; a lotus pond of seven treasures in a dream.

Having trodden the path back to the West with stability, there is not a single point of doubt remaining. Several hundred *śarīra* relics were obtained through cremation and enshrined in a stupa on the eastern corridor.
The inscription by the Layman of the Twin Huai Trees, Zheng Ji (whose "Pai Baiyun" and "Ju Chiwei" manifest his resolve): The collection of poems is titled *Guan-yuan Yuchen*.
He struck the path of the patriarchs, transmitting the legacy of Yao;

like Chao Fu and Xu You, he refused to serve as ministers. Like Shuqi and Yi Yin, he held dissenting views at the Zhou court. Thus, he reversed conventional texts while remaining in accord with the Way.
There is indeed a spirit of exhortation here; yet it is not as if black and white could ever serve one another’s purpose.
When the Dharma-wisdom was revived and the old order restored, the world and future generations approved of it.

Yet some, dwelling beneath the crushing weight of that era while clutching books moistened by their ancestors' hand-sweat, are unable to respond with even a single word of agreement, nor can they grasp a single glance without omission. This is certainly no narrow path.
Regarding those who defected [to other schools], it must be that their minds were directed elsewhere. He compiled the *Biographies of Jingue and Shenzhi*.
Renyue, whose courtesy name was Jijing and style name Qianfu, was surnamed Jiang and a native of Xia. He took the precepts under Xingxian of Kaiyuan Temple at the age of nineteen.
He studied the Vinaya under Zewu of Qiantang and became proficient in observing and violating the rules. Having heard that Fazhi was most brilliant in the teachings of Tiantai, he went to study them.

He went directly to seek him out as his preceptor. Upon reaching the Water-Moon Bridge (Suīyuè Qiáo), he cast his hat down, gathered lotuses, and said along the path, "If my studies do not reach fruition, I shall never cross this bridge again.

Fǎzhì recognized his potential; he settled him in the eastern wing of the residence and sealed all the windows and doors. Even during the day, they relied on oil lamps to facilitate his contemplation and study.
Consequently, the walls, rafters, and beams of the house were all blackened with soot. Whenever letters arrived from his home village, he would read them all...

He entered the *zhànggé* (the "Tent Pavilion"), which was opened only once every several years for the sake of the assembly’s alms-round. As he sat on the gunwale of a boat and was just beginning to stretch his legs, he experienced a sudden, expansive realization, as if opening up the void of space.
Unaware that the mast of the vessel had snapped, he felt as though the needle and the magnet had met, and the trap and the snare were both cast aside.

Day and night he listened and practiced; he questioned the Master face-to-face and sought oral instructions. Hearing what he doubted, he requested further benefit from the Great Teacher. He gathered large sandals.
Guān Dàyào was such that the multitude stood in awe of him from afar. Over the course of more than ten years, he thoroughly mastered its profound depths and mysteries, whereupon he remarked:

"Scholarly understanding is not equal to the manifest clarity and manifest verification of practicing it. Together with ten like-minded companions, he cultivated the *Guānyīn Chánfǎ* (Avalokiteśvara Repentance Method).

While lying ill, he experienced a state of vivid clarity as if in a dream, through which he deeply realized that all his previous studies were erroneous. His insight became transcendent and reached a level that ran counter to the teachings of Fazhi.
They engaged in a series of debates and cross-examinations; among these, the "Ten Admonitions" (*Shijian*) and its defense against slander (*Xuebang*) are the most prominent examples.

The preface to the "Ten Admonitions" states: "How is it that the Great Master failed to perceive my loyalty and sincerity, and instead established another gateway of doctrine regarding the Land of Peaceful Nurturing?"

To claim that the birth-body (*janma-kāya*) is identical to defilement and impurity, and to confuse the inferior response-body (*pratibimba-kāya*) of the Sahā world with the *Sambhogakāya* (She-na), is to say:

"How could one intend to pick out his shortcomings and conceal his virtues? To peddle the fame of 'exceeding the blue' and give rise to views that oppose the Path, thereby falling headlong into the mire—this is truly lamentable.
Since the Way does not accord with me, slander arises from this; I shall therefore set out on a journey to the four quarters to harmonize with my former aspirations.
Regarding his aspiration, he traveled to Tianzhu (India) to meet Ciyun (Zhiyi). Ciyun embraced him as a successor of the Dharma, saying, "My Way shall not be solitary.
The Master presented a poem, saying: "Ten years of wandering and travel— On this day, I may truly boast. In my love for mountains, I met Vulture Peak; In seeking the Way, I obtained the Ox-Cart.
The *Bai-ye* verses were translated by Qin Shi Huang; The Lotus Sutra was for the monks of Jin’s monasteries. How can the son of Zhichuan Learn to fly toward this place?"

Ciyun was invited to ascend the Dharma seat at Zhaoqing Monastery. He sent him off with a poem that read: "The oriole calls from the valley mouth; Accepting the invitation, you approach the heavy city walls.

The clouds have just turned their backs on Vulture Peak; A monk passes by to welcome you to the stone casket. Ascending the lion throne for the assembly of a hundred sons, You wave the fly-whisk, startling the four neighbors.
I rejoice that after a thousand years, In my own house there is now a Daosheng. Ciyun’s disciples and followers were moved by this.

[He spent] half [of his life]. At Stone Wall (Shibei), Lingzhi (Lingzhi), Hui’an (Hui’an), and Qingxiu (Qingxiu)—these five sites of practice were all locations where he was invited to reside by those along the way.
During his time at Lingzhi, for the sake of the benevolence of the people of Wenzhou, practitioners requested that he establish a Pure Society (Jingshe). He resided there for barely ten years;

both the monastic and lay communities held him in such high esteem that they even inscribed his name upon plaques, whether in true *kaishu* (clerical) or large *da-zhuan* (seal) script, for which he would always exert himself with his brush. [This was] the Dharma [of] Yongjia.

The flourishing of the Way was truly due to the Master’s power. As his virtue and seniority in the monastic order (*de-lak*) were both high, the Governor of Xi (Wang Fangfei) invited him to preside over Xiangfu Monastery.
Liu Congguang, the Inspector-General, memorialized the throne to grant him the rank of *min-fu* (court robe), and Hu Su requested for him the title of Jingjue (Pure Enlightenment).

Both the court and the commonalty held him in deep esteem, yet Hu Su was the most devoted of believers, observing the etiquette of a disciple. He composed the preface to the *Lengyan Jijie* (Collected Explanations of the Śūraṃgama Sūtra); indeed, this was the Master’s [work].

In my past studies of the Dharma-treasury, I have been particularly proficient in this sutra. I have compiled the exegeses of various masters to produce this *Jijie* (Collected Explanations) for its thorough understanding.
I have extensively set forth the principles of the fivefold structure and composed an exposition of the title to clarify it, desiring to propagate the divine mantras at length.

He chanted hymns with modulated tones to inspire them, vowing that the cultivation and realization of the Way would surely be achieved. He established ritual protocols to ensure their completeness, and these were practiced by all in the world.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the practice of *chánmó* (repentance). Following the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, he burned three fingers as an offering to the Buddha.

He founded the Yīnlún Hall (Retreat Hall) as a place of rest; regarding the meaning of its name, his intention was to quiet the workings of the mind. The third month of the first year of the Zhìpíng era.
On the twenty-fourth day, he said to his disciples, "I shall depart at noon tomorrow. When the appointed time arrived, he left behind a verse and passed away.
On the fourth day of the fourth month, he was interred at the western corner of Mount He. His age was seventy-three, and his years since ordination were fifty-four.
His Dharma heirs—Cifan, Lingzhao, Nairin, and Yingke—were still able to uphold the profound teachings and serve as models for others. [He] authored...
The *Shu* (Commentary) comprises fifty-five fascicles in total. The *Dàlùn Jiéwén* (Excerpts from the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra) consists of twelve fascicles.

Furthermore, there are the *Dàlùn Shū* (Essentials of the Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra), the *Jìngmíng Yīngjīng Huìcuì* (Compendium of the Quintessence of the Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra), the *Cánmén Shūyào* (Essentials of the Chan Gate), the *Zábiān Míngyì* (Miscellaneous Compilation of Terms and Meanings), and other works such as the *Jiàowǎng Zhīgāng* (Great Outline of the Teaching Net), the *Fǎyì Zhī Jīngjuàn* (Refined Excerpts on Dharma and Meaning), as well as the two collections from the Liang and Tang dynasties, the *Chuāng'àn Jì* (Notes from the Window and Desk), the *Zhūzǐ Zá yán* (Miscellaneous Sayings of Various Masters), and the *Shǐsuǐ* (Essence of History). These texts constitute the great framework of the teaching and the refined pith of its doctrine.
Those who assisted the Buddha-way and guided future generations all possessed scrolls and volumes; they were well-versed in the Six Classics and thoroughly mastered the works of the Hundred Schools.
They were skilled in poetry and capable of elegant prose, excelled in seal and clerical scripts, and steadfastly cultivated the precepts until old age without slackening.

The "Preface to the Meaning of the Name of Lingzhao" states: Even when his end approached, the Master still read these books, just as the Sage Confucius recited the *Dafayan* (Analects) as he drew near to his death.
Zhongshu [Yang Xiong] never ceased holding his scrolls even unto death; thus, he possessed the spirit of a true teacher. Yuan Ying transmits this and comments upon it, saying:

"I have previously discussed Master Shi’s (Shandao) lifelong dialectical expositions and his vigorous elucidation of the fundamental tenets. His acts of granting or withholding [doctrinal points] were, for the most part, like the striking of a mortar and pestle against one another.
Whether he emphasized the vessel-like simplicity or focused on this or that detail, how could there have been any cause for doubt? [He followed] Zhi Guan, Tianqin, and Long..."
The tree reflects with inner clarity while outwardly adapting to the needs of the times; each assumes its position through skillful means—is this not what is meant?
In the Jiachen year of the Chunxi era, Shen Daqing (Zude) renovated the stupa, for which Xiao Qianyan composed a record.
From Master Yizi Shudan: He was of the Ye clan of Pingyang in Yongjia; his mother was Pan. At the age of eight, he entered the Way.

Another nine years later, having mastered the scriptures, he received the tonsure and studied under Fuzong Zhong. After traveling extensively and conducting thorough inquiries, at twenty-seven, he resided at Miaoguo Temple to lecture.
He expounded the meanings of the four teachings and produced the *Jijie* (Collection of Explanations), which remains widely circulated to this day.

He presided over five monasteries—Dayun, Zhenbai, Wufeng, Baoji, and Miaoguo—where his disciples surrounded him in their seats. His analytical disquisitions were clear and lucid; he was steadfast, penetrating, and versatile, with a voice that was pure and resonant.

There were those who, upon hearing his recitations, were not without joy and submission. Since the Master [Zhiyi] elucidated *śamatha-vipaśyanā* through the principles of the five periods, the five flavors, the provisional and the complete, the expedient and the real, the partial and the perfect, and the Great and Small Vehicles, the meaning thereof has been profound and extensive; readers have exhausted their spirits and striven their utmost to comprehend it.

It was difficult to penetrate [the meaning]. It was only upon reaching Master [Zhiyan] that the investigation became thorough and precise; consequently, many who heard him wished to receive his instruction.

Furthermore, he lamented that since the Sui and Tang dynasties, the doctrines established by other schools had not been rooted in the sutras and śāstras, but were instead merely based on personal whims, leaving no way for cultivation and realization.

Lord Gijilang Gong, being particularly discerning, remarked: "The Master’s talent is such that, had he donned the scholar's cap to join the ranks of the gentry and served in an office of remonstrance to fill the vacancies of the state, his dignified bearing would have been as formidable as that of Han Ji’an or Tang’s Lord Jiang (Yang Jie). "Is my King in Huangzhou? Alas, he is far away at the edge of the sea, long suppressed and unable to extend his influence.

His disciple Ruoshui erected this stele at Yanqing Jingtu Monastery.

Admonition: "Take one handful at a time, and surely embody my intention. Protect yourself and others well; do not allow the lineage to be severed.

He resided there. Throughout his life, he relied upon the Great Compassion Mantra as his support. He once stood on one leg for an entire day and night reciting it;

The middle grade. This was your rebirth. On the twenty-first day of the fifth month in the sixth year of the Yuanfeng era, he changed his robes, sat upright, and wrote a verse in praise of the Buddha, saying:
"My birth in the Pure Land is certain. He then passed away peacefully. On the tenth day of the intercalary sixth month, he was enshrined in a stupa to the right of the hermitage.
He was eighty-six years of age and had been a monk for seventy-three years. His nature was tranquil and his appearance ancient; he spoke little and had few desires. Thus it was recorded.

He was grave and steadfast by nature, compassionate and harmonious toward others. Within the Tiantai school of teachings, there were particularly many divergent opinions, and masters and disciples often fell into conflict, causing great commotion throughout Jiangzhe.
Only our Master taught and exhorted with steady patience; whether matters were right or wrong, long or short, he never allowed them to take form in his speech.

He was noble yet not aloof, harmonious yet not drifting. He traveled to and from Qiantang for over forty years, maintaining his lofty character while fulfilling his duties, sustaining himself through the four requisites.

"Is he not one who is endowed with both merit and wisdom? At the end of spring in the first year of the Yuanfeng era, ten thousand people, both monastics and laypeople, sought to receive the full precepts (*mahā-śīla*).

The lecture hall was filled with light, as if rays from a crack in a wall were shooting in obliquely, or like the reflected shadows of water shimmering on the side.

they wept with sorrow and offered words of praise. Zen Master Shouyi Fazhen of Jingci recorded this as "The Record of the Light of Precepts. This was received by Vinaya Master Zhao.
Precepts are the record of one’s conduct. When Zhao Qingxian was stationed in Yue, he composed a poem that says:
"How joyful it is to have obtained this native land! I linger here at the quiet Leifeng Hermitage. Do not say, O Jiangzhe, that news is cut off; Twice a day the sound of the tide comes.
Among his ten disciples, Fazong, the master of repentance, excelled as the most eminent. The *śramaṇa* Jiezhu succeeded to his path.
Originally from Zhanglin in Jiaxing, he studied under Guoning and entered the school of Fazhi Lun. At that time, though still young, he had already begun to gain a reputation among the assembly;
his mastery of rhetoric and calligraphy struck awe into his peers. He once requested further instruction on the meaning of the *Sūtra-king*.
Fazhi said, "Serve as the monastery director for me for three years; then I shall tell you that your task is finished. He asked again, and Fazhi let out a great shout.
The Master attained sudden enlightenment and composed a verse: "Everywhere I meet the path back home, At every moment I reach my native land.
The reality of original perfection— Why wait for deliberation? Fazhi received his orders and composed a ceremonial address, saying: "Pervading the heavens..."

His literary talent flows like a rushing river; he stands alone as the preeminent scholar of his time in the examination of doctrinal meaning. When the state’s eminent scholars listen to the sutras, their worldly dreams fade;

when the monks of the riverside follow his transformation, their daytime meditation increases. Five hundred monastics transmit his new commentaries; the ancestral masters of successive generations resolve long-standing errors.
Furthermore, fearing that His Majesty might command him to share the imperial carriage, the performers would have no place to present their songs and music.
When the Cloud of Compassion arrived at Mount Zhufeng, he was granted disciples from the Dongshan school numbering five or six hundred. For thirty years, he expounded the Way;

his commentaries on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Prabhāsa-sūtra*, the *Amitāyur-dhyāna-sūtra*, the *Biexing guan shiyin jing*, the *Mohe zhiguan*, the *Guansin lun*, the *Jinbi*, and others were all...
He explained the errors in volumes six and seven of the *Commentary*. He once assembled one hundred monks and practiced the *Lotus Sūtra Repentance* for one year.

He annotated the *Ritual for the Benevolent Kings Repentance*, composed a sub-commentary on the *Sūtra of the Practice of the Way*, and had ten thousand copies carved on woodblocks for distribution. During the reign of Emperor Renzong, he petitioned for the bestowal of the Tiantai Canon upon his prefecture.

I shall petition for the bestowal of four thousand five hundred scrolls of the Buddhist scriptures (jiaocheng). The Duke of Zhangxun, Yuan the State Councilor, Ye the Hanlin Scholar, and Jiang the Vice Director of the Imperial Library have composed encomiums, records, songs, and poems [in his praise].
Prince Li, the Commandery Governor and Son-in-law of the Emperor, requested that he be granted a purple square-cut robe and the religious name Shenzhao.
Wei Guo Changzhu petitioned for an imperial edict granting him the Bailian Hermitage; two persons are to be ordained annually there. The second year of Huangyou.
He resided at Nianju Hermitage for seven years. On the eighteenth day of the fifth month, he fell ill. After a short interval, he ascended the seat to address the assembly.

That night, the rafters of the Dharma Hall, the Scripture Repository, and the Abbot’s Quarters collapsed; the bells rang out but produced no sound. Fishermen on the river saw a monk departing toward the west amidst the clouds.

At dawn on the following day, he passed into *parinirvāṇa* lying on his right side. A wondrous fragrance was never-ceasing. The following year, in the third month, he was buried to the north of the hermitage.

His disciples, out of longing and veneration, opened the lock to look upon him; his countenance remained solemn and dignified, and both his nails and hair had grown long. Lotus flowers sprouted from his stupa.

In the memorial inscription for the Great Master Fanchai, it is recorded that "a full year after his *parinirvāṇa*, his physical body remained as if alive. The Master held lightly to material wealth and offerings, and propagated the Teaching.
He took this as his own responsibility. Wearing tattered quilts and worn-out robes, he lived in ample comfort until old age.
Once, while bestowing the Bodhisattva precepts at Tiantai, light emanated from the stupa of Zhiyi and from Guoqing Temple and Mount Chicheng, intersecting and shining upon the ordination platform.

He once made offerings to the Thousand Buddhas and fed a thousand poor people; when he placed flowers upon their seats, the flowers of the Buddhas should not have withered, yet those on the numbered seats would invariably wither. As for the poor...

Human flowers are destined to wither; though some may not wither, his lifespan was seventy years and his *parivāsa* (seniority) fifty-three years. His disciples, including Chuchuan and others, were exceedingly numerous in their succession of the Dharma.
There was a disciple named Zhenfazhi (the name "Zhen" having been changed from its original Sanskrit transliteration), who resided at Longyou on Mount Jinshan.

When Wu Shidudu, the Regional Inspector of Qiantang, invited him to the Xingjiao Chan Monastery, students flocked to him in great numbers. In his lectures, he analyzed the phrasing and dissected the principles, penetrating them from beginning to end.
To raise a single point would open the way for all related meanings; to exhaust a single passage would bring all passages into harmonious accord. Those with strong memories...
This is a compilation of categorized examples. Regarding these categories, Master Ren recorded five; Jingjue added two; Cuangcong of Kuocang added three; Fohui Cai re-edited them;
and Yungjia Ji arranged them in sequence. Guangzhi once said: "The practice of compiling such collections involves an equal measure of gain and loss.
The gain lies in the student’s ability to select and search through them to understand their essential framework; the loss lies in being ignorant of the fundamental meaning of the texts."
The momentum arose. Those who exhaust their studies seek further beyond the words; it cannot be said that this alone is sufficient.

During the flourishing of the teaching, Qunfeng Taichu compiled and arranged [the texts], while Gaosuo’s *Xuyushu* and Chaoguo’s *Huixian* established separate introductory narratives (*xuannu*) to dissolve the textual difficulties.
Beneath each passage, he opened up the underlying intent. The formal commentary on the contemplation of the mind is titled *Nanping*. The preface to the *Jiajia guji* states: "Moreover..."
On this day, many students in the lecture halls read this text with numerous errors. Is this not to lose the original source while seeking only its branches and leaves?
Yet, in places where the scriptures are not available, one may "warm to the old to know the new. Thus, the fruits of one's studies will not be in vain;
by this means, one recognizes the great carriage and certainly does not prize the primitive handcart. When Śāradvatīputra of India saw this, he closed his scroll and wept bitterly.

It is said: "The 'Shattering the Bone Dharma-body' [treatise] has misled later students. Removing the *lǔ* (mortise) from the *ān* (beam) and *yán* (bracket), I recognize this as a source of affliction for later students.

I have written and sent over two thousand words to Wuxiang, earnestly exhorting him never to transmit it; it is as if the finest essence of clarified butter (*tíhú*) were being transformed into dregs."
Fazang’s transformation into a ghost-fire speech reveals how deeply he was concerned for future generations. Gaian said:

"Although this man was a teacher of men, his primary concern was to shorten the path of commerce by proliferating his doctrines to flatter those who came after him. Yet, the sin of being the first to initiate such a practice must surely be borne by someone.
The Master [Zhixu] and Jingjue debated the gates of the teachings before the authorities, requesting that a high platform be assembled and a red banner erected, following the precedent of...

The Holy Master of India contended with the non-Buddhists. Having won, he used a banner to mark the site of the victory. Those whose arguments fell into error were decapitated or their tongues severed and hung before the local magistrate.
Observing that the Master’s prowess in the battle of Dharma was so fierce and sharp, the magistrate approached him and analyzed his words, saying:
"In the composition of literary style, you do not surpass Sengyue; in retentive memory and broad learning, Yue does not surpass you. Although you have laid down your weapons, you remain superior."

Upon hearing this, my hair stood on end in awe. The Master praised the *Myōshūshō* (The Commentary on the Wondrous School), stating that its establishment of the Perfect School accords with the intent of the Patriarchs.

He composed two verses, saying: “The Buddha permitted the six stages of realization to distinguish the dung beetle; why then does one not understand both the ‘one’ and the ‘not-two’? One loses the West and loses the East as well.
If the three thousand realms are truly perfected, then all are eternally blissful. If the dung beetle has not reached the ultimate, then all [other beings] likewise remain incomplete.”

The Buddha severed the nature of evil. Initially, Lord Wu frequently invited him to lecture during his days off from official duties. He would stand outside the gate with his sash fastened and his ritual tablet held upright;

until the Master had ascended the seat, he did not dare to enter. Dongpo said: "When conversing with the Master about various texts, if there was anything I had forgotten, he would recite it from memory, flowing on without ceasing.
In his "Inscription for Biancai," he wrote: "There was both inquiry and discernment; they reached the ultimate verse."

The inscription on his stele for meritorious deeds states: "This writing is highly refined, yet it fails to mention the Master’s greatest faults. During the Chongning era, he was posthumously titled Shixiang (True Aspect).
Huizhou was a native of Danqiu. After both his parents passed away, he sought to repay their boundless kindness; he left home to become a disciple of Weiyin at Jingde Temple. At that age...

At twenty, he carried his book-satchel to study under Fazhi. After several years of diligent practice, he remarked, "Fazhi’s instruction is that the Buddha-way is exceedingly level, yet its practice is uniquely difficult;
this refers to the four samādhis. Resolving to focus his will upon these, he realized that the Pure Land is but one's own mind and that Amitābha is one's own original nature—not far away.
At the beginning of the Tiānshèng era, he gathered ten fellow students and practiced the ritual of the Great Compassion (Mahākaruṇā) for three years.

"If, while directed toward this samādhi, you would allow me to offer my own body as a burnt sacrifice, I shall faithfully receive and practice [the teaching]. Once the performance of the dharma was complete, he fulfilled his vow.

Laypeople and monastics offered several dozen types of incense, including sandalwood, which were boiled together until they formed a massive pile. It was intended for the stupas of various regions. On the final day of the fifth lunar month, Shenzhao entrusted him with these words:
"The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* is your noble gift; you must cultivate it. The *Brahmajāla-sūtra* contains clear instructions; you must follow them."
This is simply to bind the mind to the Dharma-realm. When the body is like fire, then this single mass of embers is the essence of samādhi.

Rejoice in seeing this and exert yourself; offer pure, luminous, and true offerings. May you, my disciple, practice this. The Master, having received these instructions, offered thanks to the fourfold assembly.

He led the various cremation attendants to pay homage to the Buddha and the assembly, circumambulating them three times. Then, concentrating his spirit, he sat upright. Having realized his own nature—

Fire is itself emptiness; the nature of emptiness is itself true fire. How could there be the characteristics of a burner or something burned? It was simply that all phenomena were tending toward the practice of asceticism.

After a short while, the wooden platform had been consumed by the flames, and the firelight extended across the sky. His countenance remained solemn and upright, showing no sign of leaning or tilting.

When the wood was exhausted and the flames extinguished, his skeletal remains were perfectly intact. Monastics and laypeople vied with one another to seek his *śarīra*, as they held incense burners and offered prayers.
Five-colored stars scattered like sparks. His bones were interred on the western mountain, and a stone stele was erected there. He was thirty-four years of age and had thirteen years of ordination.
Xiangfu Huixi of Quzhou had practiced together with the Master and was thoroughly familiar with the details from beginning to end; he requested that Yueshan Weibai record this account.
Danqiu Wu Ji erected this stone. Mingzhi Yanqing and Han Yingming of Guangyan Monastery received the teachings of Fazhi;
their contemplation reached profound depths, and they were acclaimed as masters of the school.
This *Sūtra of the Sublime Dharma* was written in silver; the characters for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas within the text were inscribed with gold.

Its dharma transcends mere brush and ink, and its jade rollers and lapis lazuli case inspire awe and reverence in all who behold them. During the Jianyan era, when bandits rose up and the monastery buildings were utterly destroyed, this very sūtra alone was recovered from among the rubble.
During the Chunxi era, the abbot of Lianzhian heard the clamor of thousands upon thousands of people at night.
When he rose from his seat, he saw that a fire had broken out in an adjacent room. The flames had already penetrated the roof;

while the sutras on a small pavilion atop a pillar were enveloped in fire, he grasped them and brought them down without the slightest damage. It is said that having twice escaped such conflagrations was due, in the long run, to the merit of the Mahāyāna and the protection of devas and nāgas, and in the short run, to the firm resolve and vows of the Master himself.
