His polemical correspondence reached the provincial administration; his arguments were exceptionally superior. He further authored the *Guanzheng lun* (Treatise on Governing the State) to clarify the abuses of the Ming Shen Zong’s era in deprecating the sutras and śāstras.
When he submitted these three works to the imperial court, the Chancellor at the time commended them. [The Emperor] appointed him as a Waitaizhi.
Zhu Xu was particularly detailed [in his records]. His *Cānān-lù* (Record of the Grass Hut) in ten fascicles circulated in the world.

On the seventeenth day of the fourth month in the Dinghai year of the Qiandao era, he manifested parinirvāṇa at the age of seventy-eight and with sixty-one years since his full ordination (*varṣa*). While suffering from illness, he continued to lecture, saying to his disciples:

The Flower Treasury World (Huazang Shijie) was profoundly transparent and brilliantly illuminated; it was wondrous, pure, and superior, bringing great joy to his heart. He said, "You all shall propagate the Way; my time here is now exhausted.

Someone requested that he leave behind a verse, to which he replied: "What I previously spoke was the praise of Amitābha; now, as the assembly collectively recites my own praise, I shall follow them in chanting the names of the Buddhas several hundred times.
He then directed the assembly to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* up to the section on birth in the Highest Grade, after which he sat upright and passed away.
He passed away. At midday, when the sun was at its zenith, his head and feet were both warm, and his hands were supple, returning to their natural state as soon as they were raised.

His entire body was interred at the ancestral stupa south of the city. His eulogy reads: "The boundless ocean of lands contains the void; The ocean and the void are entirely the Lotus Palace. The Lotus Palace pervades the entirety of the ocean of void;
Within this ocean of void, alone is revealed the countenance of Amitābha. Amitābha Buddha is neither born nor extinguished."
Difficult to find, difficult to grasp—like the moon in water; it is utterly beyond words, such is this body.

Such is the resonance, such is the teaching: I and Amitābha are fundamentally not two. When deluded awareness secretly arises, they suddenly appear as distinct. From now on, I shall sweep away all dust of emptiness and existence;
father and son, naturally, meet as one. I vow to cultivate the three blessings and diligently practice the six remembrances, through the karma of body, speech, and mind.
It is without flaw or blemish. "I now contemplate Amitābha with this mindfulness; until I see Amitābha, I shall never grow weary. Furthermore, the Preface states:
"The World-Honored One said that Amitābha is the Dharma-realm body, and our Patriarch said that the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is his substance.

Taking these two teachings as the essence of my heart, then the ten million billion lands appear as if before a bright mirror. The Master was stern and majestic, and his eloquence arose like a sharp blade. There was...

To encounter his sharp edge was what the world called "ascending the Dragon Gate. He recited the *Sūtras* daily; both secular classics and Buddhist teachings remained in his memory after a single glance.
When lecturing on various treatises, his words exhausted the ultimate principles and his meanings reached the very source of the profound.

Once, there appeared a perfect circle when he cupped his hands, and the soles of his feet bore wondrous patterns of two fish clearly defined. Judging from these external signs, one could fully know what was contained within. He succeeded to the Dharma of Yue.
Over thirty people, including Bo, Zian, Youlun, and others, entered his gate and his chamber by the thousands. Among them was Sun Xuecheng, Qingxiang, who styled himself Shuanan.
He composed a memorial for the anniversary of the Master’s passing, stating: "All phenomena are fundamentally empty; from emptiness, reality is realized. The Perfected Man does not die;
though he dies, he remains as if alive. Venerable Anzhu was the convergence of rare spiritual essence; his prior causes were never obscured as he sought the pearl of the precepts."
At the jaw of the dark steed, he brandished the sword of wisdom at the Dragon Gate; early on, he moved with ease through the groves of Confucian scholars, leaving no book unread.

Later, he boarded a raft upon the ocean of the Buddha’s teachings, reaching everywhere as his compassion was stirred. Having reclaimed his ancestral kingdom from the thicket of brambles, he encountered old friends upon the great road.

His mind transmitted the single thread of the Way, and his insight illuminated the delusions of the masses. Standing at the highest pinnacle of the Path, he tore away his robes and caps without a moment’s regret. For...
Doubt remained unresolved; he was shackled in prison while awaiting the dispute. He longed for the eminent seat and hastened toward it, seeking instruction by following the prevailing wind.

Yet, upon meeting the Eight Consciousnesses (the masters), not a single word found resonance with him. Intending to offer a single incense stick to the Fourth Ming (Zhili), he composed a memorial inscription, saying:
"Alas! Our Buddha’s enlightenment of the mind—Chan must employ the Teachings, and the Teachings must employ Chan. It is like the Yangtze River..."

It is like a lake: though the streams that flow into it differ, they all converge at a single source. It is like the sun and the moon: though their appearances may seem distinct at times, they both adorn the same sky.

This is comparable to using two different medicines to treat the illnesses of sentient beings; the goal in both cases is recovery. Alas, in these final times, the two schools have been afflicted by demons.
Students adhere dogmatically to partiality and establish their own sectarian titles, contradicting one another. Each insists on the exclusivity of its own gate, yet teaches...

When viewing through meditation, one finds no peace at all, like a needle stuck in felt; when meditating while viewing the teachings, one wishes to sever [the attachment] but cannot, like a goiter constricting the throat, for which no end can be found.

The teachings say, "I am [the truth]," yet who clarifies the gradual and the perfect? Those of perverse nature desire to hear it, and meditation says, "I am [the truth]," falsely claiming it to be the Separate Transmission.
Since both schools have become isolated, within each school the branches hang like stars apart; some are based on...

Some claim to clarify the Four Teachings, or boast of the Xi River; some inherit the White Lotus tradition. Yet their subtle purport of Tiantai is nothing but floating talk and idle chatter, like a drifting boat.
Some study the Guiyang and Yangshan schools, or return to Yunmen, or succeed to Caoshan; yet the Seal of the Tathāgata’s Mind is thus pushed upward and falls downward, like an inverted monkey.
Holding such a "superior mind" to oppose another's "superior mind"—attacking with a swallow—is the way of the Buddha-dharma.
At this point, what can sentient beings rely upon? It is truly lamentable. Our honorable patriarch was majestic and grand;
he was able to penetrate the subtle mysteries of both schools (and so forth).

The second patriarch of the Zhongxing lineage, the tenth in the transmission, was Congjian, courtesy name Zhengfu. He was a member of the Mao clan of Songyang in Chu. From childhood, whenever he saw Buddhist scriptures, he was able to read them immediately.

His father said, "He is a person who has returned for a second life; can he be burdened by worldly ties? Thus, he renounced secular affairs and followed Jingyin Weican. At nineteen, he underwent the examination.

After he had received full ordination, he felt ashamed that he could recite the sutras without understanding their meaning. He relied upon Biancai of Upper Zhuhang, listening and practicing day and night with such diligence that he forgot both sleep and flavor.
After three years, his reputation for excellence was established. Biancai instructed him to rely on Nanping at Mount Jinshan as he had been taught; he remained there for over ten years.
During a session of requesting further instruction, his questioning and discernment flowed like a stream. Nanping said, "The propagation of my Way rests upon this son."
During the Xīníng era, he lectured at Míngqìng Monastery. As his followers increased daily, the halls and buildings became cramped and narrow.
The local governor approved of this situation and transferred him to Jìngzhù Monastery. During the Yuánfēng era, Chùrén established Shòuśèng Monastery and welcomed him there;

the prefectural administration also invited him with generous hospitality. After three years, Biàncái retired to Lóngjǐng. Dèng Nèihàn (Rúnfǔ), lamenting that the ancestral seat of Nánpíng was not flourishing, firmly [urged him to return].
He summoned Biancai (Bianzai). Biancai said, "I am old; it is not possible for anyone other than Congjian to lead the assembly. Deng [Zhao] used the postal service to coerce him to come.

The following year, Biancai was appointed, and he passed on the teaching to his successor. Two years later, he moved again to Jingzhu Temple. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, the seat at Upper Zhihuasi was vacant.
Vice Minister Pu (Zongmeng) saw that those in power were vying to recruit him, and his private decision had not yet been finalized. Biancai urged him, saying, "Ling..."
Moved by these sacred traces, those from near and far came to take refuge there. Yet, were it not for a person of true caliber, it would have been difficult indeed to bring such glory to light.

Tong Jian was a man of upright conduct and inner clarity, well-versed in both Confucianism and Buddhism; he was revered by all quarters and naturally drew the hearts of the multitude to follow him. Had it not been for this monk, it would have been difficult for anyone else to remain there.

Pu Yunzhi studied under him and attained a profound and subtle realization through *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calm abiding and insight); he delighted in receiving Zen practitioners. Da Tong (of the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*) once...
A letter was sent, consisting only of black and white [ink]. Master Wonyang replied with a verse: "Black marks and white marks—carrying shackles, one passes through the state of transgression.
Whether it is 'understood' or 'not understood,' it is like stirring up waves where there is no wind. "If you ask what the ultimate matter is like: Mount Dongting stands upon the great lake.

When the State Preceptor Uichon sought the Dharma, the Provincial Governor summoned the Master to respond to this call. The Preceptor admired the Dharma and, desiring its future prosperity, remained in attendance.
Because his mother was anxious and urged him to hurry, the Master instructed him, saying: "The eminent monk Daoji traveled abroad to study while carrying his scriptures.
Fearing he could not leave his mother behind, he instead took her along with him. Yet, as one cannot turn one's back on the scriptures, he carried them across his shoulders."
His style name was Hengdan Ji. Today, the Monk-Administrator Xian is far superior to Ji. How could he have caused his mother to grieve and long for him by turning his back on the scriptures?

When the Administrator first developed the intention to return home, he requested a ritual incense burner, a whisk, and the transmission of the robe. The Master showed him a poem (from the *Hufa waizhuan*).

The Administrator then proceeded to Tiantai, where he made a vow before the stupa of Zhiyi, saying: "I have already transmitted the teachings and contemplations to Dharma Master Cibian of Hangzhou; I now wish to return."

Circulated within our own country, we beg for your secret empowerment so that it may be propagated. Furthermore, I have sent back a portrait of Master Miao and established a shrine hall, honoring him as the First Patriarch.
While in Huizhou, Dongpo once wrote of this matter and showed it to Hui-cheng, saying: "Compassionate and Eloquent of India."

His learning and conduct were exceptionally high, and he was thoroughly proficient in worldly affairs. When Goryeo dispatched monks at an inappropriate time, I requested that they be granted audience by the court and provided them with guest quarters;
there, I engaged them in daily dharma-discussions. Their verbal arguments arose like sharp blades, yet the foreign monks could not fathom him.

Furthermore, I fully grasped their true intentions and reported them [to the authorities]. Indeed, his talent surpassed that of others. He resided at Upper Zhushan for twenty-four years until he grew old.
He returned to Shousheng Monastery. The students from the schools of both Zhejiang, remembering him with the affection felt for a father and son, went together to visit the Master.
Upon seeing them in his room, the Master suddenly said, "I have not preached the Dharma to you disciples for a long time;

have you come all this way in vain? He then bathed, put on new robes, ascended the seat, and began to preach. His words were so fervent that everyone was moved to tears. He wrote a verse which said: Arising and ceasing...
Appearing and disappearing, he was originally without reality. For seventy-five years, like empty flowers, he transformed his bones.

Casting off his hands, he walked atop Mount Kunlun; from the beginning, he never moved from the Vairocana Cave. He passed away with his brush in hand on the twenty-seventh day of the twelfth month of the Jichou year of the Daguang era.
In the first month of the following year, his entire body was interred at his place of study. He had transmitted the Way for thirty-six years, and ten thousand [disciples] had entered his gate.
Shu Huijuebi succeeded him as his son. Zhen Shangzhu composed his *xingzhuang* (biography).
Qin Yizhi was of the Du clan from Yuyao, Yue. He took Qingxu of Longquan as his teacher and received full ordination during the Huangwu Universal Ordination.
He studied the teachings under Yun of Siming and traveled extensively through various regions, including Tianzhu Mingzhi and Leifeng Guangci.

He visited every door and entered every chamber, diligently seeking instruction for over twenty years. Upon completing his studies and returning to his hometown, the community strongly urged him to serve as abbot, but he resolutely declined.
Eventually, out of respect for his seniority, they compelled him to deliver lectures; those of his own generation who received his teachings were filled with joy and submission.

He then closed his quarters to decline all affairs and devoted himself exclusively to the practice of Pure Land cultivation. He recited the *Lotus Sūtra* five thousand times and the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-bhadracaryā-praṇidhāna* and the *Amitābha-sūtra* ten thousand scrolls each.
The Buddha’s name was Wusuan. In the seventh month of the first year of the Chongning era, he manifested illness.

On the nineteenth day, he told his disciples: "The time for me to be born in the Pure Land has arrived. I shall mount the Vajra Terrace and follow the Buddha westward. You must all exert yourselves in diligent cultivation."
They were able to see him in person as he washed his body, performed mudrās, and passed away while seated. On the twenty-fifth day, he was cremated at the western gate;

amidst the ashes and bones, his tongue and rosary remained perfectly intact. This was the efficacy of his recitation and upholding [of the scriptures]. His disciples buried him on the western peak of the monastery.
He was seventy-six years of age and fifty-two years since his ordination (*vassa*). The Vinaya Master Dazhi [enshrined] his younger brother, Tan Yue, as a monk.
Shou once participated in the consecration ceremony and composed an inscription for his stupa.

Wenqi was a native of Jinhuai who studied under Fushi; he was renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya rules. Upon returning to his hometown during the ZhiPing era, he established a monastery to the northwest of the city.

During the Jingyun era, the teachings spread quite widely throughout the land. In the summer, there was a great drought; [the Master] manifested radiant light and invoked the various great powers of transformation.

His sincere devotion moved the divine response, and sweet rain fell in abundant measure. The Prefect, Lu Ge of the Ministry of Works, memorialized that this temple be permanently established as a center for the Tiantai school.

By imperial decree, he was appointed as the abbot. He commissioned statues of the nine patriarchs, which were so exquisitely adorned with gold and lapis lazuli that they became the foremost in the region east of the Yangtze.
The scholar Lin Xi composed verses in praise of the various patriarchs; regarding our Master, he wrote: "At the intersection of the paths, the brilliance of the ancestral beam shines forth;

at the precious star, the monastery is refined. His disciples numbered seventy-two. Grand Master Puyue and Sengsong resided at Cijue Temple; having practiced the Way for a long time, they transformed [the community] into one of unity.
Jing resided at Shizhu Jingde Temple. He had a disciple named Chengji, and together with Fozhi, Ciyun, Fazhao, and Netong, they formed a lineage of masters and disciples who illuminated one another.
Each flourished in their respective regions; these were what were known as Miaozhi in the north of the city and Zhiyan in the south of the mountains.
The Dongyang Academy was second only to Danqiu and Yinshui; was it not because a spark of flame originated with this Master?
Ruoshui was a man from Quzhou who had gained renown for his studies of the Teachings (*jiao*). As the assembly had already come to revere and submit to him, he wished to seek even wider recognition;

thus, he changed his name to Ruoshui, outwardly manifesting himself as a junior student so as not to incur the disdain of those who transmit the Teachings. He resided at Chongfu Monastery on Mount Tianzhu and lectured there.

He was diligent in his external observances and possessed merit through esoteric mantras. As the anniversary of his ancestors' deaths approached, he instructed the cook to prepare fresh bamboo shoots for an offering.

The cook objected, citing that it was not the proper season. At dusk, [the Master] sprayed water from his bowl into the rear garden; that night, a crackling sound was heard, and at dawn, bamboo sprouts were covering the ground.
Those who sought them all had their desires fulfilled. When a resident fell ill, he chanted over water and gave it to him to drink, and the man was immediately cured. The multitude marveled at this.

The tree monument no longer exists, having perished due to the fire god’s wrath; only the incantation grove and Prime Minister Yu’s Dragon-Transformation Pond remain superior to the mouths of the masses.
While this is the power of the Buddha-dharma, it is also brought about by the principle that all objects are but the mind.

Xī Zuìshī was a native of Xià. He was born after his mother experienced a miraculous dream. A physiognomist remarked, "His bone structure is extraordinary; do not let him be defiled by worldly customs.
At the age of four, he received full ordination through the general amnesty of the Tiānxī era.

At fifteen, he transmitted the teachings and contemplations of the Guǎngcí school. Guǎngcí said, "My lineage has found its successor; it will certainly not decline further. He was subsequently promoted to a senior position.
His peers revered and loved him, calling him the "Tiger of Dharma. During the Zhìpíng era, he lectured at the Lóngpíng Pagoda Cloister of Qīnglóng Temple.

His conduct—whether in public or private, speaking or silent—was always in accord with the Dharma. As his reputation matched his reality, both monastics and laypeople turned toward him in admiration; even the local magistrates and officials submitted to his influence.
He brushed his robes and departed with a carefree air. Although he requested to return to his former post, he no longer took up residence there.

He gave lectures at Shengguo Monastery in the chamber of the monk Ziyun. A malevolent spirit possessed someone there; he cast enchanted earth at it, and in a short while, a slip of paper was found inscribed with these words:

"Now I have been subdued by the Dharma-master’s arrival and am sent away, though not yet entirely relinquished. If the power of the Dharma fades, I shall return. A few days later, the object struck things and flung forth fire.
A great and strange transformation occurred. When the Master arrived at the chamber, he rebuked it, saying: "What creature are you?
Are you not one who, still suffering the pains of the dark realm, seeks to beg for the power of wisdom in order to attain birth [in a higher state]? Why do you trouble people without end?

Have you not heard that those who vex a Dharma Master shall have their heads split into seven pieces? He then explained to them the causes and conditions of saṃsāra, and the assembly of monks recited incantations.
His karmic obstacles were destroyed. A thunderous sound echoed through the air, and he saw characters written in vermilion, identifying him as the Han dynasty martyr Shen Guangda.
He briefly repented and apologized, saying: "From the past until now, I have been shrouded in delusion; only today has it finally been severed.

Having received your instruction to confess my crime of harassing the monks, I am now at peace. At midnight, I shall be reborn in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations. Hereafter, this shall be my legacy."
His fruition was complete. On the sixth day of the late autumn month of the Gengwu year of the Yuanyou era, he preached the Dharma, wrote a verse, and passed away while seated.
In the early winter, his body was cremated, and dozens of *śarīra* relics were obtained, their luster brilliant and variegated. He was seventy-three years of age and seventy-six years of longevity.

His remains were scattered in Long River. Lü Yirou’s inscription on the stele states: "I have often read the *Biographies of Eminent Monks*; when I reached the section on Falan, I saw how diligent he was in the sutras..."

The Preface: The deities and spirits of the mountains all came to receive the Dharma. People said that his virtue had reached the spiritual beings, yet they privately suspected this to be a fabrication.
Upon seeing this, one knows that the Buddha’s wisdom and supernormal powers are sufficient to dispel the illusory echoes of dark demons and to rescue the sunken souls from the deep springs;
thus, both the realms of light and darkness obtain benefit and peace. Now, the sages do not speak of strange anomalies, for they would... [lead to] confusion.

This serves as a warning for those in future generations who delight in fabrication. Yet Confucius once said, "Revere ghosts and spirits, but keep them at a distance," and further stated, "In the realm of the unseen, there are indeed ghosts and spirits.

How could he have considered ghosts and spirits to be non-existent? Now that Shen Guang’s manifestations are so clearly evident, how can those who harbor malicious intent to deceive the unseen world fail to hear of this and be struck with fear? This is what [is intended here].
Although it was strange, it was recorded because it was certain [to be true]. Gaian said: "During the Qianyuan era, I visited this temple.

I paid my respects and examined the Master’s record of conduct (*xingye*), and upon viewing the back of the stele, I saw the calligraphy of Shen Guang. The characters were an inch in diameter, appearing like blossoms in a state of intoxication."

Is this not empty and exaggerated? Continuing my reading of the *Yunjian Zhi* (Gazetteer of Yunjian), I found that when Yang Ticheng (Qian) was serving as magistrate of the county, he compiled a record stating that there was a stele for Master Zui at Shengguo Temple; because the account therein involved strange and exaggerated matters, it was not included [in his work].
Could this not be because Lord Yang adhered to the view of non-Buddhist classics alone and neglected the Buddhist tradition’s extensive achievements?

Regarding the discourse on the three periods of time: I have now recorded Shen Guang’s essay in its entirety below, so that those who advocate for the Way of the Confucians and rulers may take it as a warning. (The current version of the text is not recorded here).

Jizhong, whose courtesy name was Facheng, was of the Qiu clan of Yongjia. His parents prayed at the Buddhist shrine of Zhang’an on Mount Tiantai and both dreamed of a monk who handed them a child, saying, "The Venerable of Luoxi has entrusted him to you for your care.
During her pregnancy, his mother abstained from meat and blood. When he was young, he would invariably fondle any Buddhist implements he saw.
At the age of eight, he entered the Kaiyuan Pudu Monastery; as he grew older, he studied the sutras and the Vinaya, enduring great hardship.

He fell ill and practiced the Avalokiteśvara Repentance. He beheld the Great Being (Mahāsattva) emitting light and extending an arm to bestow water for consecration (*abhiṣeka*), whereupon his illness was suddenly cured.
He studied under Guǎngzhì at Yánqìng Temple, where he pursued his inquiries with profound dedication; Guǎngzhì regarded him as a vessel of great potential.

While serving as a lecturer in his place, Xuědòu Míngjué Xiǎn saw him and praised him with admiration. He paid homage to Avalokiteśvara at Tiānzhú, whereupon his mind opened up suddenly, and all that he had learned...
He was profoundly penetrating. Nanping Zhen held him in high esteem and invited him to Tianzhu to expound the *Lotus Sūtra*.
The gentry and commoners of Yongjia invited him to reside at the Eastern Pavilion of Kaiyuan Temple. He later moved to Miaoguo Huian and withdrew to Jiangxin to refine his Chan meditation.

He subsequently resided at Faming on West Lake, where students flocked to him in great numbers. When someone wished to renovate his quarters, the Master said, "The donor shall first receive the merit."

I would rather endure his ostentatious residence than destroy it. Since the Chen and Sui dynasties, the Tiantai lineage has been passed down from master to disciple through the transmission of the incense burner and whisk.
Upon reaching the fourteenth generation, there was Master Qi, who requested that the Master (Zhili) succeed him. The Master declined on the grounds that he had received the Dharma from Guangzhi.

Consequently, Qi sealed away the incense burner and whisk and returned home. Zhao Qingxian, admiring his reputation, received him with great courtesy and composed a poem to praise the Master’s dignified demeanor.
His appearance was majestic and imposing; his voice resonated like a bell. Among the dense crowds, he stood out preeminent and extraordinary; those who saw him felt both awe and joy.

When he ascended the seat to lecture, he eschewed literary embellishment, yet his mastery of the sutras and śāstras was thorough, and his eloquence was unhindered. Every first day of the first month, he conferred the Bodhisattva precepts upon tens of thousands of people at a time.
He regularly led the masses in the release of living beings, in numbers beyond counting. His disciples followed in his footsteps, continuing his legacy for generations.

He never lacked for anything. He practiced the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, *Prabhāsa*, *Amitābha*, and *Avalokiteśvara* samādhis without a single day of omission. His recitation of dhāraṇīs to save beings from suffering and his prayers were divinely efficacious beyond measure.
Sometimes, when he entered a marketplace and sat down, those who were seated would rise; the passersby would avoid him by placing their hands upon their foreheads in reverence.

On the eighth night of the tenth month in the fifth year of the Yuanfeng era, he bathed, changed his robes, preached the Dharma to bid farewell to the assembly, formed a mudrā, and passed away while seated.

A red light permeated the sky. At the Pure Society (Jingshe), the entire community of teachers dreamed of a man in golden armor who told them, "Tonight, a man who has attained the Way will enter extinction.
Startled, they rose in alarm; shortly thereafter, they heard that the Master had passed away. Qìng'ēn Xīmào dreamed that a divine being told him he would be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven.
The Master had long provided food for the hungry ghosts; after his death, his disciples continued to provide it as before. For three days, birds and sparrows cried out in mourning.
He did not descend [from his seat]. On the fourteenth day of the twelfth month, he was buried at Mount Rui鹿 on West Peak. His age was seventy-one; he had been a monk for sixty-four years.
He authored fifty fascicles of the *Fuzong* (Aiding the School). He ordained several hundred disciples, and more than a hundred transmitted his Dharma.

The local customs of Yongjia were devoted to Buddhist affairs; they frequently held assemblies for offerings to the Thousand Buddhas and Arhats, conducted with such solemnity and meticulous preparation as if they were official government functions.

However, everyone says that these were the teachings transformed by Dharma Master Zhong. He compiled the *Ten Letters of Admonition* (*Shi jian shu*) and other works, as well as the *Ten Gates for Dispelling Delusion and Piercing the Veil* (*Zhi mi jue mo shi men xi nan*), thereby performing meritorious service for the gates of the Dharma.
Yet, the oral commentaries of the two masters were truly prolix and erroneous, and the *Ten Meanings Treatise* (*Shi yi shu*) also lacked editorial refinement;
scholars suffered from these defects. Ye Shuixin inscribed the preface to the West Lake Faming Temple as follows: [The text continues with the inscription.]
In the past, the lecturer Jichū resided at this temple. Chū was a man of virtuous conduct and possessed a powerful vow; he resolved to attain the Way through his earnest practice.
Consequently, even though the temple had been reduced to a wasteland of weeds for a hundred years, scholars and officials from the entire prefecture constantly flocked there.

Later, his son Shin established the two orders of clergy, while Master Chō renovated the halls and shrines until the monastic precincts were finally completed. Chō remained austere and diligent, his robes and sandals worn thin and his food meager.

Without prior preparation, the assembly gathered like clouds from all directions; his responses flowed forth like a spring. Even the flourishing traditions of the Eastern Gate (Dongye) and India could not surpass him.
Originally, Tiantai established the two principles of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, and those who inherited and expounded them further expanded upon them.

Consequently, Zhong and Chang each composed their own treatises. Thus, Miaozhen and Puji desired to collect the teachings of these various schools and establish them as a formal canon within the monastery.
He led the men and women to cultivate the *nien-fo san-mei* (Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi), thereby perpetuating the legacy of Jingchang and continuing the enterprise of Zhong in an inexhaustible manner;
his resolve was truly far-reaching. Now, the Buddhist practitioner regards the body as a mere lodging, yet he does not cease in his efforts to adorn its temple halls.
To treat words as mere excrescences, yet transmit them through increasingly numerous characters, is something I truly cannot understand.
I once asked Chang about this, but he too was unable to provide an answer.
Zhiyan, whose courtesy name was Zizhao, was a native of Yiwu. Before he was born, his father and mother, Chen, encountered an extraordinary monk who said to them, "You shall have six sons;
you must by no means keep the fifth one. It would be best to let him leave the household life, for he will surely propagate the Great Teaching.
During the Xiangfu era, when the Master was first born and still a young child, he immediately sought to renounce secular life. His parents found this difficult, and so...

He fell ill and only then realized the words of the extraordinary monk; he thus followed that monk’s resolve. He received the full precepts through the general amnesty of the Tianxi era under the tutelage of Huìqín of Shuanglín.

He studied the teachings and contemplation under Shénzhào and later relied upon Guǎngzhì, achieving great success. Regarding what the Great Master had attained, [Fahai] claimed, "I have already attained it.
When he ascended the hall to seek further instruction, none failed to submit to his realization. He then said: "What the Great Master has bestowed upon me..."
I have no doubt. As for the principle of the Perfect and Sudden, which is beyond all dependence, I do not dare claim to have attained it through my own deep cultivation;
yet, by refining and softening my mind, and accumulating reflections, I suddenly attained a sudden awakening beneath the words of the Patriarch.

When discussing this with those of superior standing, some would bow their heads in submission, while others would roll up their sleeves and reject me with forceful gestures. Thereupon, I sighed and said: "To attain the Buddha’s..."

When you behold those who rely on dark realization—those demons of Chan, ghosts of Chan, and teachers of the Dharma fixated on words—you will see them riding broken donkey carts, unable to rectify their errors.'"
Thus, I dare not fail to exert myself. I have carefully set forth this account of the beginning and the end. For it, I compose this inscription:

When the World-Honored One Śākyamuni entered parinirvāṇa at the Śāla Grove, he entrusted the Dharma to the *śrāvakas*, namely Kāśyapa; yet when entrusting it to the Bodhisattvas, he entrusted it to Mañjuśrī.
As for the reception of the verbal teachings, that rested with Ānanda. Since these three exist, which one could possibly be omitted? Following Kāśyapa, there were twenty-four [patriarchs].
The transmission reached Śrīlaṅka. Some say it was transmitted twenty-eight times to Bodhidharma.
During the time of Emperor Wu of the Liang dynasty, Bodhidharma first came to the Eastern Land; among the six perfections, he specifically emphasized the name of *dhyāna* (meditation).
Chen Guan praised him, saying: "He strictly upheld the *vinaya* and firmly maintained *samādhi*. He used his own body as a tongue to expound ten billion matters."
Fangu Zihufu was a native of Yining. His secular surname was Yang and his mother was Wang. She conceived him after experiencing a miraculous dream, and he was born twelve months later.

A wondrous fragrance filled the room at his birth. At the age of twelve, he took the precepts under Master Jianxiu of Puan; at sixteen, he received full ordination. He declared: "The precepts of the Buddhas of the three periods are the root.
Among the Bodhisattva’s six perfections, śīla (morality) comes first. Precepts and discipline are my grain and nourishment. How could they not be so?

He was able to forget [worldly concerns] for a day. He studied the Vinaya at Shengshou Monastery on Lake Huxin under Tongzhao, and practiced the teachings and contemplation (*jiaoguan*) at Yanqing under Shenzhi.
Moved by a sense of urgency, he traveled to various regions. At that time, the Tiantai path was flourishing in Western Zhejiang;

Biancai of Tianzhu, admiring his single-minded dedication, bestowed upon him a prophetic transmission (*jibie*). He went to Bainu to see Haihui Zhipu, who was lecturing on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the "Life Span of the Tathāgata" chapter.

In the *Pramāṇa* section, he spoke extensively on the three bodies (*trikāya*). Upon hearing his great awakening words, [the student] returned home. [Zhiyuan] comforted him, saying: "My Way shall go to the East.
You will surely cause the Dharma seat of Siming to flourish greatly. You must take care of yourself. He returned to Chengtian Temple to receive formal instruction.

In the spring of the fourth year of Zhenghe, Governor Wang Zishen summoned him to Guangshou Temple. In the following year, Governor Lü Cong invited him to Yanqing Temple. He declined both invitations.
He did not accept them. Among those who wished to follow Guangshou, there were one hundred and twenty; yet he could not refuse them.

At Yanqing, there were five hundred followers, though their flourishing was not equal to that of Fazhi. At the beginning of the Jingkang era, an envoy from Goryeo visiting the border asked after the Master, saying:
"The King sends his greetings. He gazes longingly at your great name, yet has no means to pay you homage in person. He respectfully presents this Dharma robe and sends Xiaoxiao as a messenger."
The Master had authored two hundred fascicles of commentaries and treatises. In the third year of the Jianyan era, he retired due to old age and resided at Zhanming Hermitage on Mount Mao.
He later stayed at Fusheng Monastery in Fenghua; however, Yanqing Monastery had been in ruins for many years.

The Prefect, Vice Minister Qiu, wishing to find someone to restore it, invited the Master to return once more. Unable to decline, the Master accepted, and all the officials assembled, waiting expectantly to hear his lectures.
Chou sighed and said, "These subtle words have uncovered what was hidden; I have heard what I had never heard before. Lou Daixue grasped his banner and held him in high esteem.
Yong retired and fled, leaving behind this verse: "My hair hangs down in wisps as I approach sixty years of age; The morning drums and evening gongs before me fearfully urge me to linger no longer."
He was granted leave to return to the forest to diligently tend the incense and lamps, becoming like a drifting cloud or a wild crane.

The assembly could not bear to thwart his resolve, yet Lou [Shao] said, "One must not let this opportunity slip. After his subordinates had personally entreated him two or three times, in the twelfth year of the Xianxing era, he requested to retire from the affairs of the monastery due to illness.
He entrusted the leadership to Daochen, while he himself grew old at Zheyang Wuzhen. Wuzhen, together with the Circuit Intendant Lu Zhi...

Lin had previously served as an assistant magistrate in Mingzhou and had cultivated a friendship with Wumen beyond the secular world. He frequently visited him there. In the spring of that year, he took his leave, saying:

"I have been afflicted by old age and illness for some time and have long been burdened by the needs of my physical body. I am truly unworthy of your profound regard and care, which I cannot adequately express.
Although there is no permanence, there is a destination for the mind. I entrust my final affairs to Lu Ju of Yanqing. Upon arriving at that place by boat, he bathed.
He changed his robes and sat in the full lotus position to recite the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* with the assembly. He then wrote his final instructions and entrusted them to Wuzhen, Yicheng, and others.

Having completed his verse, he led the assembly in chanting the "Peaceful and Blissful" chapter until they reached the passage on "entering deep meditative concentration. Thereupon, he beheld the Buddhas of the ten directions and passed away peacefully.
This was the eighth day of the second month in the thirteenth year of the Shaoxing era. He was eighty years of age and had been a monk for sixty-four years. He was buried in the fourth month.
He venerated the ancestral pagoda of the Dharma-patriarchs. His disciples were Zhengqin and Zhengyin; among his eight grandsons, he transmitted the Way to over two hundred people.
By nature he was simple and plain, frank and possessed of great magnanimity. In treating others, regardless of their status as noble or lowly, his courtesy and reception were always impartial.

When some found this difficult to understand, he would say: "Our Dharma takes equality as its core principle and non-discrimination as its practice. How could it tolerate making distinctions? Initially, he presided over Yanqing Temple.

During the Renyin year of the Xuanhé era, a great drought occurred. The commandery requested that he lecture on the *Yunyu jing* (Cloud and Rain Sūtra). In accordance with the ritual, an altar was constructed and the scroll unfurled;

immediately, clouds arose, and as soon as he left his seat, rain fell in torrents, bringing relief to Changguo. When the area was harassed by the spirit of the Dai clan, shamans and Taoist practitioners were unable to exorcise it through their rites.
When the Master was invited to recite mantras, the spirit was extinguished as soon as he reached the gate. This was also the case at Fusheng Dao... [text ends]

Laypeople requested him to increase his observance of the precepts. He delivered a message through a member of the Wu clan who had come to serve him, saying: "I am your ancestor; I have long dwelt in the darkness of the netherworld.
Hearing that the Dharma Master Guang was bestowing the precepts upon the assembly in the human realm, all the various beings within the underworld were liberated on that day.
I have temporarily returned from my submerged state to part from you. Many such extraordinary occurrences occurred. Whenever someone questioned him about them, he would sternly refuse to speak.
Sisi Gong was a native of Wucheng. At the age of nineteen, he shaved his head and received the precepts from Zhishenwen, who instructed him to return to Guankongxiang.
The temple had fallen into ruin due to accumulated floods, with only a hundred rafters remaining. The Master said, "What thing is not illusory? Illusions naturally decay.

If they decay and do not arise again, one must wait for them to be completely exhausted before undertaking the work. He transported earth to fill the dry land and constructed three hundred new buildings.

There were ten bays [of buildings], and the Wheel Repository (Lun-zang) was magnificent, like a great site of practice (māhā-vihāra). People flocked there spontaneously, even though he remained composed and free from seeking.
After completing his labors, he practiced repentance for three years at Jie-kong on Mount Wu. In the ninth month of the Jiyou year of the Jianyan era (1129), he passed away while seated.
His body was cremated; as the smoke reached him, all obtained śarīras. In the twelfth month, he was buried to the southeast of the monastery. He was seventy-two years of age. His disciples...
There were forty-three people including Jieteng and others. The Chan practitioner Jingduan entered the Way by observing a lion’s play;
he constantly used this as a means to guide others, and the Master (Huiyuan) held him in high esteem. Du'an also secretly conversed with him regarding the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā*).

Once, during a lecture, Du'an suddenly took a piece of incense and burned it in the incense burner. When the lecture concluded, he bowed and said, "I am old and my ears are deaf; I have never heard your words. [The Master replied,] "It was a leaf..."
The Left Vice-Director (Mengde) inscribed the stupa.
Jingguo and Fazhen were both eminent disciples; their physical forms resembled aged cranes, and their speech never conformed to worldly trends.

He composed a commentary on the *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, and whenever he wished to lecture, he would do so immediately without waiting for the assembly to gather. When his friend, Master Ju, traveled to the underworld, the official in charge of names and surnames said:

"This was a mistaken pursuit; you may return. The minister examined the register and saw that it stated: "The Ācārya Jinguo of Mingzhou has lectured on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* one hundred times.

Thinking that this must refer to his own teacher, he was both startled and delighted. When he inquired about this the following day, the master opened his robe and said, "I have only lectured on it ten times;
I merely completed one hundred recitations by reading it according to its meaning."
Zhai Ying, whose courtesy name was Yunzhi, was of the Yu clan of Tongjiang; her mother was Wang. Her mother dreamed that two suns pierced her womb and she subsequently conceived.

When the full term had passed, she gave birth to a son, and in the following year, she gave birth to another son. Considering this extraordinary occurrence, she caused both boys to enter the monastic order. Each was tested in the scriptures and received ordination.
Changming’s son was named Qin, with the courtesy name Xigu. He received his monastic training at Jingzhu in Qiantang and eventually passed away while traveling in Tai.
The next [master] was this very teacher. Having lost his mother, he followed his father to Hangzhou and left secular life at Nanshan Ruifeng.

He received full ordination under Master Shouning of Chubang and became renowned for his mastery of the Vinaya. During the Xining era, he encountered Shenwu at Baojue Temple; upon hearing Shenwu’s preaching, he felt deep remorse.

Xiu said, "I did not expect that in this degenerate age there would again be such a person; you are truly my teacher. He followed behind Xuanzang with clasped robes to request instruction, never flagging morning or night.
Shenwu took note of his capacity for awakening. [Xuanzang] spent several months without sleeping while studying the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and the *Golden Stele*.
He then reported his realization to Shenwu, who said, "The subtle purport of the *Lotus Sūtra* returns to one's own mind. You should maintain it well and do not disparage yourself."

It is so. Yet I fear that this mani-jewel of supreme value might be cast into a worn-out sack; it would not be appropriate. When learning and conduct become renowned, one’s peers look toward them with admiration;
it is like a mirror cleared of dust, where images appear, or like a bell whose interior is empty, responding to every strike and spreading its resonance.
He traveled between the north and south, his movements and halts left to the conditions of the moment. He served as abbot or gave lectures in twenty locations throughout Su, Hang, Hu, and Xiu.
Growing old and ill at Xiangfu Temple in Hangzhou, he would occasionally brandish his whisk (*chūshǔ*), drawing crowds of monastics and scholars like clouds gathering.

In the second spring of the Yuánfú era, his illness became critical; reflecting on himself, he said: "For twenty years, I have exclusively propagated the Supreme Vehicle (*śrāvakayāna*) to awaken the masses. Who would have thought I would meet with this?"
He was afflicted by illness; his strength failed him, yet he took the treatises he had composed and set them before a fire.

Rising from his seat, leaning on a desk toward the west, he commanded that the *Amitābha Sūtra* be recited. When the scroll reached its end, he passed away. This was the twenty-ninth day of the third month.

His remains were cremated, and a stupa for the numinous fungi was erected to the west of the Lotus Pond, where an inscription was placed. He was fifty-five years of age and thirty-two years since his ordination. Thus did the Master...
Listening to Shenwu’s lectures, he gained a profound realization of the Pure Teaching. He composed a ritual for cultivation and realization, praising the Buddha in verse:

"Amitābha Buddha’s body is golden in color; His marks and signs are majestic and peerless. The white tuft between his brows curls like five Sumeru mountains; His deep blue eyes are as clear as the four great oceans.
Within his light, countless billions of transformation Buddhas appear, And the hosts of transformed Bodhisattvas are likewise boundless. The four..."
The Eighteenth Vow is to deliver sentient beings, causing all nine grades to ascend to the other shore.
Jingfanzi (淨梵子) rectified this [text]. Jiahe Cashi’s mother was Gong; she conceived after dreaming of a divine being resembling a Buddha, whose radiance filled the room.

Upon his birth, he was named Fohu (佛護). At the age of ten, he took Shengguo Siyong (勝果思永), the Master of Repentance, as his teacher and devoted himself exclusively to the recitation of Amitābha’s name.
When questioned about this, he said, "I intend to take him with me to the Abbot’s quarters in another region to care for him in his old age.

At eighteen, he received full ordination and studied the teachings under Chao Guojing; he later relied upon Shenwu. During the Yuanfeng era, at the age of thirty, he resided at the West Hermitage in Xinshi.
He was transferred to the Daci (Great Compassion) Temple of Amitāyus in Suzhou, where he performed Buddha-work through vocal recitation and verbal discourse.

He would bathe and wash himself, prostrating and bowing in worship; even during the freezing cold of deep winter when wind and snow were piercing, or the humid heat of the long summer when the sunlight was scorching.
He never slackened for even a moment. When lecturing, he would complete a major scripture and begin it again, doing so more than ten times.

For other texts, he followed the same practice, establishing what was known as a "Great Dharma Assembly" where he gathered the multitude to celebrate and repent. His disciples arrived in a continuous stream, and both the gentry and commoners were moved by devotion.
His dharma-heirs spread throughout the region of Wu, while donors and those receiving the precepts filled the cities and towns. He encouraged Wang Shi of Sike to construct a stupa for him.

He constructed a monastery and carved a woodblock edition of the Tripitaka, which circulated throughout Zhejiang and Jiangsu. In the third month of the Gengyin year of the Daguan era, he gathered thirty-seven monks to perform a continuous *Fahua* (Lotus Sūtra) retreat.

Through his refined sincerity, he prayed for a response, and Puṇyakṣetra (Puxian) appeared to bestow the *karmavācanā* of the precepts, with a voice like a great bell, calling him the "Pure Brahma Bhikṣu.
Huang Gongyan, the Vice Magistrate of Baozhou, inscribed a stele stating: "How extraordinary! Such is the power of the Master’s Way."
Dharma Master Daojin of Beiping dreamed that Śākyamuni Buddha conferred the precepts upon him;

Great Master Zhiyi dreamed of forty-two foreign monks performing the *karmavācanā* ceremony to perfect his collection of precepts. That these occurred in different eras yet produced identical effects—is this not truly praiseworthy?
Regarding the ritual procedures for the *Lotus Sūtra* period of repentance, the Master was the first to establish them; all of the two Zhejiang provinces followed them. During the Yuánfú era...

In a dream, he was summoned by a man in yellow robes into the underworld. After the King had praised him, he consulted the registers of auspicious mists and found that the Bhikṣu Jingfan had recited the *Lotus Sūtra* throughout successive kalpas. He then dispatched a messenger to escort him back.

During the intense heat of the dog days, while the assembly could not rest in peace, [Jingfan] sat wearing his three robes at the Shuixin Pavilion; a wind and hail brought coolness, and he remained entirely unaffected by the summer heat. Furthermore, he manifested—

The assembly remarked, "Summer is proceeding with the ordinances of winter. The crowd was struck with amazement and marveled at the Dharma Master’s supernormal powers, noting that devas and nāgas were providing protection by transforming the scorching heat into coolness.
At times, while practicing meditative contemplation with the assembly, they would occasionally see a deity clad in golden armor kneeling before the Master;
this was because the various devas, guarding him and fearing even a moment's delay, came specifically to inspect his progress. Thereafter...
During his period of cultivation elsewhere, he observed the Vaisravana Deity scrutinizing the names and numbers of those performing the repentance rites.

There were those who did not complete their repentance, which the deity invariably predicted beforehand; these were simply individuals whose observance of the precepts was not rigorous and whose minds lacked devotion.

The Master, relying on the *Nirdeśa*, translated the *Guanzizai Pusa Pumenpin* (Universal Gate Chapter of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva) and separately composed a liturgical manual for it. He practiced it together with the assembly, and at that time, there was a profound spiritual resonance and a marvelous, extraordinary response.

1. During the Zhenghe era, a maidservant of Master Ying was possessed by a malevolent spirit (*chóng*). He requested that she receive the precepts (*śīla*), and the possession ceased. Lady Ge received the precepts from him to offer for her husband’s benefit;

she saw her husband circumambulate the Master three times before departing. During the Xuanhua era, he served as the Judicial Administrator (*zhǔfǎ*) for the district under the jurisdiction of Imperial Censor Jia, and thus was titled "Master of the Dharma" (*fǎzhǔ*).
On the fourth day of the tenth month of the Wushen year of the Jianyan era, he passed away in his chamber. His remains were cremated (*jāva*).
His relics were interred at the Bānruò (Prajñā) Monastery in Héngtáng.
Yùncí initially relied upon Shòu'ān Bì, and subsequently followed Tiānzhū Cíbiàn. Among Cíbiàn’s ten great disciples, the Master was foremost in preaching the Dharma.
Not long after leading the assembly, he presided over the Pútí Monastery on West Lake and the YuánTōng Monastery in Yuè. [This was during the] Chóngníng era.

First: When the seat of the Buddha was vacant, the great assembly waited expectantly for the Venerable Wen. Each practitioner burned two fingers as an offering to invite him to extensively bestow the gift of the Dharma.
Scholars gathered like clouds, and there were over ten commentaries; these have been followed as the established tradition until the present day.

During the intense heat of midsummer, after the fatigue of lecturing, he took a brief rest in his chamber when Master Wen arrived. He said to him, "This mountain-dwelling master who occupies the seat of the dais..."

When his formal practice concluded, he would not enter the confession hall; instead, he remained in the meditation hall, never allowing himself to lie down at will. The Master said, "How could I dare not follow these instructions?

From then on, through both bitter cold and scorching heat, he never slackened. Whether attending to the necessities of nature, bathing, or changing his robes—even in the snow—he would scoop it up with his hands to wash himself.
He passed away at Mount Dongshan. Prefect Sun Gongjian praised him, saying: "The Teacher of Tiantai."

The monk Yuanjue (his posthumous title), the true wind of ultimate reality, cannot be captured by brush or ink. With teeth like thunderclaps and the skeletal marks of a subduing rhinoceros, he stands tall like the moon reflected in water—such is his appearance.
Within the teachings of our school, there is the "Chapter on the Provisional and the Real for Guiding the Deluded."

Zongmin, courtesy name Zixiu, was bestowed the title Fayun. He was the son of Lu Tongfeng of Danghu. Having lost his mother while still in swaddling clothes, he took up the topknot of manhood and applied himself with diligence and vigor to study.
He mastered the Sanskrit scriptures and was well-versed in the Confucian classics; finding no pleasure in worldly matters, his aspirations were set upon emptiness and stillness.
At the age of eight, his virtue was profound and his demeanor solemn. At fifteen, he received full ordination. He studied under Chaoguo Zhao, Guanghua Ming, Nanping Wan, and Tianzhu Cibian.
When Cibian was about to appoint him as head seat (*śrāmaṇera*), some felt he was not yet the right person for the role; thus, they proposed that he engage in debate with [the incumbent].

His fellow disciples were awestruck and submitted to him. At the beginning of the Shaoxing era, when Minister Feng (Qiu-zhi) governed Hangzhou, he invited him to preside over Pudu Temple on West Lake.
Ti. During the Yuánfú era, Lǚ Dàwèi (Jífǔ) was transferred to Mǎnǎo. At that time, Jiǎng Shùmì (Zhīqí) visited the lakeside.
Visiting the Great Essentials of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, he presented this poem: "Whenever I have studied the *Śūraṅgama*, Gushan has been the most renowned.

To the west of the temple is the Ba'en Yuan, the residence of Master Qin; Sudō named its spring 'The Spring of the Six Friends' (Liuyi), as it was there that he and Ou-yang Hsiu were poetry companions.
Sudō retired to the spring for thirty years, sitting in meditation. When Wuzu sacked Hangzhou, the temple was destroyed..."
Reduced to ashes, he returned to Lake [Huang] to dwell in a temporary hut belonging to his clan. In the seventh year of the Shaoxing era, he manifested his passing.
He instructed that his robes and bowl be used to repair the Ba’en Pagoda, and he was buried on a mountain peak. He was seventy-seven years of age and sixty-two years since his ordination.
In the twenty-fifth year of the Shaoxing era, the local authorities converted his site into the Yanxiang Nunnery and relocated the Ba’en Temple to Niaoke on the northern side of the mountain.
The disciple Huìjìng was in charge of attending to the incense and lamps. He constructed an eastern hall, intending to enshrine the master’s remains there.

During the cremation, his countenance remained as if alive. His nephew, the Court Gentleman Chá, composed an inscription; Chá had extensively researched the Buddhist scriptures and authored the *Record of the Life and Travels of Śākyamuni Buddha*.

Zheqing was a native of Tiantai. His faculties were sharp and his intellect was brilliant. Having studied under Cibian, he established himself as a singular figure whose conduct inspired the respect of his peers.
He was thoroughly proficient in the doctrinal and contemplative systems of the [Tiantai] school. He once said:

"I have fully mastered the profound meanings and deep principles propagated by Siming; however, regarding the Contemplation for Arousing Faith, I lacked sufficient conviction, though I did not dare to disbelieve it."
[He was] the Abbot of Shousheng on Chexi. For twenty years, he did not bow his will before the local powerful families, yet his offerings and provisions never failed.
Throughout his life, he had delighted in drinking tea. One night, he said to his attendant, "Grind a bowl of tea and ring the bell to inform me when it is ready. The attendant reported this.

The bell rang. He assembled the congregation for witness. Having sipped tea from his full bowl, he wrote this verse: "From antiquity, the Buddhas of the three periods have been illusory transformations;
To this day, the five men of the Path have been illusory transformations. Human illusions and Buddha-illusions—whom can one call false or true?
East, west, south, and north—who is distant and who is kin? Fifty-four years, and the bubble has vanished; The vast, clear ocean is without peer. Then, he passed away with serene composure.
Regarding his authored work, the *Five Chapters on the Secret*, his eminent disciples were the two masters Xiangfu Xin and Pengguan.
Qi Bi, whose courtesy name was Fuguī, was granted the title Huijue; he was the uncle of Mo Neihan of Huzhou. He died when he was four years old.
When he was about to be encoffined, he lay within the straw matting; leaning his body against the coffin, he remained prostrate and suppressed [his breath].

No one knew of him. After a long time, he emerged. Those who saw him marveled at him. He was dignified and grave, never speaking or laughing frivolously. Upon obtaining Buddhist scriptures, he read them once or twice and mastered them by heart;
this was not the case with other books. His mother sent him to follow Kaiyuan Hongmin to leave the household life. At nineteen, he received full ordination and studied the teachings under him.

Xiangfu Shenzhi followed Ci-bian. Ci-bian commanded him to lecture on the Mañjuśrī, Prajñāpāramitā, and Amitābha sūtras, and sent him to the Lake region to propagate the teachings, providing him with two gāthās for that purpose.
For ten years, he presided over Chao-hua in Hangzhou, Baozang on the lake, Guanyin in Suzhou, and Shousheng in Xiu;
all submitted to his authority. Following Ci-bian’s tenure as abbot of Tiantong Zhulin, [he succeeded him].

The assembly was no longer composed of worthy individuals. The disciples deliberated, saying, "If we can obtain Master Gong, the temple may flourish. When Master Weng (Yanguo) heard this, he prepared the necessary rites to invite him.
The bells and drums were renewed, and the community quickly flourished once more. Those seated around him were as numerous as stars, exceeding five hundred in number.

As each struck, the response resonated like the tolling of a great bell. At midnight, they venerated an image of Amitābha, circumambulating it while reciting his name. This occurred in the year Jiyou of the Jianyan era.
On the twenty-first day of the eighth month, he said to the head seat: "A many-treasured stupa has appeared before my bed; what does this signify?
The head seat replied, "It is because you have regularly propagated the *Lotus Sūtra* throughout your life; it is the sign of its realization. The Master said, "I wish to see Amitābha."

He gathered the assembly and requested them to assist him in reciting the Buddha’s name. While the monks were maintaining mindfulness, he pointed with his finger and said, "The assembly may now withdraw.

He then beheld Amitābha Buddha and passed away while sitting upright. He was fifty-nine years old. On the day of Jiashen in the intercalary month, he was buried beside Caotang on the western mountain.
He was posthumously granted the title Miaobian, and his stupa was named Huiji. His disciples included Dashi Miyin and Xiuhui.

More than twenty people compiled the *Zuoyuan ji* (Record of the Patriarchal Source), a new commentary on the *Pu xian guan jing* (Sutra on the Meditation of Samantabhadra) and the *Zunsheng chanfa* (Repentance Method of the Honored and Victorious One); the *Zhu jie* (Aiding Explanation);

the *Wuliang yi jing zazu ji* (Miscellaneous Pearl Record of the Sutra of the Infinite Meanings); and the *Ji anban shouyi famen* (Collection on the Dharma Gate of Guarding the Mind through Ānāpāna). This was during his time residing in India.

There was a great drought; the springs and aquifers were exhausted, and the multitude was filled with anxiety. The Master prayed for them in secret. He dreamed that a spring had burst forth on the western slope before the mountain.

They dug there, and a clear stream gushed out; its taste was sweet and it never failed. Consequently, they constructed a square pond and channeled it to the Xiangji Hall, naming it "Dream Spring" (Mengquan) and composing a record to commemorate it.
There was a woman who had suffered from a chronic illness for a long time; she dreamed of entering the temple, where the Master, on her behalf, repented for her past transgressions. Once...

He attained awakening. Without taking medicine, he was healed. The Master had long suffered from wind-vertigo (wind-stroke). He once established a *dharmāśraya* (Dharma hall) and vowed to remain there for seven days.

Before the period was complete, his illness flared up; he fell prostrate and nearly died, yet he did not abandon his practice for even a moment. Sitting in meditative equipoise (*samādhi*) to engage in contemplation, a deity danced before him.

Shortly thereafter, he was free from ailment, and the illness never recurred. When he was in charge of the Treasure Repository, at the end of each year, he would convene a *Buddhānusmṛti-sabhā* (Buddha-recollection assembly) for both men and women.
Each [period] lasts one day and night; the monastic community’s [period] lasts one day and night, without being intermingled.

When the sun sets over Mount Heng, as if striking a hanging drum, the master leads his disciples in circumambulation, chanting with one voice while focusing their mindfulness. They set up a sixteen-foot image and recite the *Amitābha Sūtra*, the *Contemplation Sūtra*, or the "Chapter on Śrī-Ābhāsvara" (Guānshìyīn Chapter).
Thereafter, they focus their mindfulness for ten circumambulations, beginning again once completed. This is done four times during the course of a single day and night.
After more than ten repetitions, he urged them on at midnight, saying: "We do not yet know that when we practice the mindfulness of the Buddha, our minds must always remain settled wherever they are.
Yet our various faculties pursue external objects and commit various unwholesome deeds; for a single *duṣkṛta* offense, one falls into hell for nine hundred thousand years.
How much more so for other offenses, whether light or heavy, whose accumulated sins are equal to the sands of the Ganges! If you do not fix your thoughts upon Amitābha..."
Suffering is difficult to extricate; yet, by invoking the name of the Buddha, the transgressions of eighty billion kalpas of birth and death are eliminated in every moment of thought.
How much more so for those who have undergone the arduous toil of their parents in bringing them into this world, seeking only their liberation?

If I were to break the precepts and fall into suffering, would my parents not surely be filled with despair? Reflecting thus, one will no longer feel such pain. You should each practice with diligent effort. Thus it was heard.

He shed his gall and poured out his heart, prostrating his entire body on the ground. He further said: "By maintaining such focused mindfulness, one achieves the merit of a single day’s practice according to the *Smaller Amitābha Sūtra*.
Now that this has fortunately been accomplished, each person shall surely have a lotus flower grow within the pond of the Pure Land.
This is like Master Xi of Zifu in the Eastern Capital, who, while in meditative absorption, saw that Master Yuanzhao already possessed one."
The golden lotus is exceedingly large. From this day forward, you must constantly practice mindfulness of the Buddha and nurture this flower.

Whenever Master Xingfu Gui of Lingfeng heard of [the master’s] focused recitation, he led his assembly to join in sympathetic joy. He once composed a preface to the *Sūtra of Forty-eight Vows* that was rich in meaning and broad in scope;
he was also skilled at poetry, which was pure, elegant, and lovely, such as when he wrote: "This son has departed for Siming, leaving me..."
I recall Siming: for a thousand years, the Śakra-devendra has shone; for one turn, the ocean of the Teaching has been purified. The Epitaph for Vice-Director Ye Mengde states:
"In the early Zhenghe era, when I was burying my late father on Bian Mountain, I sought a man of the 'beyond-worlds' (fangwai) to befriend.
I found two such men: the Great Master Tizhen, Sigong, and this Master. Indeed, his character was alert, enlightened, and versatile; he attained [realization] through..."
By nature, he was profoundly adept at *dhyāna* (meditation) and did not labor over names or forms. He entered and emerged from the teachings of Confucius and Laozi, further elucidating their words.

Whenever he took his seat, several hundred people would surround him; his discourse was like a carriage descending a slope or water pouring from a jar—like a cascade down a steep roof—it could not be caught or questioned.
Yet his temperament was exceedingly harmonious; in his dealings with others, he never showed a countenance of joy or anger. Liu Yong, the Court Gentleman, composed the posthumous title for his stupa.

The inscription reads: The Master was solitary, lofty, and pure; his learning and conduct surpassed those of others. He enlightened the deluded through compassion and performed the work of a Buddha through his playful mastery of literature.
Monastics and laypeople alike looked up to him with reverence. He was truly one who could perfectly emulate the eloquence of [Mañjuśrī].
The patriarchal tradition of the Zǔfēng family was one characterized by compassion and discernment.
It was like that of the Hú family of Pùjiāng in Wǔlì: they received instruction from Lóngdé, were widely learned and possessed powerful memories, and their discourse surpassed that of their peers.

Relying on his compassion, he traveled to India to seek out an old friend from Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. When the friend presented the doctrines and meanings of the *Ṣaḍabhidharma-śāstra*, the Master engaged him in debate.

The spectators stood as thick as a wall. The opponent’s arguments collapsed, and he withdrew. The Master raised a pole and tied a cloth to it, saying to his fellow students: "When foreigners defeat their enemies, they hoist a banner of victory;
likewise, when one subdues Māra within the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), this too manifests the sign of victory. Now I raise this single pole. It was for this reason that...
He emulated this; the assembly marveled at his fierce spirit and dubbed him "Tiger Cub. The eulogy by Official Feng states:
"Throughout his life, he earned the title 'Tiger Cub' among the multitude," referring to his colleagues who lost their courage upon hearing of his reputation.

Initially, Cibian had received the Three Contemplations from Nanping Tongxiang and intended to transmit them to Huijue Bi, granting permission for a secret transmission within the inner chamber during the stillness of night. When the Master heard of this, [he went there].

Outside the room, he climbed the ladder and lifted the roof tiles, pressing his ear against them to eavesdrop. He mastered the essential points of the Dharma entirely. As the flying snow swirled through the air, his body felt as if clad in armor.

He then said to Cibian, "Regarding the three contemplations of the common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), if there were any remaining traces of the aggregates (*skandha*), I have already understood them thoroughly.
Cibian replied, "Are you like a bandit stealing my Dharma? He immediately intended to expel him, but the assembly interceded on his behalf.
He declined. He merely expressed his thanks and ceased. When he reached Zhuzhu, Wuzhuo had reduced it to ruins, leaving nothing but ashes and embers;

only the scripture repository hall remained. Whenever he went there to lecture, the assembly that gathered was as vast as clouds. Some urged him to solicit donations to build a grand hall. The Master said, "I am concerned only with the circulation [of the teachings];
I do not mind whether the place is cramped. There will surely be those who come later to undertake the construction. Indeed, after the Master passed away, there were those who fulfilled this.

Jue took charge of the affairs of the monastery. On the first day of the ninth month in the fifth year of the Xiangshu era, the imperial carriage visited the Hall of the Great Being (Mahāsattva) to burn incense.

The Master prostrated himself and offered prayers for the Emperor’s majesty; his responses were as fluent as flowing water. The Emperor bestowed upon him the title "Wansui Xiangshan" (Ten Thousand Years Fragrant Mountain) and granted him offerings for the Mahāsattva.
Among those in the Shanjia (Tiantai) school who were renowned as being like tigers, there were three: Dongshan Benru, Siming Daoru, and next...

This was Master [Zhiyi]. When presiding over lectures on the texts, he did not prioritize scholarly composition; he merely provided expositions and raised points of difficulty for three parts of the material.

His verse on the transmission of the Dharma says: "I inform the one to whom this is transmitted: the school of the Single Nature. The Three Thousand Real Phases (*trisāhasra-lakṣaṇa*) are the wondrous Emptiness, Provisionality, and the Middle Way.

In a single thought-moment, the entire Dharma-realm exists; the bodies of living beings and Buddhas are identical. Ordinary people and sages are of one suchness; good and evil are harmonized within principle. This is the body of Vairocana..."
The earth is as profound and empty as space. If one understands this principle, every phenomenon is perfectly interfused; whether turning left or right, its enjoyment is inexhaustible.
To honor the original aspiration of the Dharma, over several dozen people, including Bailianxian, erected a stupa at the northwest corner of the temple.
Zhai Xian of the Qian family was given the honorary title Qingbian. He was a native of Qiandang and followed Master Ziyou of Jingming on Mount Hu.
At the age of twenty-three, he underwent the scriptural examination and received full ordination. From Faming, Huixian, Cizun, and Lingwan, he inherited the teachings of the Tiantai school.

Once, while suffering from a pestilential disease that could not be cured by any medicine, he diligently recited the name of the Honored One Guanyin. In a dream, the Great Being (Avalokiteśvara) appeared, wielding an axe and chisel.
He opened his chest and replaced it with another organ; by stroking it with his hand, the ailment was immediately cured.

In his daily life, there were no subtle texts or profound meanings that he did not penetrate thoroughly. His lectures and expositions were unhindered, and his writings were composed with literary elegance.

All considered that the Great Being had bestowed upon him the *pratisamvid-samādhi* (the samādhi of eloquence). He resided at Daolin Temple in Qiantang, then at Shangfang Temple in Changshu, followed by Dongling Temple.
Next he stayed at Nanping; then at Guanghua in Gusu; then at Fushui in Sanqu; and later he resided at Shangfang. He grew old in the East.
Nanping was where he had been invited by Imperial Secretary Jiang. A poem was presented to him, which said: "The man of the Way once again expounds the Lotus Teachings."
The family tradition of Fuzhong—listen well! Fushizhu’s *Sushu* states: "He sat firmly atop Mount Ding, extending his compassion to transform the world at large.
Drawing from the waters of Dongling, he moistened the sprouts of withered grain; raising clouds from Nanping, he poured down the rain of ambrosia.

During the Zhenghe era, he composed a record on the Bodhisattva Precepts at the Upper Abode, which the world calls the *Dingshan Ji*. It contains twenty-eight verses in praise of the wondrous [Dharma].
These scriptures all encompass the essential purport of the sutras; they do not rely on mere literary elegance. As the "Introductory Chapter" states:
"Only when Maitreya and Mañjuśrī both become eloquent can one know that they have personally received the ancient majesty and authority.

On the eleventh day of the first month in the fourth year of the Jianyan era, he gathered the assembly to chant the *Amitābha Sūtra* and recite the name of Amitābha, composing a verse which said: "The wooden puppet of seventy-seven years / Meets the stage to act..."
He played freely and unrestrainedly. Now that all the threads have been gathered in, he departs with the Northern Dipper hidden from view.

His disciple Faqing divided the śarīra relics and enshrined them in the abbot’s quarters of the Shangfang Monastery. His eminent disciple Fayun of Jingde Monastery in Gusu compiled the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Names and Meanings) in seven fascicles.

Zhong Min was a monk from Xiangfu Temple in Quzhou who had long relied upon Fuzong Zhong and subsequently relied upon Nanping Wen, with whom he was renowned for his eloquent debate—referred to as "Tiger’s Cub.
During the Zhenghe era, he returned to his hometown to preside over Fushui Temple; his door was filled with visitors whose shoes lay outside, and he would often speak with great confidence, saying:
"I shall not lecture on a major treatise unless there are five hundred disciples beneath my seat. Therefore, throughout his life, he lectured exclusively on minor volumes.
As he was about to pass away, he gathered the assembly in the Xiangfu Dharma Hall and ascended the lion throne.

Just as he sat cross-legged upon the silver platform, [a being] arrived from the West and shouted, "Throughout my life, I have understood the primary meaning (paramārtha) and vowed to attain the golden terrace (suvarṇapīṭha). Having said this, he closed his eyes and suddenly passed away. This was witnessed.
Those present cried out in astonishment. As for the "Lion Throne," it was a carved wooden structure fashioned in the likeness of a lion, over ten feet high, upon which a lotus pedestal was placed.
This temple had produced many eminent masters, and this throne was always used as the step for their ascent. Since Master [Dao]xi once ascended it, no one has followed him.
Now that the tradition has been changed to Chan, it has been abandoned in a corner of the hall. Written in the *Xianzhang ji* (Collection of Ritual Precepts), with a preface by the author himself.

He said: "The disciples of Śākya, when they have something to record, invariably seek out high officials, ministers, or great officers to compose a preface for it, placing it at the beginning and appending it to the end.

They use such prefaces to drive home their records of conduct. Yet, as for those gentlemen of the world who wear the scholar's robes and caps, how could they know my rightness or discern my wrongness?
If what I have done is correct and lacks a preface, can Heaven cause me to perish? Even if what I have done were incorrect and yet possessed a preface, could a man ever suppress it?"

Alas! I am biased in my practical conduct, and thus my mind does not accord with what is right. Why is this? If something accords with the Sage’s mind, it will naturally circulate without obstruction;

if it slightly deviates from the purport of the teaching, one can surely expect it to be submerged and not practiced. To fail to obstruct what is right while offering but little praise—this is my failing.
"When the true wind does not prevail, yet one avoids misleading those who come to study—whether this is right or wrong, whether it is practiced or not—among these, who can truly be said to know me?
How ultimate! This is a public statement of universal truth. Even the Duke of Zhou’s deliberations on establishing the capital at Luo could not surpass this."
