The fourth patriarch of Zhongxing, the fifteenth-generation Dharma successor, was named Fulin (also known by the title Huizhao). He was a preeminent disciple of Mingzhi. When the Sengtong Yitian came to seek the Dharma, he first arrived at Siming.
The Prefect ordered Mingzhi to serve as his host, while Yitian took Mingzhi as his teacher and befriended the Master. [Yitian] requested...

He compiled a treatise on the various categories of the Buddhist teachings (*bājiàochénglèishū*) and circulated it upon his return to his country. The text read as follows: "Writing is the vessel through which the sages lodged the subtle Way.

Even its authors cannot be treated with negligence; those who govern ought to devote their full hearts to it. In the past, when the trigrams were drawn and writing was created, the response from Heaven was most manifest:
either the River yielded the diagrams, or the spirits wept. This continued down to the times of Yao and Shun, when they toured the four quarters..."
I have examined my late father’s writings on the text of the *Spring and Autumn Annals*. Confucius composed the *Chunqiu* with ever-increasing care;

his method was inherited from the *Zuozhuan*, which clarifies various principles and precedents such that there is hardly a single word that was uttered casually. Even down to the formation of "武" (wu) from "止" (zhǐ) and "才" (cái), "蠱" (gǔ) from "皿" (míng) and "蟲" (chóng), and extending to "天" (tiān) from "一" (yī) and "大" (dà), and "王" (wáng) from "三" (sān) and "貫" (guàn)—here again we see that the application of written characters is not something created by human beings.

Regarding the texts of the *Shi* and *Shu*, the *Erya* provides their glosses; as for the legacy of the Yan and Liu dynasties, the civil culture flourished greatly. It was then that Xu Shen compiled the *Shuowen*.

During the reign of Emperor Wu of the Liang, the *Yupian* was produced by one of heavenly endowment, and its four tones brought further benefit to the world—a system which even ten thousand generations could not alter.
Thus we know that the enterprise of writing and characters is indeed great! Under the Great Song, there are the offices of Proofreader (*Jiaoshu*) and Corrector (*Zhengzi*).

The Official: Dong Gu was the functionary of Sima Qian and Ban Gu; it is for all such reasons as these. Cao’an said: "This composition is exceedingly lofty; it almost rivals the brush of the Grand Historian.
Regarding his presiding over the Three Studies, he was concerned that students were unable to advance in virtue and cultivate their practice. In their youth, they were indolent and weak in spirit;
in their later years, they would speculate on fate and compare appearances. He therefore said in jest: "I have two great prohibitions while presiding over the Dharma seat. At thirty—"
In the past, one was not permitted to recite the name of Amitābha Buddha; after the age of seventy, one was not permitted to maintain the incantations for dispelling calamities.
Although these [prohibitions] resemble the frivolous, they are in fact timely remedies for the ailments of the age.
Jue Xian was posthumously granted the title Chengzhao. He was born into the Chen family of Cixi; at nine months of age, he lost both his parents.

Wang comforted him, saying, "This child’s bone structure is extraordinary and magnificent; he shall surely leave the household life. At seven years old, he took the precepts from Master Jingzhenzi Nan and received the scriptures;

upon reading them once, he could recite them by heart. After receiving full ordination, he studied the teachings under Mingzhi, followed by Qingbian of Naping, and finally Cibian of Tianzhu, who bestowed upon him a prophetic prediction of his future enlightenment.
Successively, at the beginning of the Jingkang era, he presided over Baolin Monastery. Every day he lectured on the Mahāyāna sūtras, and his disciples filled the hall.

When the masses requested him to lecture on the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* due to a spring drought, as soon as the assembly concluded, rain fell for three days. News of this divine miracle spread joyfully for a hundred li.

He erected a banner of the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* and requested monks to recite ten thousand sections of the scripture to lead the entire district. Subsequently, he presided over Yanqing Monastery, where he greatly propagated the ancestral teachings.
Xi. In the eighth year of the Shaoxing era, he retired to Baolin Temple due to illness. He constructed a small chamber behind the abbot’s quarters and named it the Miaolian Hall, where he resided.
He committed himself to reciting the scriptures for a set period of ten thousand fascicles, and further chanted the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* forty-seven times.

In the fifteenth year, at the age of [seventy-]five, he gathered the assembly to preach the essential points of the transmission of the Dharma. On the sixteenth day of the first month of the following year, he sat in meditation.
He passed away at the age of seventy-eight, with fifty years of ordination. His stupa was erected beside his quarters. Dr. Lian Bu composed the inscription.

Later, during a quiet night, someone heard the sound of sutra recitation coming from within the stupa. Upon opening the sarcophagus, they found that the sacred remains were bound by cords that had not decayed; their color was like that of bronze.

Zongzhao was close with Cān’ān. On his behalf, he composed a petition for the invitation to Xingjiao on Xiaoxi, which states: "His profound spirit nourishes within; his solitary style overflows without.

He has investigated the subtle points of the five thousand scrolls [of the Lotus Sūtra] without falling into the trap of mere words. For twenty years, he has burned with intensity of mind, yet it felt to him as if it were but the duration of a meal.

Having served at Zhuanqing Monastery for many years, he has twice lectured upon the fundamental tenets of the Tiantai school: the Eight Teachings, the Five Periods, and the Ten Modes of Profound Contemplation."

His three contemplations were the whetstone upon which he moved with ease; his commentaries were clear, meticulous, and profound, penetrating and encompassing all matters such that his contemporaries acknowledged his excellence.

In the *Bingchen* year of the Shaoxing era, the military governor of Mingzhou invited him to reside at Shoujing Monastery. Having suffered during the Jianyan disturbances, only the main hall remained.

Three successive administrators had taken charge, yet no affairs had been consolidated. With only a few thousand thatched rafters and a dozen or so emaciated monks remaining, he settled there with ample composure. Not long after...

I have often harbored this hope. I used to say: "The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas establish Buddha-works throughout the entirety of empty space and the pervasiveness of the Dharma-realm, yet they cannot accomplish them on a mere span of land like that of Yunxi.
This is surely due to the power of one's own capacity. Even if I were able to do so, what would it amount to?
The lands bestowed by Prince Jeta and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada are beyond reckoning—amounting to hundreds, thousands, tens of thousands, millions, and billions."

He devoted himself solely to diligent study and thorough mastery of the teachings, pursuing his cultivation with earnest resolve. Students arrived daily, and his spiritual influence spread far and wide.
Those among his disciples and lay patrons who wished to engage in the work all contributed their resources until it was completed in four years.
On the twenty-fifth day of the third month of the fourth year, he passed away at Falian Temple. A general account of his virtuous achievements may be found in Xue Chengji’s record.
Commentary. The Commentary states: Venerable Chaoguo’s myriad practices were as firm as gold; his solitary standard stood like a towering wall.

Having departed from the seat of Mount Ling, he early on proclaimed the patriarchal style of Mount Tai. Admiring the Way of Fazhi, he ascended the Hall of Mingzhi. There was no separation between life and death;
he encountered the mechanism of Chengzhao and entered the chamber of Yuanzhao. Master and attendants intermingled, and he thrice received the title of "Name."

Lan’s fame spread far and wide as he expounded the precious volumes of the secret treasury; his attendant was clad in blue robes, and white-haired elders joyfully followed him as he contemplated the deep marks of the Buddha.
He cleared a hundred mu of wasteland to establish a pure monastery; when the first snows of winter filled the air, his bones were warmed by the lotuses that floated upon the flames.
Just as he looked forward to the universal nourishment of the rain of compassion, who would have thought the bridge of the Dharma would suddenly collapse?

[The lineage] was broken. Yet the oral teachings of seventy-two years still remain as surviving fragments; the mind-to-mind transmission of several thousand years has once again been linked to the orthodox succession.
Daochen, styled Yuanchang, was granted the honorary title Yuanbian. He was of the Peng clan of Leqing; his mother, Lady Wang, dreamed of purple vapors swirling around her.

He was born with a disposition toward the supramundane. In his childhood, he pursued the path of transcendence; upon receiving full ordination, he studied the Vinaya and mastered its great principles.

He received the transmission of the teachings and contemplation from Xi’an Yuan, who regarded him highly, saying, "This is a person who has returned for a second birth. Later, he met Yuanzhao Guang at Yanqing.
He resided at Guangji for twelve years and subsequently moved to Guangci. In the third year of the Jianyan era, when the imperial carriage visited Yongjia, an edict was issued [to appoint him].
The former residence of Lin Ling-su became Zifu Monastery. When it was necessary to select a master for it, Prime Minister Lü responded to the imperial decree and renovated it.
Initially, funds were insufficient; he pledged his *saṃghāṭī* robe to a merchant, who, seeing a brilliant light shining from it one night, returned the garment to the mountain at dawn.
There was originally no well there; [Lin] pointed to the ground and had it excavated. This has been passed down since ancient times.
There was a spring named Tiankang, from which water gushed forth below; it was sweet and clear. Yuanzhao, having retired from public life, invited the Master to preside over it.

The area, once adorned with gold and azure tiles, had been ravaged by war and reduced to weeds and brambles; the site for meditative contemplation had become intermingled with the common ways of the populace.

He sighed, saying, "How can this field where Buddhas are selected be allowed to remain abandoned for long? With sincere heart, he prayed to the Sage, and as days and months passed, those who turned their hearts toward him [increased].
The assembly was completely renovated and restored. For those whose illnesses were so severe as to be difficult to cure, he would preach the Dharma and offer consecrated food;
their ailments would then be healed accordingly. The Prefect, Qin Hui, was harsh in his administration, and the prisons were filled with inmates. None of the subordinate officials dared to speak out.

During a summer drought, [the Master] offered prayers for rain and spoke to him with tactful persistence. Qin was moved to realization and immediately released over a hundred prisoners. That very night, rain fell in abundance, and the year’s harvest was saved.
There was a year of great abundance. At Zifuleqing, the riverbank collapsed several times. It was rumored that a spirit resided there;
when the officials and commoners requested that he confer the Mahāyāna precepts, the spirit sent word through a medium to express its gratitude, and the bank no longer crumbled.

Later, while returning from visiting Master Yinchi (Yuwang Shen) who was ill, he said to his disciples: "Grand claims are often without substance and ultimately prove useless. On the twenty-third day of every month...
He established a ritual for focused mindfulness and exhorted both monastics and laypeople to participate; at each assembly, nearly ten thousand people would gather. He practiced this for many years.

When he manifested illness, he instructed the monks to take turns chanting the *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra*. He sat upright and chanted along with them, continuing day and night without ceasing, seeking a vision of the holy countenance.
On the seventh day, he said to his head seat, "I have attained the sign. When the assembly heard a wondrous fragrance, they saw a small body of Amitābha, and subsequently, they saw a large one.
His body was suffused with a radiant joy that manifested upon his brows and eyelashes. He bathed, changed his robes, and wrote a verse which said: "The Pure Land is but the mind;

fundamentally, there is neither delusion nor enlightenment. When not a single thought arises, one enters the first stage [of the Bodhisattva path]. He then had [his disciples] recite the *Anle-xing* (Peaceful Practices) chapter. Suddenly, he sat up and passed away.
His remains were kept in a shrine for several months, yet his countenance remained as if alive. This was the sixteenth day of the twelfth month of the Guiyou year of the Xiangshu era.

His lifespan was sixty-eight years; his *dharma*-age was fifty-one. He had three junior disciples and over two hundred *dharma*-heirs. He was buried beside the stupa of his ancestral teacher, Chongfa.

Initially, while at his place of study, he practiced the Amitābha Repentance. During a period of meditative contemplation, he dreamed of an elderly monk sitting upon a rush mat who said, "I am Siming.
The Master prostrated and asked, "Regarding the habitual tendencies within this one school, [how shall I proceed]? Daochen... [text continues].
"I have not yet attained a deep understanding of these signs. I pray that the Venerable One will reveal their subtle and esoteric meaning. The Venerable One nodded his head in agreement.

Upon this, [the student's] mind-ground was awakened and the ice of doubt melted away; thus, though coming from different paths, they were all brought back to the Correct Way. Furthermore, the monk Qingshun of Zifusi dreamed that the various Patriarchs came to visit the Master.
An attendant stood by holding a chart of their positions, yet the eighth position was missing. Shun pointed to it and asked about it. The attendant replied, "You..."
The Master succeeded him in that position and presided over Yanqing Temple; he was indeed the eighth patriarch. Wang Boxiang recorded his deeds and virtues, noting that the Master once wrote:
"The Pure Land of the Mind is but one and the same. This is truly because Amitābha realized that my own mind is the precious land."
My mind possesses the blissful land of Amitābha. Though distant, it is near; not separated by even a single thought-moment. Though near, it is distant, spanning ten trillion *kṣetras*.
It is like the bright moon in a clear blue sky reflected in all waters: the water does not rise upward, nor does the moon descend;
the water and the moon are of one and the same realm, naturally illuminating and reflecting one another.
Jixian’s courtesy name was De’ao, and his posthumous title was Zhengjiao. He was born into the Ji family, whose hereditary occupation was wine-selling at the market.
There were three siblings in the family, and the Master was the youngest; he suddenly sighed and said, "Can the turbid wealth of this world truly sink my lifelong pure aspirations?
He then went to a teacher to shave his head and receive full ordination, studying under the Chief Seat Mingyi of Tianzhu, and later followed Baiqing.
Lianhui listened to the *Mahā-śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Mohe zhiguan), transmitted it, and practiced it. At the age of forty-one, he succeeded to the seat of wisdom.
He lectured for thirteen years, diligently applying mindfulness twelve times each day, reciting the ten recitations while facing west each time, and dedicating the merit through the making of vows.
Someone asked: "The Lotus Samādhi involves one land being all lands, one body being all bodies, and one Buddha being all Buddhas.
Why does the Master not rely on the *Mohe zhiguan* (Great Calming and Contemplation) to cultivate the wondrous practice of the Lotus Sūtra as the cause for rebirth? The Master replied:
Jingxi said: "For instance, in the 'Chapter on Distinguishing Merits,' one directly contemplates that within this land, the four lands are fully present.
Therefore, this Buddha-body is itself the bodies of the three Buddhas, and this great assembly is itself all assemblies.

Because delusions have not yet been severed, the 'Peaceful Practices' (Anle Xing) represent the functional aspect of practice within the Sahā Pure Land. Thus, without leaving the defilement of the Sahā world, one perceives [the pure realm]."

Purity through Co-residence. Question: There are many categories of lands where beings co-reside; why must it necessarily be the Land of Ultimate Bliss? Answer: Because the teachings speak of it extensively;

because of the capacity of sentient beings; because it gathers in and nurtures living beings; because it causes them to focus their minds single-mindedly; because past affinities are profound; and because it refers to the majority of cases.

When the Master was about to enter the retreat (jie), he felt slightly unwell. He then entered the city to take leave of the officials of the prefecture and county, returned to his quarters, closed his door, and cut off all visitors. His...
He summoned a physician in vain. The Master was startled. The assembly said, "We merely wish to have him administer medicine; we pray you comply with worldly convention.
After the physician had completed his examination, they sent him off with generous gifts. The Master had his bed moved so that he faced west and set up an image of Amitābha.

Suddenly, he asked his attendant, "Has the *gaṇḍī* been struck at the Upper Hall for the repentance service? The attendant replied, "It has already been struck. The Master said, "Please have a practitioner recite a sutra for me. Before the sutra was finished—

His life came to an end. At the two monasteries on East Mountain, the bells and drums could be heard from one another. At the Guantang Hall of Nengren, the sound of the Buddha’s voice was heard as a swelling roar, and the sounds of celestial music were clear and resonant.
Passersby opened their windows to gaze out, sighing at such an unprecedented occurrence. When the news of his passing arrived at dawn, it was verified that what they had heard and seen was not false.
His remains were enshrined in a stupa to the northeast of the monastery. He had more than thirty dharma heirs, whose deeds are recorded in the *Baizhu ji* (Treasure Pearl Collection).
Liaoran was of the Xue family of Linhai; his mother was surnamed Hu. She prayed for a son at the Stone Avalokiteśvara Image in Wugai Monastery at Zhang’an (arriving by sea from the Tang dynasty).
She dreamed that she ascended the Buddha hall, where a monk with a thick beard and white teeth stood upon the steps holding a lotus flower and said to her, "When you eat, you shall conceive.
On the thirteenth day of the month, she gave birth to an extraordinary child. At the age of seven, he studied the Way under Master Zhongyuan of Xiangfu.
At sixteen, he received full ordination under Huì of Ān-guó. Huì took him as a disciple. He dreamed that he was sitting upon a stone platter while floating across the sea;

the mountains of the sea rose majestically, and he was endowed with wondrous marks. Sitting amidst a grove of bamboo, he thought to himself, "This is the abode of Avalokiteśvara, where I have spent my life receiving, upholding, hearing, and seeing [the teachings].
He rose and, with palms joined, offered praise in a hundred verses. Upon waking, he still remembered half of them. From this time on, his eloquence flourished.
Tài was unimpeded in his eloquence. He attended Huìqiān at Bái-lián Temple; when Huì passed away, he went to visit Lì of Yǎnqìng Temple. Lì received him with exceptional courtesy.
He once inquired about the textual meanings of three passages: the ten dharma-realms from the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, the three worlds, and the "ten suchnesses" from the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*.
Together they reached three thousand [verses]. Jingxi asked, "Where does the 'pointing out' of the wondrous object (*miao-jing*) originate?

The Master replied, "The *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* are dead dharma-gates; the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* with its 'ten suchnesses' (*daśa-tathatā*) is the living dharma-gate. Li Shou nodded in agreement.

When Chao Shuo was serving as the Prefectural Official of Ban, he had little official business and severed all external attachments; he frequently discussed the Tiantai teachings with him. Mingzhao of Siming was a lecturer.

Dao Ru was as courageous and fierce as a tiger when debating with his teacher, ultimately besting him. When he traveled to Guangyan, he was invited [to serve], saying, "I dare not betray what I have learned;
I regard a single eloquent disputation as wisdom. He resided there for six years, during which time the position of White Lotus was left vacant.

Li Fu-ma’s grandsons were particularly fond of Chao, and it was through them that Chao’s reputation as a teacher became widely known. When letters of recommendation arrived, he declined the invitation.

He did not accept. After twenty-four years had passed, students vied with one another to seek his guidance; his stūpas and temples were magnificent and eminent. Neither drought nor flood required ritual intervention;

when performing *yú* and *róng* sacrifices, they prayed solely to the Master. In the Wǔwǔ year of the Shàoxīng era, a Great Dharma Assembly was established in Nínghǎi, and the Master delivered lectures there.
Seeing someone holding a warrant, he said, "The Tuṣita Heaven invites you to preach the Dharma. The Master replied, "The assembly has not yet concluded.
The messenger said, "There must be no delay; you should go first, followed by the next in order. He looked at the warrant and saw that several people were named. The Master tore out his own name.
On the fifth month of the year *xīnyǒu*, he dreamed of two dragons playing in the air. One dragon transformed into a deity and descended from the sky, producing [a scroll] from his sleeve.
The document reads: Chang said, "The Master shall return in seven days. Ying replied, "Yes, yes. Upon waking, he preached the Dharma for the assembly and declined visitors to practice contemplation.

He wrote more than two hundred words and showed them to the assembly; at the end of the writing, he said: "When the World-Honored One entered nirvana, he taught the *Śāriputra-parivarta* (the *Yijiao jing*).
When the Great Master Zhi [Zhiyi] was approaching his end, he taught the method of contemplating the mind (*guanxin fa*). I now speak this writing. Having finished, he bathed and changed his clothes.

He sat upright and gathered the assembly; while reciting the *Amitābha Sūtra*, he passed away upon reaching the passage on the Western World. On the *renshen* day of the eighth month, he was buried at Donggang.
He was sixty-five years of age and forty-nine years since his ordination. He was posthumously granted the title Zhizhong.

On the evening of his passing, practitioners of the Nengren lineage heard extraordinary celestial music and beheld auspicious light illuminating the heavens. The power of his vows and the strength of his path were truly vast.

He was widely known; those who sought him at his door numbered in the tens of thousands, and those who transmitted his teachings exceeded two hundred. He presided over many famous monasteries, and there were no high-ranking ministers who protected the Dharma who did not honor and revere him.
Prime Minister Fan named the hall where he resided, and Vice President Xie composed a eulogy for his true likeness, which was carved upon stone.

He authored the five-fascicle *Shi Nanyue Zhiguan Zongyuan Ji* (Record of the Perfect Source of the Nanyue Tradition of Calming and Contemplation) and the two-fascicle *Jie Shibu’er Men Shuyao* (Explanation of the Essential Pivot of the Ten Non-dual Gates).

The *Jiaoyi Huxi Qianhou Ji* (Collected Works on Doctrinal Principles from Before and After Huxi) consists of eight fascicles. When local residents fell ill, he would recite incantations over them, and they invariably recovered.

The Hu family of Ninghai cleared a room for him, where a divine being took up residence; however, when he preached the precepts, the spirit moved elsewhere. Later, the path to the Dragon Pond in the rear garden was perilous, making it difficult for those who came to pray.

He recited incantations to relocate it to a more accessible spot; thereupon, a great wind and rain arose, with sand flying and stones rolling, blocking the old site so that it could be moved. This remains convenient to this day.
As for Zhanzi (湛字), he was from the Jiao family of Yongjia. His mother dreamed of swallowing a precious pagoda and gave birth to him.

He left home at a young age, passed the scriptural examinations to receive ordination, and pursued his studies in the monastic academies. He studied under Lingqin, Lupu, Cihui, and others in western and eastern Zhejiang, eventually arriving at Hengshan.

He was a senior disciple of Huìjué and presided over Shòushèng Temple. His door was filled with visitors' shoes, and he lectured without a single day of omission. Whenever he performed Buddhist rites, there were invariably miraculous responses.
He maintained a daily regimen of reciting the *Lotus Sūtra* in seven fascicles and chanting the name of Amitābha twenty thousand times, recording these as his practice for purifying karma.

He authored the *Huguo ji* (Record for Protecting the State) in four fascicles as a commentary on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, and another four fascicles each for his commentaries on the *Guanjing* and the *Guangming jing*.

He also wrote the *Jiaming ji* (Collection of Pseudonyms) in three fascicles, the *Fuzong qi yi* (Reinstating the School and Resolving Doubts) in one fascicle, and the *Jingang banruo hui jie* (Exegesis of the Assembly on the Diamond Prajñāpāraṃitā) in two fascicles. In his daily life, he slept little;

even during the height of summer, he would set aside his drowsiness and cease fanning himself. Sitting amidst the weeds and brush, he recited the *Amitābha Sūtra*, offering his body and the two kinds of wealth (Dharma and material) as alms to the mosquitoes and gadflies.
His disciples, finding his advanced age unbearable, requested that he cease his ascetic practices. The Master said, "How could a mere creature of the air be worthy of the Sublime Vehicle?
I wish for my blood to be consumed, so that it may become a karmic connection upon passing through your ears. To this day, the "Mosquito Feeding Platform" remains.

During the Jianyan era, he composed the *Shengwenhuiyi* (A Record of the Miracles of the Śrāvakas), at the end of which he wrote: "The Xiongnu left Hangzhou and entered Xiu; the fires of war followed the dikes, plundering like swarms of bees."

I have risen and, sighing that my life may end this very morning, have hastily written this. How does this differ from when Zhāng’ān was describing the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra Xuányì* while bandits were rampant?
When he was building his carriage-cottage at Chēxī, his bright windows and clean desks had already been taken by others;

During the summer months, he would bury a large jar in the ground, filling it with cold spring water and leaning against it to refresh his body.

He practiced this without ceasing for several years, until the multitude jokingly named it the "Hall of the Five Warmths. He was able to stand out as a peerless leader in his field, expanding the ancestral Way;
it was truly here that he cultivated his character and nurtured his virtue. In his later years, he resided in seclusion at An-yuan Monastery during the Geng year of the Shaoxing era.

In the seventh month of the year [Shen], he passed away while sitting in meditation without illness. When his body was cremated, śarīra relics were found wherever the smoke reached, fulfilling the wishes of those who sought them.

Fajiu, whose secular surname was Zhao, was from Yuyao. At the age of seven, he took the Dharma name Zoujiu and became a disciple of Zongwei of Longquan. At fifteen, he passed the scriptural examination and was selected;
the following year, by imperial decree, he received the tonsure and was enrolled at Kaiyuan Temple in his home prefecture to receive full ordination. Thereafter, he relied upon Zhizhong at Guang...
Yan saw that Huijue was enlightened in the practice of Guanyin. When [Huijue] traveled to India, Yan accompanied him. Upon his passing into *nirvāṇa*, Yan again followed Nengren Fazhao.
During the Jianyan era, when the state was in turmoil, many Zen monks fled to Fuzhou; Yan also traveled extensively there to broaden his learning and experience.
He long followed Furuo of Furi, who would summon Yan for night-time sittings and invariably inquire about the Tiantai school.
His *Jingguan* (Contemplation of the Objects) and the general meaning of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* were highly praised.

When He Gui of the Ministry of Personnel heard that he had achieved merit through his recitation of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra*, he tested him on the anniversary of his parents' deaths; indeed, there was a profound spiritual response. Invited by the Luo family of Cixi to preside over Yuanzhan Hermitage, students flocked to him from all directions. [The year was] the thirteenth of the Shaoxing era.
In the [blank] year, the Prefect Mo Jiang invited Qingxiu [to reside there]. Qingxiu’s retreat was located about one *she* from Xiaoxi Town, deeply hidden among crags and gullies.

There, the springs were clear and the rocks cold; mist and clouds obscured the landscape even by day. He lived there for seven years, during which time his Dharma hall was renovated and students flocked to him like spokes converging at a hub.

Troubled by the fact that the individual quarters for practitioners were numerous and fraught with many defects, he opened up a communal hall, equipped with clean desks, bright windows, meditation boards, and *pú-tí* mats.

Whether sitting on meditation cushions, reclining, or walking in meditation; whether speaking, remaining silent, looking, or listening—everyone was dignified and solemn. Even those who were ill or frail did not dare to slacken in the slightest.
This was surely the result of his personal leadership. Furthermore, seeing students clinging to the literal words of the texts and merely flapping their lips and tongues, he sighed and said:
"The Way of Tiantai, though it flourished through Siming, has also declined because of him. Unless a sage returns..."
He was born. Who could have supported him? To the left of the monastery is Lion Rock (*Siṃha-śilā*); he constructed a small chamber there and named it "Fearless" (*Abhaya*), dwelling within it.
Daily he recited the seven scriptures. He passed away in the winter of the nineteenth year; his age was fifty, and his *dharma*-years were thirty-five.
His stupa was erected to the west of the monastery at the foot of the mountain. The recluse Chijue Yan Shengtú claimed that he had reached the master’s threshold.

He composed an inscription and seven elegies for his funeral. His successor in the Dharma was Mizhimiao Yunzhu Yanqing, who intended to have [the texts] engraved on stone but was dissuaded by public opinion.
The Master possessed a naturally sharp intelligence and a memory that surpassed others. In ordinary life he was grave and silent, appearing as if unable to speak;
yet when resolving obstructions, his eloquence flowed like a stream. His deportment was graceful and unhurried, never offending those around him. His fellow residents had long...
He lived there without showing either joy or resentment. Yúnjiě’s conduct was exceedingly lofty; he remained hidden for a long time at Míngzhōu and Língfēng.
He authored the *Direct Commentary on Perfect Enlightenment* (*Yuánjué zhíjiě*), which scholars esteemed as authoritative.
Shenhuan, whose courtesy name was Yaowen, was a native of Anji in Huzhou. He studied under Huijue and was recognized by his fellow disciples as one of the most eminent.
During the Xiaoshing era, he presided over Siqi Juewu Monastery. Beyond his lectures and exhortations, he devoted himself solely to literary composition.

Regarding difficult passages in the great Mahayana scriptures where preceding masters had provided interpretations that were not yet exhaustive, he thoroughly analyzed and clarified them. In total, there were one hundred chapters; these are known in the world as the "Huan Bai Zhang" (The Hundred Chapters of Shenhuan).

The deities of the various directions have no fixed order for their seating. Having examined the Great Canon (*Tripitaka*) and consulted the words of the Patriarchs, I have composed these "Biographies of the Devas" entirely according to my own judgment.
The preface states: According to the *Baolu*, the seat of Guṇakāraṇḍavyūha-devī (Gongde Tian) is placed to the left of the Buddha.

If the ritual arena is spacious, the seats of Mahāprajñāpāramitā (Dabian Tian) and the Four Heavenly Kings are further placed to the right; thus one knows that among worldly people, some [arrange them] in groups of seven.
Whether there be sixteen, eighteen, or twenty-one positions, they all belong exclusively to the category of ghosts and spirits; their increase or decrease is merely a matter of convenience.
Now, if one wishes to establish a hierarchy of honor and precedence and arrange the ancestral seats (zhāomù), it is truly very difficult. For instance, Guizimǔ is in fact a rākṣasa.
How could they possibly be ranked alongside Mahābrahmā? There is a goddess named Puṇyadattā and a son named General Vaiśravaṇa.
Now, Puṇyadattā is placed at the top, followed by Brahmā and Śakra, with General Vaiśravaṇa and Hārītī listed last—is this not a violation of the proper order?
I lament the delusions of conventional practice; as no one has yet clarified this, I have searched through the Tripiṭaka and composed this [text] on the various devas.

Biographies. They are arranged according to their respective ranks, and each is explained in its proper place. Generally speaking, among the heavens there are hosts and guests, males and females, fundamental and manifested, and the manifest and the hidden.
Mahābrahmā is the lord of the three realms; Śakra is the lord of the Heaven of the Thirty-three; and the Four Heavenly Kings are the lords of the eight classes of spirits.
As for Guṇakara and Mahāmati, they are merely guests and sojourners. Guṇakara resides in Northern India, while Mahāmati...
They dwell among mountains and marshes, having originally no presiding leader; this is what is meant by "having a host.

Figures such as Guṇakāra, Mahāprajñā, and the Tree Spirits are all female in form, while Brahmā and the Four Heavenly Kings are all male in form; this is what is meant by "having both male and female.
The five hundred followers of Vajrapāṇi and Guhyapada are all originally great bodhisattvas; they currently manifest in the traces of divine images. This...

This is what is meant by having both the fundamental and the manifest. When Mahāprajñāpāramitā expounds the True Dharma before the Buddha, although her rank is that of a guest-deva and her body is constrained by female form, her words and deeds are manifest;
yet at other times she merely acts as a responsive influence among the assembly and does not engage in public proclamation.

Even when exercising authority as a sovereign king and appearing in the form of a man, her words and deeds remain obscure. This is what is meant by having both manifestation and concealment. One should know this.
Regarding these four deities, one may speak of them as "Heaven. Because the light of the sun and moon illuminates the world;
because Kārttikeya provides protection against military calamities; because Sāgara protects against wind and rain;
and because King Yama presides over the netherworld—these constitute twenty-one positions. If Hārītī is combined with Mātṛkā (the Mother of Ghosts), there are then twenty positions.
[The text] ends here. Master Guan remarked: "In only a few hundred characters, it encompasses all the heavens; the intent of the vow to protect and uphold [the teachings] is fully expressed therein.

Furthermore, there is one fascicle of the *Anleji* (Record of Peace and Bliss) and two fascicles of the *Yuanjue shu* (Commentary on the Perfect Enlightenment Sutra). His eminent disciple Jue’an, Jianyan, propagated the teachings at Jiaoyuan.
Sun Jian was held in high esteem by him, while Tang Siyi was close to him. [Jianyan] presided over Tianzhu Monastery.
Sishi’s courtesy name was Qiushan, and his style name was Yuantong. He was born into the Zhan family of Linping in Hangzhou. At the age of seven, he took the monk Guoyang Shenying as his teacher.

At sixty-six years of age, he received full ordination within the Dharma and transmitted the Vinaya teachings of the Great Wisdom (Mahāprajñā). Aspiring to the Way of Tiantai, he served Puming Jing at the Pure Society.
When Puming ascended the seat, Sishi became his dharma heir. He then requested Qian Juewu to accompany the Master on his travels, and they subsequently moved to another location.
Shangzhu said to him, "The seat of awakening is vacant; no one can replace you. An official summons from the commandery has arrived and cannot be declined.

He opened his door to receive disciples until his straw sandals were filled with followers. King Tan offered him boundless respect and gave him countless gifts, yet he dismissed them all to provide for the community, leaving no store in his own bags.
Yuanjue and Cishou held a deep mutual admiration for him, and the fourfold assembly turned to him as their refuge. For ten years he practiced the Way, and then he built—
He returned to Guiyun Monastery on Mount Xishan. His physical remains were purified there; his shadow did not enter the dust of the world.

When Master Hu, who possessed the mark of emptiness, invited him repeatedly, he did not respond. In the fifth month of the fourth year of the Qiandao era, a diviner came to visit and said, "The full moon of the sixth month is the day your death will occur.
The Master laughed and said, "Can the Creator truly control me? For now, let us wait until the coolness of autumn. He then composed a verse:
It was thus. He said, "I shall pass away in the sixth month and wait for the eighth; see whether you believe this or not. This was likely because [the two months] were equal in length.

On the twenty-sixth day of that month, he bathed and purified himself further. Sitting cross-legged in his coffin, he solemnly addressed the assembly at Guangyan Monastery, recited the Buddha’s name, and then passed away.

In the ninth month, he was enshrined in a stupa within the Abbot’s quarters. His disciples Zhichong and Zhiquan transmitted the Way, and those who heard their fame were numerous. Initially, when the Master returned to his hometown...

His intention was to deliver his kinsmen from the house of suffering. His thatched hut barely provided shelter from wind and rain; yet, as offerings were received in a continuous stream, the dwelling was expanded several times.

His residence, located on the eastern side, was less than ten feet square. During the first chills of autumn and the height of summer, he sat upright all day long, comparing and deliberating upon the sūtras and śāstras of the Buddhas and patriarchs, as well as the recorded sayings of the Chan school.
He thus composed the *Huizong ji* (Anthology of the Convergence of the Schools), for which Chao Gongwu, the Commissioner of Sichuan, wrote a preface.
It was published in Chengdu. When the Master performed rituals to avert calamities and illnesses or to dispel baleful influences and malevolent spirits, his responses were as swift as an echo.

He himself said, "Throughout my life, I have gained much from the Bodhisattva precepts. Whenever there are strange apparitions or demonic forces that cannot be controlled, once I have recited the precepts for them, they cease their activity immediately."
Zhongjiao’s style name was Fazhao. He was of the Zhang clan of Cixi. His mother dreamed of falling from the moon when he was born. At eighteen, he shaved his head.
At the beginning of the Yongming era, he studied under Mingzhi and traveled to Tiantong and Tianzhu monasteries. Yuanjue Ci served as the head seat (shouzuo) and lectured with him;

he attained profound realization, such that their seals and circles, or needles and holes, were without the slightest discrepancy. At the beginning of the Jingkang era, Liu Du invited [Foguang] to serve as the governor of Tai.
The Sage (Śākyamuni) left his seat vacant, entrusting the task of lecturing to Ai Jushou. Zhi Yong was summoned by the Master to provide the morning and evening meals;

had these not been provided, he could not have settled the assembly. He reclaimed saline wasteland and transformed it into fertile soil; twenty *qǐng* of land became as abundant as the Hall of Fragrant Accumulations (*Gandhakuṭī*).

The scrolls of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna scriptures were expounded and analyzed without interruption. In the summer of the year Yimao, there was a drought; when he administered the precepts at a pond, sweet rain arrived immediately, and the harvests of that year were bountiful.
In the Gengshen year, he retired to Sinam Hermitage in Jangmil. After only six years, he passed away while sitting in meditation after composing a verse. He was seventy-nine years old;
the epitaph was composed by Yi Nam-su.
There was Mingzi Youshui, whose style name was Muchuan. He was a native of Jinhuai. Having received instruction from Shanyin, he studied under Nengren Yuanyue.

Upon meeting Chexi Qing, he obtained the *dharma-entrustment* (ji). He presided over several monasteries, and his disciples vied with one another to emulate him. Whenever he gave a lecture, he would not look at or read the text beforehand.

He merely instructed his attendants to record the beginning and end [of his lectures]. With his eloquence and analytical skill, he expounded without exhaustion, such that all were moved to sigh in admiration and submission.
He once said: "I have led my disciples here seven times for the *Mahā-zhiguan*; during the actual practice, I have never uttered a single word.
He further remarked: "Within this great treatise, if one wished to raise even a minor objection as small as a scrap of paper, it would still be impossible."

It cannot be established. This is because the nature of words and letters is detached; all are liberation. The principle of the matter was thus established. Having clarified the doubts and dispelled the obscurations, the cases were similar to this. Initially, when Zhuzixian was traveling toward Tianzhu, he relied on an old man for alms and moored his boat there.
Hearing the sound of the lecture drum, he went to the temple to observe and took a seat at the side to listen.

Upon reaching the section on "Pervasive Destruction of Dharmas" in the *Zhiguan*, he saw that it extensively refutes nine types of *dhyāna*, all of which are not the gates for practitioners of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching to enter the Way. He stood up in admiration...
He said, "In my life, I have never heard such a wondrous Dharma. He paid his respects and departed.
Later, while presiding over a lecture at Yanqing Monastery on the subject of the "Tamed Man" (*puruṣadamyasārathi*), several men suddenly arrived to listen.

The Master said, "If we were discussing the 'Tamed Man' in the context of Confucianism, it would be like a loyal minister who does not fear death, or a brave warrior who does not cling to life, establishing great undertakings for the world and accomplishing billions [of deeds]."
Those who manifest their names for the sake of others, and are not deluded or submerged by sound, form, fame, or profit, are all called "great men" (*puruṣa*).
However, if one is within my teaching, they take the single mind and the threefold contemplation as their vessel, and the six periods of the fivefold repentance as their oars and rudders.

Only by subduing the various māras, restraining the non-Buddhists, and no longer being confined within the cage of birth-and-death—whether through the mundane cycle of segmentation or the subtle cycle of transformation—can one truly be called a great man. Thus it is said of the scholar.
When he wore [the robe], he also established the rites for its removal. His ability to seize the opportune moment to preach the Dharma and transform others was like this.

On the anniversary of his passing at Yanqing Temple, his Way was honored and his practice perfected; yet he did not announce himself to the assembly at an improper time. Instead, during the four seasons, he would admonish the junior students in the Qixin Hall, saying:
"Do you know why I do not repeatedly announce myself to the assembly? Have you not heard it said that 'thunder does not strike the heavens too frequently'?"
He lost his prestige. If those beneath him could maintain the rules and regulations, they were like swans and cranes in the azure heavens;
even if a net were spread out, they would all be startled and look upon one another with mutual reverence. His instruction of the assembly was likewise such.

On the third day of the twelfth month in the fourth year of the Qiandao era, while seated in the Green Jade Pavilion, he ordered an attendant to invite practitioners of the Sixteen Contemplations to recite the *Amitābha Sūtra* until the passage on the "True" [Contemplation].

The contemplation on the Dharma-body caused him to cease his recitation. He summoned the *vinaya-dhara* (ritual master) to assemble the community. As they gathered, he thought of the Buddhas of the Western Paradise to assist him in his rebirth there.
The assembly then surrounded him. The Head Seat said, "For fifty years, the Master has preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings; as you depart, how can you have no words?
The Master replied, "Since you know that for fifty years I have preached the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, yet you still wish to grant me [a final word] at my departure—"
"Jue, what shall I do? [Wuzhuo] entreated him incessantly. [Wuzhuo] then left behind this verse: "Having lived in the world for eighty years, I have become like a snake with its feet bound.

I leave this message for those yet to come: let the resonance be transmitted through the empty valley. He was buried beside the stupa of his dharma-ancestor, Chong. His disciple, Tianwang Yongxue, studied under him.

However, there were many others such as Fushi Hui and his peers; the abbot of Yanqing had not been in office for ten years and was not admitted into the Patriarchs’ Hall, yet the Master had not even reached two years.
Consequently, the assembly harbored doubts regarding his enshrinement in the temple. [The Master] spoke in a stern voice, saying, "The Great Way is propagated widely;
how can it be restricted by mere months and years? Thereupon, he entered the hall.

One may observe that his courtesy name was Yiweng and his style name was Jiekong. He was of the Qi clan from Huating. He left home at Baoyun Monastery and received full ordination at the age of sixteen.
He relied upon Nanping Jingwei Yan; Yan’s reputation resounded throughout Jiangzhe like the sound of a carriage wheel. [Yiweng] carried his book-cases to follow him, and once he proclaimed in song:
Prajñā is silent and desolate; upon these words, he attained realization. It was like taking a cup of qi-subduing decoction.

Later, he was invited by Xi to stay at Xiangfu Temple. After two years, he returned to the forests of Danghu in Hunan due to illness.

He said, "The sound of pines in the wind and the mountain moon are my own inexhaustible robes and bowl; why speak of the meagerness of pickled vegetables and salt? In the seventh year of the Qiandao era, the Chancellor Wei [Mi] presided over the court.
In Pingjiang, he was invited to preside over Beichan Temple. It happened to be the ninth day of the month. Pointing to his seat, he said: "An inch of ash within my breast has long since grown cold;
