Regarding the three great works of the Mountain School (Shanjia): the *Xuangu* (Mysterious Verses), the *Zhiguan* (Cessation and Contemplation), and [the *Mohe Zhiguan*].
Section. Although the Benevolent Emperor bestowed the imperial decree upon the two masters, Dongye and Zengwang, they were unable to establish the Tripitaka at Nanhu Xiazhuzi.
Consequently, those who had not previously participated in the turning of the Great Being’s wheel-canon had never beheld it.

In the third year of the Chunxi era, an imperial edict was issued to Dongchan Monastery in Fuzhou to carve woodblocks so that it might circulate eternally alongside the Great Canon in the sutra markets. When the two sets of the canon arrived, one was used for...
Presented for Your Majesty’s perusal. One portion was bestowed upon the followers of Awakening so that this great collection might be widely disseminated; this was due to the Master’s efforts.
The two Yuanjue Temples on West Lake were established as monastic academies through the meritorious deeds of various empresses and consorts, which was likewise a momentous auspicious occasion.

Throughout his life he suffered little illness, and in his later years he became increasingly firm and lean. On the first day of the tenth month in the second year of the Shaoxi era, he said to his attendant: "This floating and illusory..."
The Emperor, whose worldly affairs were extensive, had long revered the *Lotus Sūtra*. He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* without ever being separated from it for even a moment.

Since he had made this his practice from beginning to end, he summoned thirty-seven monks to perform a period of repentance based on the *Lotus Sūtra*. Taking ritual implements, they proceeded to the two palaces to purify their bodies through ablution.

He composed a verse and passed away while seated. His age was eighty-two; his years since ordination were sixty-nine. He was buried in the main hall of his residence. His posthumous title was "Religious Teacher Guangci" (Broadly Compassionate).
The stupa was named "Puzhao" (Universal Illumination). Song Zhi Rui, a Court Attendant, composed the inscription.
Duanxin, whose courtesy name was Fuso and sobriquet Zheng’an, was a native of Yongjia. He received the Dharma from Yian Chu-gong, who in turn had received it from Yuanbian.

His grasp of the fundamental tenets was clear and lucid; his discourse was fluent and unhindered. While presiding over Nanhu, as he prepared to depart this life, he gathered the assembly of monks and chanted the "Peaceful Bliss" (Anle) Sutra.
Upon reaching the passage, "Entering deeply into meditative concentration, one beholds the Buddhas of the ten directions," he passed away. His verse says: "Life is thus; death is also thus."

The clouds have dispersed and the sky is a single expanse of azure; the sun’s orb is precisely at midday. In his preface to the *Teaching and Contemplation* (Jiaoguan) by Master Duanxin, Ye Shui wrote:

"The Master [Duanxin] studied the teachings and contemplations of Tiantai while simultaneously practicing the various other schools. His understanding of their essential meanings was thorough and penetrating, and his eloquence arose like a sharp blade."
At the beginning of the Chunxi era, there were many veteran and renowned masters of Chan and doctrinal study in the capital. The Master, though young, took up the spear and entered their chambers;
his citations from antiquity and the present all struck upon the essential points. Those who debated with him were startled and said, "He is truly a library of books; do not try to contend with him.

Inspector Zhen (Liangyou) was lax in his understanding yet eloquent in his speech, asserting high and low positions according to his whim. The Master never once conceded to him, suddenly confronting him with suspicious and devious questions.
He was certainly one who rectified and broke [the cycle of delusion]. From the beginning he did not allow arrogance to arise, and his spirit remained subdued; thus, he was profoundly revered by all.

He lived for many years with his doors closed, such that no one recognized his face. He taught his disciples only to pursue the emptiness and stillness of the Western [Paradise], free from worldly fame and profit.
Speaking thus, he passed away.
(Seventh Generation) Huiming, style name Wuhui, styled Huian. He was of the Zhao clan of Yanguan; his mother was Lady Wang. At his birth, there were extraordinary signs of light.

At the age of eleven, he served Yuanzhi of Huadu Monastery as a disciple. While Yuanzhi was in retreat at his country villa, the Master recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and requested the four requisites with the utmost diligence to serve him.

When Yuanzhi passed away during a period when the ordination of monks was prohibited, some urged him to pursue the study of Confucianism. The Master merely raised his sleeve to show them [the insignificance of such pursuits].

He said, "I have completed my duties and shall now wear these robes. I shall further attend to the auspicious rites and succeed in upholding them, strictly observing the prohibitions and bestowing the precepts.
Not long after Master [Zhao] arrived at Upper Zhushan, his quarters were filled with visitors. Although Huitong of Xie had invited him to a secluded retreat, he only responded later.
When Zhang Duanjing (Zi Zheng) established the Fuchun Hermitage to honor him, offering a vast amount of land, he declined to accept much, fearing the confusion of mixed uses. At Upper Zhushan...

Successive generations had inherited his lineage, and the vacant seat was originally intended for him to succeed as the presiding master. However, the Master fled at night; though the temples of Dezhang and Cigan vied to invite him, he accepted neither.
He shared a bond of pure friendship with Changzhao, and when the latter retired from public affairs, he relied upon him. At that time, they were both known as the two eminent monks of the Great Song.
On the twenty-second day of the second month in the fifth year of the Qingyuan era, he recited a verse. Celestial music resounded in the void, and...

He passed away. Those who sought his *śarīra* through cremation obtained them according to their wishes. His eminent disciple Benjing enshrined his bones in a stupa; at Liangzhu, he established the Zhenji Monastery.
Ten thousand people joined his society for the recitation of the Buddha’s name. The Master emerged as a leader of the mountain gateways; the tally-sticks [for ordination] filled his hall.
He composed the "Record of the Kongji Hermitage" and the "Essential Methods for Cultivating the Mind," achieving merit in both lands (China and Japan). The details are found in the "Zunsu Zhi."
In the Inner Transmission of the Dharma Protector, Nanyue said: "The Dharma was entrusted to the Dharma-minister; the Dharma-king has no affairs. My descendants are valiant and diligent;
they don armor and helmets, resent their enemies, take charge of the lectures, and excel in composition. They take the *Suan-shu Kong-mu* as the standard for correct faith."

Taking the setting sun as the signal for their drum, they set their minds upon it; they concentrated their spirits on the field of the three sublime contemplations and suddenly halted their reins at the domain of the four samādhis—all were Dharma ministers.
Now, I record their words and deeds so they may be examined. For those whose eras are difficult to clarify, I rely on their biographies.
As for those who have buried their brilliance and erased their traces, yet whose writings cannot be suppressed by others, I continue to record them here.
He had no expectations regarding his fellow practitioners.
Facheng was a native of Yongzhou. He studied under the monk Senghong, a man of divine anomalies from Lantian. Following his instructions, Facheng recited the *Lotus Sūtra* and practiced samādhi.
In a dream, Samantabhadra exhorted him to transcribe the Great Teachings; he immediately ordered the transcription of the eight divisions of the *Prajñāpāramitā* and the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.

He experienced auspicious omens. His own hand-copying of the *Lotus Sūtra* was particularly extraordinary in its manifestations of these signs. When he fell ill during the Zhenguan era, he expressed his aspiration to be reborn in Tuṣita Heaven, saying, "A youth has come to welcome me;
I am departing. A light issued from his mouth, and a wondrous fragrance filled the room. He passed away peacefully while sitting upright.

During the summer retreat, the Master would invariably recite the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* three hundred times; on other days, he would maintain this practice as well, still managing two recitations even when occupied with guests.
Feng. He would not speak until he had completed a section of the scripture. In ten years, he had recited more than ten thousand sections.
Faxiang was a native of Yangzhou who left home to become a monk at the age of sixteen. He served his master with diligence and recited the *Lotus Sūtra* through arduous effort.

He established the "Lotus Hall" at Qixia Temple and practiced the *Lotus Samādhi*. After seven days and nights of diligent cultivation, he obtained great spiritual responses and auspicious signs. Tigers were rampant among the populace.

The clergy and laity had prepared a vegetarian feast (*zhāi*). Suddenly, [a tiger] entered the hall and seized a person. The Master called out, "Do not act so rashly! A vegetarian feast has been prepared today;
you may release this person. The tiger released him. Tigers then gathered there in great numbers. He struck their heads with a staff and preached the True Dharma (*saddharma*) to them.
Consequently, he did not cause any harm.
Hengjing was a native of Wenhui in Dangyang; in the twenty-second year of the Zhenguan era, he received imperial permission to enter the monastic order.

He studied the Vinaya under Wen Gang, being able to recite what he heard once and contemplating its meaning as he practiced. Later, he went to Yuquan Temple to follow in the footsteps of Zhiyi, where he cultivated *śamatha-vipaśyanā*.

Ten *li* south of the temple stood Longxing Monastery. During the reigns of Empress Wu Zetian and Emperor Zhongzong, he was summoned three times by imperial decree to serve as a preceptor for the precepts.

In the third year of the Jinglong era, he submitted a petition requesting to return to the mountains. An edict was issued for the Secretariat, the Chancellery, and the Academicians to hold a vegetarian feast at Lingguang Palace;
the Emperor composed a poem to see him off. Li Qiao, the Minister of the Secretariat, and others joined in composing verses. The Master received the poems, shook his monk’s staff, and departed.
He passed away in the first year of the Tianxian era (702).

He was buried to the west of the temple. His demeanor was lofty and his spirit transcendent; his discernment and capacity surpassed those of ordinary men. Initially, he studied the Vinaya, and later, together with Chujin, he researched the teachings and contemplations (*jiaoguan*).
He entered the capital and resided at Caotang Temple on Mount Zigai in Zhongnan. By imperial decree, he was appointed to reside at Qianfu and Fahua Temples for nearly three years.
For ten years, while Amoghavajra translated new scriptures, he selected the most eminent and talented individuals, frequently entrusting them with the duties of scribe and stylistic refinement.

At the beginning of the Yongtai era, by imperial decree, he joined Liangben and others to participate in the translation of the *Ratnatriparitrāṇa-rāja-sūtra* (Renwang huguo jing) and the *Ghanavyūha-sūtra* (Miyin jing) within the Daochang at the Tianming Palace.
Together with Amoghavajra and the scholar Liu Kang, he further refined and finalized the texts, serving as a verifier of their doctrinal meaning.

A member of the official staff, his literary compositions were beyond reproach. In his later years, he composed the *Nianfo Sanmei Baowang Lun* (Treatise on the Jewel King of the Samādhi of Buddha-Recitation), which sets forth twenty sections of questions and answers to resolve doubts;
therein, he provides profound illumination regarding what to delight in and loathe, and what to adopt and reject.

Chujin was of the Cheng clan of Guangping. His mother, surnamed Gao, conceived him after dreaming of the Buddha. At the age of seven, he left the household life; when he performed obeisance to the Tripitaka and searched for a scripture, the Lotus Sutra came into his hands.
At nine, he received full ordination at Longxing Monastery in the Western Capital. One night, while reciting the sutra, he reached the "Treasure Stupa" chapter.

His body and mind were serene and still when a jeweled stupa suddenly appeared. Śākyamuni’s transformation bodies filled the realm of empty space. Having sat in meditation for six years, he vowed to erect this stupa.
As soon as his sincere aspiration was expressed, donors and believers arrived. On the night of laying the foundation, he recited sutras and practiced the Way.

The multitude heard celestial music and a wondrous fragrance. Emperor Xuanzong dreamed of golden characters descending from the heavens. When he inquired about them the following morning, everyone pointed to the Master.
Thereupon, the Emperor personally inscribed the plaque for the temple and bestowed vast quantities of silk. On the day of its completion, five-colored clouds gathered above the spire of the pagoda.
He said to his fellow students: "When one digs a well and encounters mud, the water is not far off. When wood is drilled until it grows warm, obtaining fire is but a matter of time.
Let us seven persons unite our resolve; reciting the sutras day and night with incense smoke never ceasing, let us do so during both the spring and autumn seasons."
He assembled forty-nine people to practice the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-samādhi*. By imperial decree, this was permitted to become a permanent ritual standard.

During the preceding and succeeding stages of the *dharmakṣetra*, three thousand and seventy grains of *śarīra* were manifested. When they planned to enshrine these relics, another one hundred and eight grains descended.

While painting a transformation image of Samantabhadra, nineteen grains were obtained from the tip of his brush; they were perfectly spherical, moving of their own accord, and possessed a radiant, crystalline luster. He also used blood to write [the scriptures].

The Bodhisattva Fahua [Fahua] answered the ninefold inquiries and those concerning his spiritual lineage. He transcribed one thousand copies of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, thirty-six of which were written in golden script to enshrine within precious stupas.
Furthermore, he transcribed another thousand copies to distribute for the practice of upholding the Dharma. Once his work of conversion was complete, he passed away lying on his right side.

When the new wood was exhausted and the fire extinguished, his countenance remained as white as snow, appearing as if alive. He was sixty-two years of age and thirty-seven years since his ordination. Tian...
The Emperor dispatched an envoy to offer condolences. A stupa was erected to the west of the city, and Cen Xun composed an inscription for it. Since childhood, the Master had transcribed scriptures;

he never wore silk or fine fabrics, adding only hemp or coarse cloth to his garments during the cold. In the thirteenth year of the Zhenyuan era, Dou Wenchang, the Commissioner of Merit for the Left Ward, memorialized that the late Master Chujin, at the beginning of the Tianbao era, had built a stupa for the sake of the state and established a place of practice (daochang). For over sixty years, he had [transcribed] the scriptures...
His voice was uninterrupted. We beg that you grant him official recognition and bestow upon him the posthumous title "Dàyuán" (Great Perfection).

Zhìyǎn’s secular surname was Sòng; his mother was Zhang. She dreamed of ascending to the pinnacle of the Tōngxuán Pagoda and sitting there when he was born. At the age of eight, he left the household life.

He recited the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* twelve times through to its conclusion; everyone regarded him as a divine child (*śiśu*). Having shaved his head, he listened to the lectures, whereupon his wisdom blossomed and was fully developed.

He lived in seclusion at Mount Huqiu, where he preached and performed repentance rites. Externally, he recited the *Lotus Sūtra* three thousand times. Before the incense burner had even been lit, fragrant smoke would naturally arise;

when the evening water jar was just empty, it would mysteriously overflow with water. It was as if the Celestial Youth (*Devakumāra*) were attending to him. He practiced the three pure deeds and cultivated the sixteen [precepts].

Hui guan organized over five hundred people to hold daily fasting assemblies and lectures for more than ten years. He lectured on the *Lotus Sūtra* and the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa Sūtra* thirty times each, and on the *Avalokiteśvara Sūtra* one hundred times.
When his karmic conditions were exhausted, he passed away.

Xingman (行滿) was a native of Nanpu in Wanzhou. Having received full ordination, he relied upon Shishuang. Arriving in Yuzhang, he gazed up at the sacred traces of Tiantai and took up residence at Zhizhe Yuan on Mount Huading.
For ten years, he showed no sign of resentment toward his tea stove; he lay upon the ground in the manner of a recluse, burning refuse to warm himself beneath it.

He would say, "Take off your clothes and sit upon this mat," and would even feed the fleas and lice. Once he had put his robes back on as before, they were found to be intact. His physical frame remained robust.

Outside, a large pine tree with spreading branches had a small tree growing as an epiphyte upon it. Whenever [the Master] sat in meditation, that tree would invariably lean over him in a graceful, swaying manner.

People said, "The tree is paying homage. Man Cha-tou did not believe this and waited to observe it; he saw that when [the Master] sat, the tree would indeed pay homage as before, but when he withdrew, the tree would stand upright and tall once more.
For forty years, he ate his meals with the assembly and never once relieved himself. During the Kaibao era, he spoke thus.
"I shall now depart; let me call upon the name of Mañjuśrī to assist me. After a short while, he passed away in silence at the age of over eighty.
Prime Minister Wang Anshi, the Prince of Shu, was his disciple. When he first governed Ningbo, he listened to Guangzhi’s lectures and thus cultivated the principles of nature and phenomena.
Discussions concerning essence and function often appear in his commentaries on the scriptures. He maintained an unceasing correspondence with the Master Shan of Chongfa Temple.
Chongfa left this inscription for him: "A small pavilion overlooks the water amidst tall bamboos; lush and fragrant, the remaining flowers perfume the ground."

I only wish that people of this age would contemplate this realm, so as to transform all afflictions into refreshing coolness. He buried the girl of Yinqiu at Chongfa Temple and took leave of his official post with a poem, saying:
"Now I launch my boat across the gate to bid you farewell; from this moment on, life and death shall part ways, one to the west and one to the east."
He had the lay attendant Lingzhao guard it. Later, when Faxiang delivered the letter to Dharma Master Chongfa, the Master called for Lingzhao.
Upon his arrival, Chongfa was greatly pleased and asked, "Are you able to read, recite, or transcribe? Lingzhao replied that he could do none of these, but only prepare seasonings. The Master said:
The cook was a slave. He sent him back with a letter to Hui, which read: "Lingzhao has returned.

I give you one copy of the *Lotus Sūtra*, one scroll of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, two thousand sheets of paper, and one hundred writing brushes. When the King passed away, the Lady finally gave Lingzhao to the monk Xuyu.
[She said,] "A true recipient of the Buddha’s entrustment does not give [the Dharma] to just anyone. This monk is now a foolish man and a weakling; he is a mere executioner."
Those with physical disabilities were generally included among the fields of merit within the Golden Realm, yet those in office paid them no heed.

Some may argue that the Three Jewels are like a great ocean—equal and without distinction of high or low—but this refers to the Three Jewels of Essential Nature (*tattva-ratnatraya*), not the Three Jewels of Institutional Maintenance (*prajñapti-ratnatraya*).
When the King was collecting national calligraphic works of Avalokiteśvara, half of one was consumed by fire; he subsequently visited a forest hermitage (*aranya*).
Between the feet of the Vajra [statue], he obtained a half-body; when joined together with it, there was not even the slightest discrepancy. The King rejoiced and circulated the account.
Yin Pan obtained the original carving and had it inscribed on stone for exposition. Chen Tianyu praised it, saying: "The physical marks of a Bodhisattva are fundamentally neither separate nor joined.
Taking material things as their marks, separation and union appear vividly. Sometimes they reveal the entire body, and sometimes they manifest a half-form, according to conditions."
Responding to conditions—all this is my own mind. One should know that writing arises from the mind and burning ceases within the mind.

It is only because sentient beings do not know the single characteristic (*ekalakṣaṇa*) and remain stuck in the two extremes that the Bodhisattva manifests two bodies while returning them to a single essence.

This single essence is not an essence; nor is it something other than an essence. This, too, is not what is called a "Bodhisattva. Furthermore, the *Fazhi jisū* (The Commentary on the Dharma-Wisdom) states: "Dharma..."
The essence is suchness; fundamentally, there is neither arising nor ceasing. Yet, as worldly conditions drift along, there is meeting and parting.

Since the Great Wise One entered nirvana at Tiantai, the Way has been like a suspended thread. However, from Yinzhi to Daotong, the master’s fragrance was transmitted to the waters of Yinqu, its sound resonating like a bird emerging from a valley.
As those who ascended to the heights grew sparse and the remnants of the Semblance Dharma became vast and distant, Nanhui shone upon the Tiantai tradition beneath Mount Jingxi.
Regarding Master Dongshao Li: although there were no other authors who could surpass him, his dwelling in this world was unlike that of others, and so forth.
He was like the blazing sun at the zenith of the sky, or like a sudden clap of thunder emerging from the earth; grasses, trees, tiles, and pebbles all manifested the true dharma.
Even birds, beasts, insects, and fish all receive the subtle and wondrous teaching; by tasting its words, one may divine what they have attained.

You, Fazang, are a man of Wu and a high disciple of Jingjue. However, [the monk] Song Mingjiao composed the *Dingzutú* (Chart of the Determined Patriarchs) and the *Zhengzongjì* (Record of the True Lineage), using the *Fofazangchuan* (Biographies of the Dharma-treasury) to delude the world.
I condemn these as works that should be burned, for they rely exclusively on the *Damo duoluo chanjing* (Dhyāna-sūtra of Bodhidharma) to form a faction.

Appended to the *Zhiju Baolin Zhuan* (The Baolin Tradition of the Torch of Wisdom), the Master [Daoxuan] cited scriptures and examined treatises to establish his own interpretation of the patriarchs, thereby attempting to rescue the *Fofa zang* (Treasury of the Dharma Transmission).

Furthermore, three years later, when Sengsong encountered difficulties regarding the *Chanding jing* (Sutra on Meditation), he would simply claim that there were errors in the transcription; he then altered and reshaped the text to suit his views, using evasive phrasing for his private interpretations.
Relying upon Sengyou’s *Sanzang ji* (Record of the Tripitaka) and the names of masters in the Vinaya school, he composed a deceptive commentary. The Master [Daoxuan]...

He also produced the *Zhizhe* (Cessation of Error), refuting it by comparing it with the *Dahui Chanjing* (Great Assembly Chan Sutra) and presenting the *Chusanzang jiji wen* (Preface to the Collection of Records Concerning the Tripitaka) to demonstrate its flaws;

thus, [Hu]song was utterly defeated. During the Jiayu and Zhiping eras, Shen Qi of the Dugu Department and Shi Miao composed prefaces for its earlier and later sections, establishing it as an indelible classic of our school.

Furthermore, his correspondence with Master Yan of the Translation Academy and his responses to Master Zhen of Xingjiao Temple, which provide detailed analysis and refutation, are particularly [significant].

Following the compilation of the *Lìfù jí*, the Master’s defense against insults was indeed diligent and thorough; thus, those who would venture upon invasion could not help but be deterred by the thought of the Ten-thousand-li Long Wall.

Yang Jie, courtesy name Cigong, was a native of Wuyuan. He took "Chu" as his style name. Having passed the imperial examinations at a young age, he served as Director of the Court of State Ceremonial and later as Commissioner for Criminal Justice in Eastern Zhejiang.
Naturally endowed with a brilliant intellect, he had extensively sought instruction from Chan masters and deeply mastered the profound principles of the Three Contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
When the King of Goryeo, Uichon, sent an envoy requesting that he travel to China to study both Chan and doctrinal Buddhism, the court appointed Yang Jie to serve as the reception officer.

Upon arriving at the White Lotus [Temple] on Mount Tiantai, he found full accord with Fazhen and observed the rites of a disciple toward him. He paid homage at the stupa of Zhiyi, inscribing its epitaph as follows:
"By Imperial Decree, Prince Youse of Goryeo, the State Preceptor Uicheon, visited the regions of Wu and Yue to seek the Way.

Having traveled extensively throughout Tiantai, he ascended the ridge of the Buddha Dingguang and beheld the *Pranidhāna* (Vow Text) written by Zhiyi’s own hand. There, the State Preceptor prostrated himself before the stupa."
He vowed to transmit the teachings and contemplation to the Eastern Land; this truly reveals the Master’s dedication.

Compared to those nowadays who call themselves "wandering monks" (xingjiao)—who are preoccupied with plotting their routes, seeking only abundant food and drink, comfortable lodgings, and whose feet carry them aimlessly from place to place until they grow old and die without awakening—the difference between them and the Master is vast indeed.
(The Five Verses on the Master’s Family Lineage). When [the Master] entered nirvana, the Duke...

While guarding Jingkou, he received a bequeathed letter. The postscript sent with it said: "The three contemplations are universally clear and perfect in every thought; the patriarchs' incense burner and whisk are transmitted only through the mind.
Having sealed the bequeathed letter, he sat in the full lotus posture; not abiding in the white lotus, he gave birth to a white lotus.

He further composed the inscription for the Wuxiang Monastery, stating that the purport of Śākyamuni’s transformation throughout his entire life was as clear as pointing at one's palm. He further remarked: "The wisdom of the founder [Zhiyi] is the heaven of transformative edification."

I take the Lotus Samādhi as my ultimate goal and the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) as my refuge. For without reading the *Lotus Sūtra*, there would be no way to clarify that the wondrous Dharma is inherently possessed by my own mind;
and without being born in Sukhāvatī, there would be no way to realize that the wondrous Dharma is inherently possessed by my own mind.
When I gazed upon and paid homage at the Twin Śāla Trees, the Tripitaka suddenly turned of its own accord. At the request of the monks, I composed this eulogy: The Twin Śāla Trees.

The Precious Treasury turns into Vairocana; there is no need for others to exert force to support him. Let the eminent monks of the four seas not be moved to wonder: he is like a single bright pearl within a bowl.
In his later years, he devoted himself exclusively to the Pure Land practice. While traveling on official business, he carried with him a painted image of the sixteen-foot Amitābha.

At the time of his death, he passed away while sitting upright, moved by the vision of the Buddha coming to welcome him. His verse says: "In life, there is nothing to be attached to; in death, there is likewise nothing to be feared."
Setting it aside: in the vast void of space, there are "zhi-hu-ye-re" (the particles of discourse). Taking what is mistaken for what is right, one reaches the Western Land of Ultimate Bliss.

At that time, the consort of the Prince of Jing dreamed that she was wandering in the Pure Land with a deceased maidservant; she saw those wearing court robes sitting upon lotus flowers, their bodies transformed by necklaces of jewels.

His robes fluttered and were scattered by the wind until they vanished. His maidservant said, "Yang Jie. When [the master] woke up and inquired about him, several days had already passed since his passing.

Apart from his collected works, there are the *Śrāvakayāna-piṭaka* (Sheshi bieji) and the *Zhuanfudao ji*. In the prefaces to the *Ten Doubts* (*Shiyi lun*) and the *Collection for Resolving Doubts* (*Jueyi ji*), he discusses the Pure Land teachings with particular vigor.
It is said: "If attachment is not profound, one will not be born in Saha; if mindfulness is not singular..."
To be born in the Pure Land is the goal. It is all the more lamentable when virtuous persons abandon the three types of lack of faith and fail to seek rebirth there.
The first is: "I shall transcend Buddhas and patriarchs; the Pure Land is not a place where I ought to be born. The second is: "Everywhere is the Pure Land;
there is no necessity to be born in the West. The third is: "The Land of Ultimate Bliss is a sacred realm; we commoners cannot be born there."
These words are truly worthy of being taken as a mirror for reflection. Master Zhao’s eulogy states: "Virtue, Way, Benevolence, and Righteousness;

Teaching, Contemplation, Chan, and Vinaya—whenever he grasps at them with his hand, they flow forth from a single source. That Superior Man is difficult to repay; who would dare to enter the chamber of Vimalakīrti?
The Inscription on the Formless Stele says: "There was one named Shenqin, who, because the monastery was facing decline, informed the local commandery of the situation."

The Magistrate requested that a man of extensive learning and noble conduct be invited to preside over those who lecture on and contemplate the teachings of the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*, and that he be honored with the title "Qin" (Diligence).
When Qin resided at Jingming, Yan succeeded him; when Yan resided at Chicheng, Liyun succeeded him. When Yun went to Baozang Monastery, the messenger returned to report to Qin.
Finding no room for him among the masses, they divined a superior location to relocate and renovate his residence. Those who understood the situation...

That is to say, if it were not for the assembly of pure practitioners who expound the contemplation of the wondrous teaching, such a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) could not have been accomplished;
yet no genealogical record of them has been heard of. It has long been a deficiency in the annals of the Tiantai school that this standard account is missing.
Neng was a man from Jiahe. In his youth, he studied under Pusa Nengren (Śākyamuni) and practiced repentance in a meditation chamber for nearly forty years.

His reputation as a practitioner spread throughout Jiangzhe, yet he did not dare call himself a "practitioner. Zhiyi practiced the Way during the six periods of the day and sat in meditation during the four periods;

Even after the age of seventy, though scattered by the fires of war, he never slackened in his morning and evening devotions. During the Qiandao era, he was granted a sacrificial stipend.

From childhood, he was exceptionally brilliant and resolved to pursue the Way of Learning; whenever he opened a scroll, he immediately mastered its contents. Those with whom he associated were all renowned figures.

He withdrew to Zuoxi. Moved by the letters of Han Yu that had rebuked and rejected [the teachings], his resolve became as firm as the grip of a skilled archer’s thumb and forefinger.

Suffering from an eye ailment, his elder brother Sengru urged him to pray to the Bodhisattva Yuan Tong. The deity immediately declared, "One who remains unchanging in the face of peril is a true great man. Someone then informed him of Zhu Tai...
The physician spoke to Du Qigong. "Your Excellency has not yet read Buddhist scriptures; how do you know that [Buddhism] does not surpass Confucius and Mencius?

When Emperor Gao of the Qi dynasty ascended the throne, he summoned [Hui] Qiu with a carriage drawn by a *pú* ox and bundles of silk to serve as a *tōngzhí-sànqǐ-shìláng*. Qiu did not accept the appointment.
Subsequently, when Prince Jingling sent a letter to urge him, Qiu replied: "I, Qiu, lie ill during the four seasons and tend to my irrigation and planting during the three seasons.

I enjoy the lingering shade of the mountains and marshes and entrust my twilight sentiments to fish and birds. Is this not surely the profound grace of the Tang and Yu dynasties, and the magnanimity of the Zhou and Shao ministers?"

This was the stage of his spiritual cultivation. He built a hut and called himself the "Future Bodhisattva of Liberation and Wise Intelligence Beneath the Twin Sala Trees," where he planted fruits and vegetables for others to take as they pleased.
He worked as a hired laborer for people; together with his wife, Miaoguang, he would work by day and return home at night.

He expounded the Buddha-dharma. After seven years of ascetic practice, while sitting in meditative seclusion, he beheld the three Buddhas—Śākyamuni, Suvarṇa-śālī, and Dīpaṃkara—approaching from the east.
They emitted light like the sun, and golden radiance descended from heaven and gathered upon his body.

From within his clenched fist, he occasionally exhaled wondrous fragrances, and between his chest and belly, a golden hue suddenly appeared. A voice from the sky proclaimed: "On the day you attain enlightenment, you shall succeed [to the lineage]."

When Śākyamuni sat at the site of enlightenment, the fourfold assembly arrived in great numbers to pay their respects. The local governor, Wang Xiu, considering this to be a delusion and a fabrication, imprisoned him.

For over ten days he did not eat; filled with remorse, the governor released him. Upon returning to the mountains, he redoubled his ascetic practice, and those who took him as their teacher increased daily.
He then declared: "I have come from the Tuṣita Heaven to preach the Unsurpassed Bodhi. Formerly I concealed this matter; now [I reveal it]."

Without concealment, he acted with sincere intent. In the sixth year of the Datong era, he sent an envoy bearing a letter to the Imperial Court, addressing the Emperor as "Lord of the Empire" and "Bodhisattva Who Saves the World.

He further remarked that the Great Being had vowed to propagate the orthodox teaching and universally deliver all creatures, and having heard that the Emperor’s will was virtuous, he desired [to meet him].
They came to discuss this. The Emperor issued a decree, saying: "Shan-hui wishes to deliver sentient beings and untie all their fetters. As a Great Being, his conduct has no fixed location;
let him come as he pleases. In the twelfth month, he arrived at Mount Zhong. On the eighth day of the third month of the following year, he reached the palace gates.
The Emperor, having long heard of his divine wonders, had previously ordered the gates to be locked so that he could not enter. Shan-hui struck the gate with a large mallet once.

All the gates were opened wide, and he entered directly into the Palace of Kind Words (Shanyan Dian). Although the usher thrice urged him to prostrate, he did not bow; instead, he ascended straight to the imperial couch. Their conversation was extraordinary.

A meal was prepared for him, and when it was finished, he departed for Mount Zhong, where he sat beneath the pines of Dinglin Monastery. The local officials provided him with all necessary provisions.
Virtuous men gathered like clouds. When he first entered the capital, he carried two wooden mallets; these were later called "knocking-at-the-door mallets.

The Vice Minister of the Imperial Secretariat asked him why, and he replied: "If the ground of the Dharma were to move, then all phenomena would likewise move."

He felt uneasy. Shortly thereafter, he engaged in a dialectical debate that was like an echo responding to a sound. When the lecture concluded, the Emperor bestowed upon him a "water-jewel" and a "fire-jewel," each an inch in diameter, which drew their light from the sun and moon respectively.
The following day, the Emperor invited him alone for further conversation. At the Shouguang Palace, they emerged when the night watch had already passed.

In the fifth year, he entered the capital and discussed with the Emperor the principle of "cessation without extinction. He said to the Emperor: "All forms and appearances inevitably return to emptiness; it is immeasurable..."
The Sublime Dharma does not transcend True Suchness (*tathatā*). Throughout the world, nothing is more secure than the Way; nothing brings greater joy than the Principle. The Emperor remained silent.

In the third month of the second year of the Taicheng era, he announced to the assembly that he would observe the fast and burn his body as an offering of a great bright lamp to the Triple Gem, for the sake of universally delivering all beings.

During the famine and chaos at the end of the Liang dynasty, he and his disciples daily gathered acorns and chestnuts and kneaded grass to make porridge to sustain themselves; the villagers and local thieves could not bear to offend them. He once said: "I..."
He was one of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa. If one wishes to be born among these thousand Buddhas, one shall immediately behold me.

His disciples Huirong and others wished to establish a Longhua Assembly (Dragon Flower Assembly). The Great Being said, "You may instead hold an assembly for the Buddhas who have suspended their radiance;
the Longhua Assembly is my own concern. If you follow my words, you will certainly behold the Dragon Flower. He further said, "I attained the Way forty [years ago]."
Eon ago, Śākyamuni first resolved his mind [for enlightenment]. It was solely because Śākyamuni was able to sacrifice his body that he attained Buddhahood before me.
In the second year of the Tianjia era of the Chen dynasty, while practicing the Way in the mountains, he constantly saw the Seven Buddhas before him and Vimalakīrti following behind.
He said to his disciples, "Among the Seven Buddhas, only Śākyamuni frequently converses with me. In the winter of the second year of the Guangda era, Song manifested himself.

He was presented with an imperial edict of praise and commendation; not long after, he was summoned to the capital to reside at Tianshou Temple. In the second year of the Chunhua era, he was appointed as a compiler for the Historiographical Institute.

In the first year of the Zhizhao era, he served as the Superintendent of the Buddhist Teachings in the Western Capital. When Emperor Zhenzong ascended the throne, he was granted an audience with special honors. In the Xianping era...
Initially, he was appointed as the Superintendent of Monks for the Right Ward (*youjie senglu*). Three years later, he was promoted to Censor-in-Chief for the Left Ward (*zuojie canzheng*).

Su Yijian composed a petition on the deeds of the sages and worthies of the Three Teachings, entrusting the Master and the Daoist [official] Han Dechun with the task. They compiled the *Record of Sages and Worthies of Vulture Peak* (*Jiuling shengxian lu*) and its supplementary biographies in one hundred fascicles.
The Master was subsequently appointed as the Head Seat (*shouzuo*) of the Left Ward. In the second month of the following year, he passed away in his native village.
He was buried in Longjingwu, Qiantang. In the fourth year of the Chongning era, he was posthumously granted the title Yuanming.

His writings include the *Biographies of Eminent Monks of the Great Song* in thirty fascicles, the *Brief History of the Sangha* in three fascicles, and the *Collected Buddhist Scriptures for Inclusion in the Canon* in one hundred fifty-two fascicles.

The *Wàixué jí* (Collection of External Studies) in forty-nine fascicles, the *Zhēngpǔ* (Zither Scores) in ten fascicles, and the *Wùwài jí* (Collection of Transcending the World) were all circulated separately.
Duke Wang wrote a preface to his collected works, stating: "At the age of eighty-two, the Master’s hearing and sight remained undiminished.

Having served fourteen successive reigns in the capital and four generations of the Wu-Yue state, he was ultimately able to receive the blessings of being 'employed by the Great Plan' (*Hóngfàn xiàngyòng*). While occupying the position of one universally looked up to among the Buddhist clergy..."
It is said that one must surely attain longevity and surely attain high office.

Wang Wenzheng wished to have portraits of nine long-lived men from Chaoshou painted to succeed the "Nine Elders" of Le-tian, and the Master was also included among them. A poem for the portrait at Gushan says:
"In silence he returned to the realm of truth; his transformation in the human world is now complete. The two courts revered his supreme achievements; the four seas looked up to him."

His fame is lofty; his ancient traces remain in the Flower Society (Huashè), and his collected writings fill the imperial capital. Pausing and lingering, I reflect on past events as the evening crows cry from the trees in the courtyard.
The Master compiled the *Jieshe Fajijiwen* (Text on the Dharma-Assembly for Forming a Society), noting that the name "Society" originated with Huiyuan of Mount Lu.

During the Qi dynasty, Prince Wenxuan of Jingling recruited both monastics and laypeople to form the *Jingzhu She* (Pure Abode Society). During the Liang dynasty, Sengyou compiled the *Fashe Jian Gongdeyi Huiwen* (Text on Establishing the Merit Township Assembly of the Dharma Society).
Since ancient times, people have invariably held dharma assemblies within monasteries. The principle of such an assembly (*shè*) is to unite the many into a single, weighty body.
In accomplishing tasks and achieving success, nothing is more effective than an assembly. Today’s *gòngshè* (collective assemblies) together cultivate fields of merit;

their regulations are strict and clear, surpassing even public law. When members encourage one another and are diligent in practice, the assembly fulfills the function of providing sustenance and growth.

At the local shrine of Zhou and Zheng, he established a vigil for the Gengshen day, wherein they played bells and cymbals, sang hymns of praise, recited the Buddha’s name, and practiced the Way, remaining awake throughout the night to avoid the Three Peng demons.

To report to the Emperor regarding transgressions and the subtraction of one's allotted lifespan was, in fact, the method of the Daoist school. Vulgar monks, seeking profit, do not seek the fundamental source;
they mistakenly practice heterodox arts—how deeply lamentable this is! The Master’s meticulous protection of the Teachings reached such an extent as this.
Gaian said: The *Gui tian lu* states that when Emperor Taizu visited the Minister of State, he lit incense before the Buddha and asked whether one should prostrate.

The Master replied, "One bows to the Buddha present, not to the Buddha of the past," and consequently, the act of prostration was abolished. He ordered that whenever the Emperor went on inspection tours to burn incense, no prostrations were to be made.
Since the Master entered court during the Taiping Xingguo era, the *Gui tian lu* records these events; however, this is merely the work of those fond of such anecdotes.
This statement is merely Ou-yang’s mistaken citation. When viewing the lanterns on the night of the Yuanxiao Festival, Imperial Secretary Wang mocked [the monks] without any leniency;
how could he have been indulgent toward the Dharma? When the emperors Gaozong and Xiaozong visited Tiantong Mountain, they never failed to kneel at Mingqing Temple.

Jie Zhu was the daughter of the Huang family of Changle. She was devoted to learning, reciting ten thousand words daily. She took Fashi Ziguang as her teacher and received the tonsure after passing the scriptural examinations.

Delighting in the cultivation of goodness, she possessed a vast memory and was skilled in composition; whether expanding or contracting, advancing or retreating, she always acted with perfect appropriateness.

It was titled *Moshu* (Silent Writing) and consisted of several hundred thousand words of miscellaneous essays. He suddenly remarked, "One need only know the Way; what is the use of accumulating such writings?
and he burned them all, leaving behind only inscriptions on steles and prefaces. Having received the Dharma from Fahai, Huaiyao resided at Huangbo.

When Yao passed away, [Zhili] composed a funeral inscription for him and also wrote a *Biézhuan* (Separate Biography). [This concludes the section on] the deliberations regarding the distinction between Chan and the Teachings following the editing of the *Zhi guan* by Xiazhu.
Qi had profound insights and realizations. On the twenty-third day of the ninth month in the tenth year of the Xining era, he manifested nirvana.
He was ninety-three years old by secular age and seventy-three by monastic seniority. His remains were interred at Feishan. Li Xiao, a Court Gentleman, composed the inscription.

Faduan’s secular surname was Qiu; he was a native of Xia. From childhood, he abstained from meat. He underwent the ritual examination for ordination and shaved his head at Jiekong on Mount Wu, where he received the teachings and contemplations of Jingjue.
He studied the Chan methods of Huanglong. Having entered the monastic world, he moved through three successive appointments before arriving at Xiuyu, where he constantly let out the lion’s roar.

He was playfully nicknamed "Master Lion. Retiring to Guiyun Hermitage, he recited the Lotus Sūtra day and night. He composed a poem saying: "In old age, my mind remains alert and my spirit even clearer;

Deep in the night within my secluded chamber, I recite the Lotus Sūtra. My children and grandchildren will surely find me annoying when they wake up, So I strike the stone slab three or four times from time to time.
His mother’s tomb was before the mountain. Every morning, he would walk slowly and recite one complete volume of the sūtra.

Upon his return, he requested that those who recited [the scriptures] be given five hundred coins. When the case-study index was opened, he would count a few lines and depart with the money, which he distributed to those suffering from hunger and cold.
He was fond of singing the "Fisherman" (Yùfù) songs, often continuing until dawn. The monk Huítóu of Zhà and the scholar-official Ānqíshòu found his eccentricities to be charming.
There were madmen who used the pretext of preaching the Dharma to deceive the world, all of whom he thoroughly exposed; thus, he commanded Yú Xiùlǎo to open the hall for formal sermons.
The Commentary says: "Pushing over and turning back; kicking over and not relying. Before the seven fascicles of the Lotus Sūtra have been recited, the single cry of the Fisherman is first heard.
Having heard this, he ascends the seat and quotes a verse, saying: "Originally a descendant of one who fished on the Jī and the Xiāng rivers; east, west, south, and north, wherever I go.
The assembly acclaimed this as excellent. He then descended from the seat and said: "I contemplate the Dharma of the Dharma-King; the Dharma of the Dharma-King."
Thus it was. After seventy-two transmigrations, he was enshrined as a "Scattered Sage" (Sangseong) at Insa Shrine.

His secular surname was Yi, and his royal name was King Munjong Renxiao of Goryeo; he was the fourth son of the king. Having renounced worldly glory and taken the tonsure, there were no internal or external classics that he did not study.
He often lamented that, having been born in the eastern frontier, he had previously lacked knowledge of the fundamental tenets of the Buddha-dharma and sought [to learn them].

He traveled to the capital to seek out spiritual friends. At the beginning of the Yuanyou era, he submitted a memorial to Emperor Zhezong requesting that the teachings of the Xianshou school be transmitted back to his country for circulation.
Upon reaching Siming Prefecture, Mingzhi Li and Huizhao Lin served as his official escorts.

They visited the Yuyang Monastery to pay homage at the Śarīra Stūpa and requested Dajue Liaoyi to ascend the seat and proclaim the Dharma. By imperial decree, the two monastic districts were ordered to nominate a candidate capable of transmitting the Dharma.
As for this, Jueyan Cheng of Dongjing responded with sincerity. Cheng recommended Huiyin and Jingyuan of Qiantang to stand in his place;

by imperial decree, Yao Jie, a Chao-feng-lang, was appointed to escort them there to receive the Dharma. When the various monasteries of the Wu region welcomed and saw them off, they treated them as honored guests.

Upon meeting Tianzhu Cibian, they observed the etiquette of disciples, inquiring about the teachings and contemplations, and presented him with a "cloud-phoenix" *mò'nà* robe, a pure water jar, and other offerings.

Regarding the collection of scriptures and other items, Cibian presented this verse as a gift: "The Supreme Chant of the Ultimate Cream is most honored; The Lotus Flower is a wondrous metaphor for its merit.

In years past, the Fifth Patriarch personally attained wondrous enlightenment; Today, O King of Monks, you joyfully succeed to his lofty traces. The fragrance of the precepts flows forth from the golden incense burner;
The Dharma words are personally transmitted within the fly-whisk. In the days to come, wherever they are expounded in the land of海东 (Haidong), May the lamps of wisdom be arrayed."

The blazing light shines without end. Master Jiang (Zhiqi) shared a meal with him and also presented a quatrain: "Exquisite penetration reveals the emptiness within; A single realization penetrates all that is not penetrated.
Send word to Dingguang: do not beckon with your hand; The site of practice is flourishing as you settle in Liaodong.
Lingzhi Dazhi ascended the seat to propagate [the teachings] and requested that his written works be returned to the country for circulation. He then visited Foyin at Jinshan. Yuan.

Wuen sat down to receive the master’s ritual greeting. When Lord Yang asked for the reason, Wuen said, "Yitian is merely a monk from a foreign land; such is the custom for monks arriving at a monastic community.
Lord Yang said, "Be modest and conform somewhat to local customs. To seek to differ from other regions—how can that be following the teacher's mind?"
Yuan said, "Not so. To bend the Way to conform to worldly customs is already to lose one eye first; how can you show this to the Middle Kingdom?

He presented the Master with a *kāṣāya* robe and a set of scriptures, to which the Master replied with two verses: "From whom did you obtain this famous robe from beyond the seas? A prince who leaped over the city walls, a man of true stature.
Its brocade pattern was once exchanged for something of priceless value; It is surely fit to be worn upon the Vajra Seat. [The scriptures...]
The book-cases are spread with brocade and embroidery; the yellow scrolls, nestled in water, open at times. Yaoshan merely wishes to idly shield his eyes;
when has the True Eye ever been able to be shielded? Upon arriving in the capital, he was hosted by Attendant-in-Ordinary Fan and Director Su, and they reached the Prime Minister’s residence.

Huilin visited Yuanzhao, who likewise revealed the essential tenets of his school. The Master had entered the gateways of all the various sects; indeed, [Yuanzhao’s] critical evaluation would not have escaped him.
He presented a twenty-verse regulated poem in the "gu" style to Lord Yang, which was elegant, robust, fresh, and refined, capturing the diction of a poet of the *sao* tradition.

The Lord replied with a verse, saying: "Who could compare to the World-Benefiting Master, who has exhausted the subtle principles of the five schools? I am ashamed to accompany him. *Mi*... [text fragment].
The genius of Bian was not merely that of Zaochi; the two respected one another and were like brothers.

Xu Ba, who transmitted the meaning of the *Feishan Beizhuan*, had the merit of refuting [the errors of] Xian, stating in his preface: "How great is the disparity between the names and realities of ancient Chan and modern Chan!
What was called 'Chan' in antiquity referred to those who relied upon the teachings to practice meditation. What is called 'Chan' today refers to those who speak apart from the teachings."
He was a master of Chan. Those who discourse on Chan cling to its names while neglecting its reality; those who practice Chan follow its explanations to grasp its essential meaning.
To remedy the current malady of hypocrisy and artifice, and to restore the ancient, pure, and refined Way of the Sages—Master Zhu’s critical exegesis reaches this very pinnacle.
Recently, the Great Liao Emperor issued an edict to the relevant authorities, commanding the śramaṇa Quanzhu to [expound] the study of the principles of the teachings.

Xiao and others recompiled the catalog of scriptures. All those commonly known as the *Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch*, the *Baolin Zhuan*, and so forth, were burned and eliminated along with their spurious and false regulations.
They then re-edited the three-fascicle *Continued Catalog of the Zhenyuan Era*, in which these matters are recorded in detail.

There are those who, by observing the Buddha’s heart of entrustment and the Emperor’s resolve to propagate and protect [the Dharma], have noted that the Chan school texts currently practiced in China are largely permeated by heterodox elements. This is why the masters of Silla doubted that there were any worthy ones in the Middle Kingdom;
yet upon seeing the *Feishan gaoyi* (The High Discourse of Mount Fei), they finally realized that there are indeed Bodhisattvas who protect the Dharma. Yesterday, I received the Imperial decree.
He carved [the text] upon green stone slabs, yet fearing that its circulation might not be widespread, he engraved it upon wooden printing blocks. Alas!

Will those who preside over the Dharma in the final age after a hundred generations not surely rely upon the power of Master Zhu? After returning to his own country, their correspondence never ceased, and he dispatched envoys to present offerings.

When first departing from that land, the memorial he presented to the King in his farewell address read: "I do not consider the difficulties of practicing in this present age; I have merely ventured to admire the ancients..."
People’s profound faith makes them thirst for the morning news of enlightenment and find it sweet to die that very evening; they value an inch of time more than a foot-long jade disk.

Daring to emulate the legacy of Xuanzang and yearning for the lofty footsteps of Yixiang (who sought the Dharma in Central India and transmitted the Huayan school of the Nature-Doctrine to China), I have resolved to cross the vast ocean, fearing only that I might miss the opportune moment.
Thus, seeking the sublime realms of the West shall encompass ultimate insight, while hearing of the turning [of the Wheel] in the East...

The Wheel of Dharma: To propagate the benefits of perfect penetration for eternal circulation throughout the ages, and to provide support for awakening and understanding within the minds of all beings.
When traveling to Mount Fulong to visit Zhiyi, he personally composed a vow at the pagoda, pledging to transmit the teachings and contemplation to the Eastern Land.
How magnificent was his resolve! Gaian remarked: "This is an appended commentary on Dongpo’s discourse on the state of Goryeo."
Huang said: "Regarding the inquiry about the causes for attaining wisdom: the presiding monk Jingyuan was originally an ordinary man.
It was solely because of his frequent socializing with merchants that they engaged in reckless talk while in the kingdom of Goryeo, which led Yiian to travel from afar to study under him.
Consequently, our monastery has received generous offerings, yet the local government offices in Huai and Zhejiang have suffered widespread disturbances. In private, I say of Yiian:"
The pursuit of the Dharma is no trivial matter. The monk Jingyuan also rendered service to the gates of the teachings. Dongpo’s discourse on affairs of state was merely a single instance of speech.

Yongdao (whose protection of the Dharma led to his being honored by the court and the restoration of the monastic order) was of the Mao family of Shunchang in the Western Capital; in his youth, he received instruction from An Lohan of Chengtian Temple.
Gong received full ordination in the third year of the Chongning era. He traveled to the capital, where he studied the two treatises on *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* and the *Śata-dharma-śāstra*.
He mastered them through a single reading and committed them to memory. Once, while entering a village, a pharmacist and a Daoist practitioner addressed him with malicious words;

he countered them with grand rhetoric, struck their cheeks, and departed. Those who discerned his character remarked that he would surely become a pillar of the Dharma gate. In the third year of the Zhenghe era, he was granted purple robes.
The Master presided over Chongxian Xiangji Chan Monastery on Left Street. In the fifth year [of the Zhenghe era], he was granted the title Baojue.

During the reign of Lin Lingsu, whose illusory arts deceived the sovereign, the first month of the first year of the Xuande era saw an imperial edict ordering all monasteries throughout the realm to reform their Buddhist teachings; the temples were converted into Shenxiao establishments.
The Buddha is the Golden Immortal; the Bodhisattva is the Great Being; the Sangha is titled the Virtuous One. They wear caps beneath their robes and hold wooden tablets.
The various mountains announce to the assembly: "We temporarily withdraw the field-robe from our shoulders and briefly roll up the conch-like topknots at our crowns.
Although we remain the same people as of old, we joyfully add these new titles to our names. In the eighth month of the third year, a great flood occurred in the capital city.
The aquatic creatures emerged from their dwellings in the marketplace. Ling Su’s methods for subduing the waters proved ineffective, causing the officials and citizens to grow increasingly fearful.

The Great Being Saṃgha appeared within the palace and was invited to perform rites for the suppression of the waters. The Great Being shook his monk’s staff and ascended the city wall, chanting secret mantras;

the force of the waters suddenly abated until they were completely exhausted. Ling Su’s spirit was disheartened, and he further provoked the Crown Prince by disparaging him, leading to his banishment back to Wén.
He died in Daozhou. He was restored to his original Buddhist name, Shi. The various monasteries expressed their gratitude, saying:

"We return the wooden tally to Minister Pei; we withdraw the crown-pin from Great Master Fu. We shall once again perfect the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of a *arhat*, and don once more the field-robe of hemp cloth.
When the imperial decree first went forth, who did not bow and obey? Only the Master resisted the edict; he was branded and exiled to Daozhou. The guards said:
"Traversing ten thousand li, it would be appropriate to consume meat and wine to bolster one's physical strength and vigor. The Master said, "My sins are great and my retribution heavy;

that Your Majesty’s grace has been so lenient as to allow me to prolong these final gasps of life is already a great fortune. To perish from the miasma of this land would likewise be the decree of Heaven. How could I violate the precepts?

I am guarded by those who protect me even more than I can; the journey is about to begin. That night, the Master dreamed that a Buddha statue carried a *bimba* fruit into the city. His subordinate also dreamed of...

The following morning, the Master arrived. The Master said, "This monk must be an extraordinary person. Before long, many among the soldiers and civilians suffered from cold-related illnesses and sought his help.
The Master received the *vidyā-mantra* and ritual manuals of the Tripitaka Master Mingyin Miaoshan Pujie from India;
his spiritual responses were like echoes. He also transmitted the Sudden and Perfect Precepts (*yuantun jiejfa*) to Great Master Yuanzhao. Thus, those who were ill...

Those who drank the consecrated water or had their heads rubbed by him were invariably cured and restored to peace. As those seeking his aid became numerous, he established a pond within the temple grounds to accommodate them.
There was a ruined monastery in the prefecture which he intended to rebuild; it was completed in several months. In the second year, he was transferred to a neighboring prefecture.
While passing through Xiangtan, Hong Juefan presented him with a poem that said: "Master Dao’s courage exceeds his physical frame; He dares to write a memorial against the dragon’s scales.
Willingly baring his shoulders to bear the Buddha-Dharma, He gladly extends his neck to receive the axe. After three years of exile, his heart remains without shame;
Returning ten thousand *li* away, his countenance shows no decay. In days to come, he shall be one who upholds the discipline Of the teachings of our school. *Nian* (near).

Hearing that he was hurrying to court in his ceremonial shoes and tablets, in the sixth month of the seventh year [of the Shaoxing era], he returned to the monastic life and resided at the Zhaoxian Chan Monastery in Zhaokeng.
He was granted the administrative quarters of the Śākyamuni Cloister at Xiansheng Temple in the Right Ward to manage concurrently.

At the beginning of the Jianyan era, when General Zong Ze was the Regional Commander-in-Chief (Liushi), he requested him to preside over Tianqing Temple in the Left Ward; meanwhile, Pu, a Xiaojiao Lang, served as the Commissioner for Recruitment and Debate for the Liushi.

General Manager and Military Counselor to the Imperial Commissioner. He performed *kaji* (empowerment) for the state to protect and assist the military forces while residing between the Huai and Ying rivers.
He exhorted the local elites to distribute grain to aid the army; before long, they returned laden with supplies, and the three armies raised shouts of joy.

When the imperial carriage toured the south, he was repeatedly summoned to the Hall of State to participate in deliberations on matters of great importance for the military and the nation. He requested to be invested with the crown and granted command of the troops to restore [the realm].
He returned to his former domain. He declined the honors with a poem, saying: "In years past, for the sake of the Dharma, I suffered the brand of the penal mark.

By divine decree, I changed my robes to assist the ranks of armored soldiers. In shackles and fetters through the barbarian wilderness for half a decade, I traversed a thousand stages across waters and lands.

Ice and frost could not alter the integrity of pine and bamboo; Furnaces and coals could not shift the resolve of iron and stone. I wish to become a disciple of Gautama; I cannot endure these official hairpins and tablets."

Upon his return to the capital, he was granted the honorary title "Chuantong Fajie" (Enlightened Penetration and Dharma Aid). (In accordance with the imperial regulations of the Zongzong era, this six-character title was added to the rank of Shi Honglu Xiangchong, corresponding to the official grade.

In the fourth year, the Military Commissioner of Ming requested that he reside at Baolin Monastery. During a summer drought, he was commissioned by imperial decree to pray for rain at Yuantong Monastery in Yue.
As expected, he responded with a torrential flow [of eloquence]. When he was granted an audience at the Xiangshou Palace, the Emperor said, "The late Emperor was deluded by demonic arts;

he stripped you of your clerical robes and appearance. Would it be acceptable for Your Majesty and I to remove his branding and tattooing? The Master replied, "Though I am grateful for Your Majesty's grace, I cannot bear to destroy or remove the late Emperor's calligraphic legacy.
The Emperor remarked, "This monk remains stubborn to the end. He was subsequently invited to reside at Donglin Monastery in Jiangzhou.

Regarding the combined affairs of Pingxinglong Chan Temple and Guangfu Monastery: the Master once read the *Sengshi lüe* (Abridged History of the Buddhist Clergy of the Great Song), which states that whenever there was a court assembly, the clergy always preceded the Daoists.

Furthermore, when they stood side-by-side in the palace courtyard, the clergy were on the east and the Daoists on the west; however, when encountering them alone at the suburban sacrifices, the Daoists were on the left and the clergy on the right.
This was originally based on the regulations of the imperial ancestors. Recently, following the Chongguan era, because of the Daoists...
Having unwarrantedly received official rank, Wang Zixi, Lin Lingsu, and their ilk threw the imperial administration into disorder.

Consequently, they established precedents to abruptly exclude the monastic order from its ranks and took advantage of this momentum to destroy the long-standing institutions of our ancestors. Since the Jingkang and Jianyan eras, the official titles of Daoists have already been rescinded;
as for their positions within the court hierarchy, they ought to be restored to their former status, and thus [the monks] shall once again stand alongside the Daoists.
Liu Ruojian went to the imperial court to present his defense. He submitted a short petition requesting that an official decree be issued to specifically grant a correction.

An imperial edict was received, ordering that the matter be handled according to the revised regulations, permitting monks and Daoists to assemble so that their respective ranks and roles could be properly established;

all of this was due to the Master’s efforts. In the fifth year, he was granted an audience at the inner palace to pray for rain. He established the ritual altar and ascended the seat, chanting incantations.
He placed fresh carp in four golden vases, sprinkled water while reciting secret mantras, and dispatched four swift-footed messengers to release them into the rivers and ponds.
Before the messengers had even returned, the rain had already fallen in profusion. The Emperor specially bestowed upon him a golden bowl.

The Master constantly maintained that the Imperial Preceptor of Xiangguosi Temple preserved the three imperial compositions (by Taizhen and Renzong) praising the Vinaya Master Daoxuan of the Tang, which had been secretly transmitted to him by a celestial deity from Śākyamuni Buddha.
The "Numinous Tooth" was kept as a personal object of veneration. Whenever anyone sought relics, he would pray with devotion and grant them.

The Master wished to construct a pavilion and, at Xiangfu Temple in his residence, enshrined three thousand transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇakāya-buddha*) there. He opened a grand lecture hall and traveled to propagate the teachings in Bird Town (*Niao-zhen*).

A monk from Pujing Temple prostrated at his feet and requested [the tooth]; the Master placed it within a golden basin and brought it out for the monk to pray before. The monastics and laypeople of the entire town acclaimed this.
The ritual was performed for three days, yet there was no manifest sign of response. He rebuked his disciples and redoubled their diligence in the three karmas.

At midnight, there was a resonant sound. The Master said, "The Tathāgata has appeared. Looking, he saw eight grains [of light]. He extinguished the candles, and the bottom of the basin was seen to emit a radiance reaching toward the heavens;
it subsided after a short while. He enshrined them in a wooden stupa. To this day, on the seventh day of the third month, the Ritual Stupa Assembly is held. (Ge Dazhi [Shengzhong])

The preface to the *Shu* (Commentary) recounts the origins of the undertaking, stating: "Only here in Zhendan do we uniquely treasure the sacred tooth relic. Formerly, while it was in the capital, it received the offerings of humans and devas;
now it remains in Wuhui, having survived amidst the remnants of war and fire. Moreover, ten thousand households have gathered for the third day of the Dharma assembly.
Thus, leading my fellow practitioners, I have reissued this *Sengshi* (History of the Sangha), briefly prefacing it with this introduction. This is recorded separately.

He established a Chan residence and transmitted two methods of Chan contemplation. His commentary states: "When rites, music, and military expeditions proceed from the Son of Heaven, the Way of the King flourishes.
When the monastic regulations of Buddhist temples follow the precepts of the Tathāgata, the True Dharma abides.

One who does not obey the King’s commands is called a rebellious subject; one who does not follow his father’s footsteps is called a wayward son. How could anyone dare not to conform to the Buddha’s teachings?"
These are called the followers of Māra and the heterodox. Thus, the Dharma of the Buddhas of the three periods of time has no divergent teachings;

the various sages of the ten directions have received and studied it through identical texts. Indeed, the scriptures of Śākyamuni are the root, while the words of Dharmatrāta are the branches. To turn one’s back on the root and pursue the branches is truly lamentable.

I, a fool, have long practiced among the multitude, exerting my strength upon the palm-leaf manuscripts (*palm-leaf*); I have extensively inquired about the *Nidāna* (the "coming from the West") and have further examined [the texts].

A Record of Seeking the Dharma Throughout Antiquity and the Present: The practitioners of dhyāna in India all receive the teachings of the Buddha-vehicle; thus, those who enter the ranks of the sages do so without ceasing.
This is because they rely on the Dharma and not on persons, and they strive for reality in their practice. The words of the Buddha and the true Dharma will surely not mislead future students.
I venture to address my fellow practitioners who study the Buddha and cultivate dhyāna: may you swiftly leave the ford of suffering and ascend high to the other shore.
Do not deceive others with clever speech, nor delude yourself. The *Lingfu jing* (Scripture on the Spirit Mansion) says: "If you wish to attain the Way, you must rely upon the Buddha’s words.
It is impossible for one to attain it by contravening them. How could this be refuted?
On the twenty-first day of the seventh month in the seventeenth year, he told his disciples: "The upholding of the Dharma depends further upon all of you; I shall now depart. He sat upright and...
Transformation. The verse says: "The myriad dharmas are fundamentally empty; the one truth is devoid of delusion. It is like the vast void, originally identical to the echo in a valley.
After the cremation, his remains were enshrined in a stupa at Jiulisuong.

Zi Guang was a native of Lanxi. He studied the teachings of the Tiantai school and traveled south to seek instruction from Dahui Zonggao. While residing in Putian and Fucheng, he composed the *Yituo Mingshi Shengdi Lun* (Treatise on Relying upon Enlightened Masters and Auspicious Sites) in three fascicles.
