Possessing supernatural insight and understanding, at the age of twenty-nine in the second year of the Zhenguan era, he submitted a memorial requesting to travel to Western India. The Emperor granted his request.
Taking up his staff, he set out and reached Mount Xiliang, where the accumulated snow had not yet melted; there were venomous dragons and flying sands that blocked the path.

He ascended and descended the precipitous heights, looking back to see that they were all thousands of *zhang* high. In dangerous places, he crossed by means of ladders seven times, using ropes as bridges with each step.
Then he crossed a body of water eighty paces wide. Next, he ascended the Snowy Mountains (Himālaya), which rose sheer for a thousand fathoms. At every step there were pairs of notches in the cliff;
holding onto four such notches, he placed his hands and feet alternately into the crevices in the rock and passed over like a monkey with its arms.
On the third day, they finally reached level ground—a place not even visited by Zhang Qian or Gan Yanshou.

Crossing the River of Sand, they encountered various malevolent spirits of strange forms and diverse species, which swarmed around them before and behind. With single-minded devotion, they recited the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the *Prajñāpāramitā-hṛdaya Sūtra*.
Furthermore, traveling northwest for three hundred li, they crossed a desert expanse and arrived at the northern corner of Mount Ling, on the edge of the [Xi] Ridge.
The precipices are steep and reach their utmost height. Since the beginning of time, ice and snow have accumulated there to form glaciers that do not melt in spring or summer;

they are vast and expansive, merging with the clouds until their boundaries cannot be seen. When the peaks of these glaciers collapse and fall, some lie across the sides of the road, reaching heights of a hundred feet or widths of several *zhang*.
The paths are rugged and uneven, making the ascent arduous and perilous; as wind and snow fly together, one must tread upon them.
Though he wore heavy furs, he could not avoid shivering with cold; when he wished to sleep or eat, there was no dry place to do so. He cooked his meals on a precipice and slept upon the ice.
After seven days, he emerged from the mountains, and fourteen of his companions had perished from cold and hunger. Furthermore, they traveled three hundred li through the mountains.
One enters the Iron Gate Peak (*Tiéménfēng*). Its cliffs are narrow and precipitous, and there is much iron ore; these are used for the door panels, which are further plated with iron.
Iron bells are cast and hung in great numbers above them. This is the frontier pass of the Turks.

Having traversed one hundred and thirty kingdoms in their entirety—all lands converted by our Buddha, including the Forest of Nirvāṇa’s Firmity (*nièhuán jiāngù zhī lín*) and the Bodhi Tree where Māra was subdued at Kāla...
They paid homage to the sublime stūpas and Mount Nāgārjuna, beholding many miraculous wonders.

They obtained precious images, śarīra relics, and seventy-three works totaling one thousand three hundred and thirty fascicles of the *palm-leaf* (pattra) scriptures—namely, all that was spoken by the Tathāgata throughout his entire life:
the teachings of the Vaipulya from Vulture Peak, the *ardha-akṣara* texts from the Deer Park, and [the works of] Aśvaghoṣa and Nāgārjuna.
He collected and researched the works composed by Asaṅga and Vasubandhu, as well as the doctrines of the eighteen heterodox schools and the principles of the five distinct Nikāyas.

He mastered their essential meanings and obtained their texts; even regarding the sounds of the seven cases and eight inflections, or the phrases of the three genders and six types of derivation, there was nothing whose subtleties he did not exhaust or whose wonders he did not fully comprehend. Consequently, the King of the Mauryas bestowed upon him a blue elephant.
White horses were provided to assist with the transport. On the twenty-fourth day of the first month of the nineteenth year, he arrived at the capital.

The Palace Commissioner Fang Xuanling prepared banners, streamers, martial music, and the ceremonial regalia of the Buddhist order. With several hundred thousand monastics and laypeople, the Master rode in a precious palanquin as if descending from Tuṣita Heaven.
He was quartered at Hongfu Monastery. The following day, he had an audience with the Emperor at the Yiluan Hall, where the Emperor personally comforted and honored him for his diligent service.

Upon his arrival, all necessary provisions for the translation bureau were ordered to be supplied by the Office of the Imperial Guard. He first advanced the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and marveled at it, saying:

"In surveying the heavens and gazing upon the sea, nothing can surpass its height and depth. Although I have been occupied with military and state affairs and have not yet had the leisure to examine it in detail, I now know that its fundamental source is profound and vast.
Looking back at the nine schools of thought, they appear like small marshes and ponds compared to the great ocean. By imperial decree, he was ordered to produce an abridgment of the translated text.

Each volume of the sutras and treatises consisted of nine sections, which were bestowed upon the governors-general of the nine circuits to be circulated and disseminated throughout the land, in the hope that all within the realm might receive instruction in what had not yet been heard.
An imperial decree was issued to establish the Hongfa (Great Dharma) Court separately to the west of Ziwai Hall, where the Master was invited to reside.

He was permitted to select seven men of renowned virtue to accompany him; in addition to discussing the Way with the Emperor, he was authorized to engage in translation as he saw fit. Furthermore, an imperial decree was issued regarding foreign regions...

He said: "My primary concern is to ensure accuracy in correspondence [with the original]. If it were not for such a person, who could discuss the teachings of sound? Therefore, whenever those of the Middle Kingdom have doubts, they all rely upon me;
I then translate my Chinese words according to the Western Indic [language], so that those who read it there may revere China.

Furthermore, I was commanded to translate the *Laozi* into Indic to transmit it to the Western Regions. The Master replied: "The ultimate goals of the two teachings of Buddha and Lao are vastly different."

"What use is it to employ the Buddha’s words to explain the principles of Laozi? Moreover, as a humble person from a foreign land, hearing this would bring disgrace upon the Great State. Thus, he desisted.

In the third year of the Yonghui era, he submitted a memorial requesting to build a stupa at Cien Monastery to enshrine the Sanskrit manuscripts of the sūtras and śāstras that he had obtained, as well as the two Emperors’ "Prefaces to the Holy Teachings" (Śāsanānuśamsā).
The Emperor granted permission and further ordered that the clothing and belongings of deceased persons from the seven palaces be collected to assist with the expenses.

In the first year of the Xianqing era, a prince was born (the future Emperor Zhongzong). A divine light filled the chamber, standing tall and illuminating the heavens. He was granted the title "Prince of Buddha-Light" (Foguang Wang).

After one month had passed, the Prince submitted a memorial requesting ordination to ensure the flourishing of the Triple Gem; an imperial decree granted his request. His hair was shorn and he was conferred the precepts of refuge.

The Emperor further presented him with the Heart Sūtra inscribed in golden characters, along with Dharma robes and a begging bowl. In the second year, when the Emperor visited Luoyang, he issued an edict for the Prince to accompany the imperial entourage.
He then announced his intention to reinter his parents in Chenliu, whereupon an imperial edict was issued providing the necessary funeral equipment.

In the fourth year, he established the Yuhua Palace as a monastery to honor the late Emperor; by imperial decree, he resided there and translated the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. After four years, the work was completed in six hundred fascicles.
On the ninth day of the first month of the first year of the Linde era, he addressed the assembly, saying: "All conditioned phenomena must inevitably return to extinction."
Extinction. How could a body, like a bubble or an illusion, remain for long? He caused those nearby to recite: "Namo Maitreya Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha.

May all sentient beings swiftly behold your compassionate countenance. On the fourth day of the second month, he lay on his right side with his feet stacked, supporting his head with his hand, remaining steadfastly motionless.
When the assembly asked, "Will you certainly be reborn before Maitreya? he replied, "I shall certainly be reborn," and—
He passed away. His lifespan was sixty-four years. The Emperor mourned him with great grief and suspended court for five days. He provided funds for the funeral expenses.

Upon the burial, five edicts were issued in praise and consolation. On the fourteenth day of the fourth month, following Buddhist custom, he was interred east of the San River in a silver inner coffin within a golden outer coffin.
At first, when he was lying ill, Master Mingzang questioned him. [The Master] saw two tall figures together supporting a white lotus before him and saying:
"Since beginningless time, you have harmed sentient beings and committed various evil deeds; because of this minor illness, they shall all be extinguished."

"You should give rise to joy and celebration. The Master looked toward the great assembly, who joined their palms and listened. "Is it not through the power of translating the *Prajñāpāramitā* that heavy offenses are transformed so they are received as light?
When he first traveled to India, he stroked a pine tree by the path with his hand and said, "As I go west to seek the Dharma, may your branches grow toward the west;
when I return, they shall turn east, so that my disciples may know in advance. After he departed, the branches indeed pointed westward.

One day he suddenly headed east. His disciples said, "The Master is returning. They called it the "Buddha-touching Pine. Upon reaching that land, he encountered the school of Nāgārjuna and wished to study under him.
The master of that school commanded him to take medicine and seek immortality before he could exhaustively master their fundamental tenets.

Reflecting that he had originally sought the sūtras but failed to master the arts of the immortals, and thus felt he had betrayed his former vow, he subsequently studied the Dharma-lakṣaṇa under Śīlabhadra and transmitted the principles of Vijñaptimātratā.
Furthermore, he bestowed the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* upon Kuiji, transmitting the principles of the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* and also bestowing the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* upon his disciple Guang.

Although the *Ratnagotravibhāga-mahāyānottaratantra-śāstra* (Qixin lun) was originally composed by Aśvaghoṣa, it had not been seen there before; consequently, he translated it into Chinese during the Tang dynasty.
He served as a *brahman* and propagated [the teachings] throughout the Five Indias.

His secular name was Daohong. He was the younger nephew of Weizhi Gong; his father was General of the Imperial Guard (Jinwu Wei Jiangjun), and his mother was Lady Pei, who conceived him after dreaming of swallowing the moon.
At six years of age, his intelligence surpassed that of others; he was of dignified and noble appearance, with clear and elegant features. He stood eight *chi* tall.
He was six feet tall. His vital energy surpassed that of ten thousand men. He had a jade pillow upon his neck, and the lines on his ten fingers were coiled and folded like seals.

When he encountered [Hui]yuan at the age of three, [the Master] said: "Truly the seed of a general. If by fortunate coincidence we meet again and you are ordained as my disciple, then my Dharma will have a place to rest."
As he was contemplating returning to India, Xingburen said, "Master, simply return east; your disciple shall be born.
Since this prophecy coincided with the hidden signs, he presented it to Sengzong. Sengzong said, "That kind of person is coarse and violent; how could they receive your teachings?

Paramārtha replied, "It is precisely because of your own capacity that such a person would not have been born had it not been for you, nor would I have recognized him had it not been for me. Sengzong agreed, yet the Master had not yet accepted the child.

Ming spoke in a stern voice, saying, "Only if you can observe three matters may it be granted. These were: not severing the mind of desire, abstaining from meat and blood, and not eating after midday.

[The Master], mindful that he might be lured by the hook of desire, feigned compliance. At the age of seventeen, he was commanded to shave his head and reside at Guangfu Temple. At twenty-five, his great virtues flourished; the three branches of his learning ran both lengthwise and crosswise.

He established the *Lipang* (Chapter on the Mandate) to expound upon the principles of affirmation and refutation, such that none before him could compare to him. He was devoted to his studies and received the full precepts.

Inheriting the core tenets of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratā-siddhi* as transmitted by Śīlabhadra, he composed several hundred treatises—whether as independent works or commentaries—and was thus known at the time as the "Master of the Hundred Treatises.
He traveled to various regions to propagate the teachings, benefiting many followers.

While traveling east to Boling, he was invited to lecture on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, for which he composed the *Xuánzàn Dàshù* (Great Commentary on the Profound Meaning) in ten fascicles. On the tenth day of the eleventh month of the first year of the Yongchun era...

Third: He passed away at the Ci'en Translation Institute at the age of fifty-one. The Emperor composed a eulogy for his portrait and issued an imperial decree that his likeness be depicted and enshrined in monasteries throughout all circuits.
He was interred in the cemetery of the Tripitaka Master. He once commissioned a statue of Maitreya, saying:

"Facing this image, I shall recite the Bodhisattva Precepts and pray to be reborn in the Inner Court. He also commissioned a statue of Mañjuśrī made of jade and transcribed the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* in gold ink; both [were completed].
He attained the state of responding to conditions. Gaian said: "Asanga frequently ascended to Tuṣita to consult Maitreya regarding the fundamental tenets of Vijñaptimātratā;

his younger brother, Vasubandhu, was enlightened by his guidance. Deeply repenting for having composed treatises on the Small Vehicle, he subsequently authored works to propagate and praise the Mahāyāna."
From generation to generation, sages and worthies have succeeded one another. Reaching the time of the Great Dharma-Treasury, the Master Śīlabhadra was one hundred and three years old;

having been entrusted by the Great Being Mañjuśrī, he endured death to await the arrival of the Tripiṭaka Master. When the Tripiṭaka Master arrived there, he transmitted the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* in their entirety to him.
The Master then synthesized previous teachings and extensively composed commentaries and treatises, following the three periods of the Dharma as established by Śīlabhadra.

Regarding the classification of teachings (*panjiao*): first, existence; second, emptiness; third, non-emptiness. It was not through the brilliance of "existence" that he illuminated his era, but by means of [the doctrine of] names that he established his school.
These are known as the Five Patriarchs of Ci'en: Maitreya, Asaṅga, Śīlabhadra, Xuanzang, and our Master [Kuiji].

Nevertheless, in his commentaries and exegeses on the sutras, he extensively heard and practiced the establishment of conduct, the subsuming of dharmas into the mind, and the formation of contemplation; in these explanations, he exclusively employed the *Vijñaptimātratā* treatises to establish [his system].

The passage concerning the extinction of the seeds of nature (*prakṛti*) is interpreted as being consistent with the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. This, however, is merely to cite provisional scriptures (*neyārtha*) to substantiate the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*);

such an error is indeed grave. Nevertheless, his discussions regarding the breadth and narrowness of the eight consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) in relation to their objects, as well as the transformation of consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), the integration of wisdom into the bodies [of the Buddha], and the doctrines of the creation of karma and the reception of retribution, have achieved considerable merit.
Regarding the records concerning the Vinaya school, who can emerge without passing through the door?

Who does not follow this path? How much more so when the eminent Great Wisdom (Dazhi) serves as the chronicler for that record—having personally witnessed the divine awakening of Guangci (Guangci Shenwu) and being thoroughly versed in the Tiantai lineage—is he not surely worthy of esteem? One must therefore examine and categorize these matters accordingly.
Differences in perspective arise; who can avoid occasional discrepancies in the *Jiangmu* (Outline and Details)?

Yet, if one discards these myriad variations to return to the single principle, how could those with aspirations for the tradition of the teachings remain aloof from the foremost of the Three Studies? Thus, I have composed this *Record of the Vinaya School*.
Daoxuan’s courtesy name was Fabian. He was of the Qian clan from Jingzhao. His mother, Yao, became pregnant after dreaming that a moon pierced her womb.

She further dreamed of a Buddhist monk who said to her, "The one you carry is the Vinaya Master Sengyou of the Liang dynasty. He remained in the womb for twelve full months. At nine years of age, he had read through all manner of books;
at twelve, he was proficient in calligraphy and literature; and at fifteen, he took Dayan Yin as his teacher. At sixteen—

He focused his mindfulness on the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and mastered it within two weeks. He further recited other sūtras and simultaneously understood their meanings. At seventeen, he shaved his head; at twenty, he received full ordination under his preceptor.
His three robes were made solely of coarse cloth, and he maintained the practices of constant sitting and eating only once a day without change from beginning to end.

When walking, he always took short steps, leaving fleas and lice to roam as they pleased. In the fourth year of the Wude era, he again followed his preceptor to study the Vinaya; nevertheless, he was particularly fond of dhyāna meditation.

Delighting in mountains and waters, he intended to live in seclusion and practice meditative concentration. Huīyǐn said, "Only when the precepts are pure and concentration is clear does wisdom have a foundation.

You have only recently begun to listen and are not yet proficient in observing what is transgressed or maintained. [Huìyuǎn] replied, "I shall simply focus on listening; you yourself may take charge of the monastic affairs for me.
They went back and forth three times together, listening to the Vinaya-piṭaka forty times before finally reviewing the texts. In the seventh year, he moved his residence to Zhūzhù on Mount Zhōngnán.

Mālanya compiled the *Xingzhisao* (Abridged Commentary on Practice) in three fascicles. In the fourth year of the Zhenguan era, he practiced the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi* at the Qingguan Vihāra for ninety days.
A dragon transformed into human form and, accompanied by its retinue, came to pay homage and listen to the Dharma.

A novice monk felt lustful and cast a lingering glance at the dragon’s female consort, who intended to kill him. Suddenly, she recalled her teacher’s instructions, immediately ceased her evil intent, and withdrew her venom.
Tujing said, "Do not drink this water. When the Master examined it, the water was surging and boiling; he immediately ordered it to be sealed off.
Furthermore, at Yunji Temple, he practiced this samādhi for twenty assemblies. He served as a celestial youth attendant for Yinqinbu for nineteen years.

Together with Master Xuanzang at Hongfu Monastery, he translated scriptures, serving as the scribe and editor, and was ranked as the most excellent among them. In the first year of the Yonghui era, he resided at Zhu...
Má Láo Fā received from Vaiśravaṇa Deva-rāja a prescription for restoring the heart. He said:

"In this age of the Semblance Dharma (xiàngmò), wicked bhikṣus merely establish monasteries but do not cultivate meditation or wisdom, nor do they engage in recitation; moreover, they do not even know how to read or write.

Even among those who do know, there is perhaps one or two in a thousand. He further stated: "The sacred sites of this land and the holy traces of the Western Heaven are calculated to number three thousand."
There are over eight hundred entries, recorded as they arose in response to inquiries, forming the *Gantong Zhuan* (Biographies of Miraculous Responses).

During his summer retreat, he achieved such merit that *zhicao* (mushrooms) grew in the courtyard and white springs gushed forth from the earth where he dwelt in seclusion. Sometimes, when he took up his brush to continue the biographies, eminent scholars were moved to adopt his teachings;

at other times, laypeople erected altars and mounds, while foreign monks offered their praise. Occasionally, miraculous flowers and exotic fruits arrived with swift dispatch, or non-human beings presented him with ambrosia.

(Mingxiang’s Biography): In the second spring of the Qiandeng era, a celestial being informed the Master that his karmic conditions were nearing their end and that he would be reborn in the inner palace of Maitreya.

He subsequently established an unrestricted great assembly (*anāvaraṇa-mahāpariṣad*). On the third day of the tenth month, he addressed his disciples, saying: "My breath is failing and my strength is exhausted."
He was on the verge of passing away. Monastics and laypeople beheld empty banners, extraordinary flowers, and celestial music resounding in unison.
They entreated the Master to return to the Tuṣita Heaven, to the inner courtyard of Maitreya. He was seventy-two years old and had fifty-two years of ordination.

After his cremation, his relics were divided into three portions and enshrined in stupas. The inscription for the portrait hall reads: "A eminent monk of the Liang dynasty, a supreme virtue of the Tang; though of different eras..."
Fellow practitioner, his ritual deportment was never erring; he commissioned portraits and statues for monasteries throughout the empire to serve as models.
Initially, while performing circumambulation at night in Ximing Monastery, his feet—though with cracked heels—were protected by a supernatural being, allowing him to walk upon the void without harm.
Looking closely, he was a young boy. The Master questioned him, and he replied, "I am Nanda, the prince of King Vaiśravaṇa.

My father the King has commanded me to serve and protect you, O Master. The Master said, "I am practicing the Way; there is no need for the Prince to trouble himself. Your majesty possesses sovereign power;
if there are those in India performing Buddhist services, I pray that you bring them here. The Prince said, "I have a Buddha..."

He had possessed his ivory and jeweled palms for a long time; yet he was willing to sacrifice even his head and eyes—how could he not offer these? The Master treasured them and made offerings with them.

At the beginning of the Longshuo era, he requested the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* from a spirit at Qingguan Temple. A dragon transformed into human form and came several times to listen in secret, seeking to receive the precepts of refuge.

While the Master was sleeping briefly in his room, a novice monk peeked inside and saw a red dragon that was extremely long; terrified, he informed the Master. The Master stopped him, telling him not to speak of it.
According to Liu Yuxi’s *Jiahua*, a Vinaya Master was foremost in upholding the precepts. Suddenly, thunderclaps resounded incessantly around his door.

The Master said, "I have upheld the Vinaya without transgression; if this is due to past karma, I do not know of it. He removed his three robes from outside the door, fearing that they might be possessed by a dragon or a water-sprite.
When the robes were brought out, the sound did not cease. Upon examining his right hand, he saw a black spot on his small fingernail, like a sesame seed. He tried—

He extended his finger; with a single tremor through the aperture, he lost the point. Emperor Muzong composed a eulogy for him, saying: "In successive generations there have been awakened beings who act as envoys of the Tathāgata.
Dragons and ghosts submit to them; celestial deities receive their service. Their fame flies to the Five Heavens; their words startle ten thousand li.

As the golden sun sinks in the west, the Buddha-sun rises in the east. I bow my head in refuge to the Master Zhaolü, the Patriarch. Emperor Yizong posthumously conferred upon him the title Chengzhao (Illuminating Clarity).
Li Yong composed the *Xingzhuang* (Biographical Account). The *Songzhuan* states: "The reputation of Vinaya Master Xuan for upholding the precepts shook the land of India;

the excellence of his compilations and revisions flowed throughout the world. Thus, when Tripiṭaka Master Vajrabodhi first arrived at court to have an audience, the Emperor asked, 'Having come from so far away, are you not weary?
In which quarter do you wish to rest? Vajrabodhi replied, 'I have heard that Vinaya Master Xuan of Ximing Monastery maintains and upholds [the Dharma] with great integrity.'"
First, he wished to go and rely [upon him], and the Emperor granted his request. He spread out cotton paper to catch the lice and wrapped them up before throwing them to the ground.
Wèi said, "This is the sound of striking sentient beings upon the earth. From this, one can clearly understand that all secret practices involve either restraint or prohibition.
(There was another person named Wèi during the Zhèngguān and Xiǎnqìng periods. It is also said: "Fǎlì of Yèzhōng and Huáisù of the Táng era—these two names, 'new' and 'old,' are renowned."
Each excels in its own beauty. The *Śāriputrābhidharma-śāstra* establishes the Sarvāstivāda; the *Prakaraṇapāda* presents both aspects of the substratum (*āśraya*).

The *Jñānaprasthāna* alone opens the school, its doctrine of "existence" (sarvam asti) standing peerless. The eminent master of Zhongnan, Great Master Chengzhao, whose spiritual resonance spanned three lifetimes, traveled a thousand li to meet him.

Standing at the juncture between the celestial and the human, he moved with ease within the midst of the fruits of realization. There was nothing he did not know, and he corrected errors with a guiding cord.
Zhòu Miù, who took it as his personal mission to protect and uphold the teachings of the Dharma, was truly a great figure of his generation.
Consequently, those engaged in religious practice throughout the realm have taken Mount Nanshan as their compass.

During my reign in the Daxiangfu era, the Indian śramaṇa Juechēng arrived at the capital and was housed in the Translation Court (Fanyuan). He was approximately forty years of age and had mastered over forty [scriptures].
The original text states that in the *Sūtra-śāstra*, it says: "Śrīghoṣa was born into the Kṣatriya caste in the ancient kingdom of Ku-lan.

When Minister Ding Jin asked what he had seen during his mission, Śrīghoṣa replied, "I wished to pay homage to the stupa of Vinaya Master Xuán. The Minister said, "There are many sages and worthies in this land; why focus solely on this one?
He replied, "The Vinaya Master’s reputation is preeminent throughout the Five Indias. Kai-an remarked, "As for the Nanshan school, it originated with Upāli."

Regarding the compilation of the Vinaya Piṭaka: since the time of the Cao Wei dynasty, the *Mahāsāṃghika-vinaya*, the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya*, and other vinaya texts were transmitted to this land, whereupon the precepts and regulations became somewhat complete.
During the early years of the Li Tang (Tang) dynasty, the Vinaya Master Chengzhao frequently experienced the descent and manifestation of celestial deities.

He deliberated upon matters such as the Vinaya and its related doctrines, eventually consulting various heterodox schools and taking the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* (Four-Part Vinaya) as his primary authority.
He composed commentaries and sub-commentaries to refute the positions of other schools and widely propagated their essential tenets.

However, relying on the traditional interpretations of the masters of the *Mahāsaṃghika-vinaya-saṃgraha* (Hongcheng lun), he asserted that the five meanings of the "emptiness school" (śūnyatā-yāna) partially accord with the Mahāyāna, and thus established the precept-substance (*śīla-tan-mūla*) of the Perfect School (*Yuanzong*). [He was subsequently challenged by a Japanese Dharma Master to establish a formal inquiry, which he was ultimately unable to answer.]

Furthermore, three types of repentance methods were established. Rather than relying on the *Vaipulya* (fangděng) teachings of Samantabhadra, they instead adopted the teachings of the *Vijñaptimātra* (weishí) school as the repentance for beginners in the Dharma-ending age.
Their emphasis on the "Contemplation of Dharmas" (*zhòngguān fǎ*) was judged by some to be of excessively high standing, which is not without its points of contention.
During the Huángyòu and Yuánhòu periods, the two masters Kān and Zhào emerged in succession; each composed commentaries and gathered disciples to lecture upon them. Later...

The masters Yinsheng and Zhao engaged in a debate regarding circumambulation to the left or right and the length of monastic robes; thus, these two matters were divided, resulting in the two schools of Huizheng and Zichi.
I have personally investigated this and found that it was established by the Patriarch Nanshan, as well as Master Gong of Dazhuangyan Monastery and Vinaya Master Zhenyi of Ximing Monastery:
they determined that circumambulating toward the east and turning toward the north constitutes circumambulation to the right (*pradakṣiṇā*). Furthermore—
In common worldly practice, entering through the eastern gate of a city and exiting through the western gate is cited as proof of sincerity.

Furthermore, based on the grass hut, the right side of the patriarch’s body, and the clockwise coiling of the hair of the virtuous and holy ones—these three meanings serve as evidence to demonstrate that [the direction] is to one’s own right.

As for the *Nirvāṇa* Sūtra, where the golden coffin is circumambulated to the right at Kuśinagara, this is said to be from the east toward the south; however, this is merely an error on the part of the translator.

Moreover, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that the sun, moon, stars, and the twenty-eight lunar mansions constantly revolve around Mount Sumeru from the east, through the south, and to the north;
this clearly fails to grasp the principle that the celestial bodies revolve counter-clockwise while the sun and moon revolve clockwise (as recorded in the *Jin Tianwen Zhi*).
Thus, the errors in his translations are even more severe than those in the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*’s *Paścimabhāga*. How can they be relied upon?
Indeed, that *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-uttaratantra* (Golden Dhāraṇī), as adjudicated by the Tripiṭaka masters, is likewise merely the text of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*. Cao’an further states:
